### Abstract

This thesis explores the deaths that occurred during the Klondike Gold Rush (KGR) of 1896-1900, and the sociocultural influences that led to these individuals being either remembered or forgotten through time. Analysis of archival sources and grave markers in cemeteries in the Yukon and Alaska provided a demographic dataset for those who died during the KGR. With the principles of secondary agency in mind, mortuary practices and commemorations of these dead are shown to have been influenced by five primary sociocultural categories: Indigeneity, relationships to family/friends, membership in social organizations, the mode of death (and environmental conditions at time of death), and “other factors.” This analysis demonstrates that race, gender, affluence, and community ties played a significant role in individual long-term commemoration. However, unique to the KGR, the influence that the environment and associated causes of death played on commemoration could supersede any privileges held by an individual in life. This combination of influences on the commemoration of individuals, and resulting biases in who has been remembered or forgotten, has contributed to the inaccurate and romanticized view of the KGR that permeates popular perception through heritage and tourism today.

Keywords: Klondike Gold Rush; Mortuary Studies; Identity; Agency; Social Memory; Yukon

[iv]

#### CHAPTER 1 Introduction & Background

The Klondike Gold Rush (KGR) was a fleeting event that profoundly shaped the country that we know as Canada. When I began this project in the spring of 2022, it sprang from a need to understand how it could possibly be that we have no reasonable estimate of how many people died in an event as significant as the Klondike Gold Rush. The popular perception is that 100,000 people had left for the Klondike and, at most, 50,000 had made it. Though I understood that not all of the remainder had died, it seemed inconceivable that so many people and their stories had been lost. There are dozens of books, movies, photographs and records associated with the event, and yet we do not know how many people had died. Perhaps I was battling with my own humanity and the inevitability that 125 years after my death, I, too, will likely be forgotten.

My initial goal in the earliest stages of this project was to compile a detailed database of those who had died during the Klondike Gold Rush; through that process, learning about these people, and seeing gaps in the data, I was left with a question. What factors associated with the Klondike Gold Rush influenced and, in some cases, continue to influence whether people are either forgotten or persistently remembered after their death?

What I have learned nearly three years on is that to be remembered after death is a privilege, and not a privilege that is afforded to all. At its core, this thesis explores how different social and cultural factors impacted the chances that an individual would have been remembered or forgotten in death during the Klondike Gold Rush, and how the Klondike’s natural environment also played an important role in the deaths, and commemoration, of those involved.

Death, and its commemoration during the Klondike Gold Rush, represents a complex interweaving of the social and cultural strands that make up individual identity, combined with the unalterable natural environment of the region. People brought with them the customs of both Victorian and frontier society, all influenced by the agency the dead hold over the living. Combined, all of these factors created a basis for both remembrance and forgetting that is profoundly individual.

[2]

BACKGROUND

What is a Gold Rush? Many events have been referred to as gold rushes throughout time, from the Brazilian Gold Rush, which began in the 1690s, to the South Kivu Gold Rush, which began in 2021. 2 Even so, time and individual perception can muddy what defines a gold rush. According to Stephen Tuffnell, a gold rush is characterized by "scale – the speed and pace – of the mining that takes place." 3 For Tufnell, the gold rushes of the second half of the 19th century, beginning with the California Gold Rush (1848-1855) and ending with the Klondike Gold Rush (1896-1900), are the most representative of this, "triggering huge transfers of population, which in turn resulted in the large-scale transfer of goods, capital, property and ideas." 4 Beyond scale and speed, Tufnell suggests that these events should be seen as true representations of gold rushes because the people involved defined and experienced them as such. Tuffnell sees gold mining after this period as much more based on capitalist ideals and, I would add to this, much more industrialized, as we can see with the mining companies that began operation in the Yukon in the early 20th century. 5 That said, the gold rush was not only a North American phenomenon in the 19th century; significant gold rushes took place in Australia, New Zealand, Africa, and Finland, among other locations. Many of these events were linked together through fervour and crowds of prospectors who participated in two or more rushes, travelling from one to the next. 6

A Brief History of the Klondike Gold Rush 
Gold was discovered by a Tagish man named Keish (Skookum Jim Mason), his brother-in 
law George Washington Carmack and their nephew Káa Goox (Dawson Charlie) on the 16th of 
August, 1896, at Rabbit Creek, now referred to as Bonanza Creek. 7 News travelled slowly, but 
prospectors had an honour code between them; as such, in 1896 and 1897, all of the most 
2 Helen Reid and Hereward Holland, “Congo Bans Mining in South Kivu Village after Gold Rush | Reuters,” ed. Peter 
Cooney, Reuters, March 4, 2021, https://www.reuters.com/article/congo-mining-idUSL5N2L27AI/. 
3 Stephen Tuffnell, “Everything You Wanted to Know About the Gold Rush,” BBC History Revealed: Your Essential 
Guide to the Gold Rush, December 2022, 28. 
4 Tuffnell, “Everything Gold Rush,” 28. 
5 Tuffnell, “Everything Gold Rush,” 28. 
6 Tuffnell, “Everything Gold Rush,” 28. 
7 Porsild, Gamblers and Dreamers, 3, 35; Douglas W. Allen, “Information Sharing During the Klondike Gold Rush,” The 
Journal of Economic History 67, no.4 (December 2007), 496; H.M. Cadell, “The Klondike and Yukon Goldfield in 1913.” 
Scottish Geographical Magazine 30, no.7 (1914), 345-346; Kenneth Coates, Best Left as Indians: Native-White 
Relations in the Yukon Territory, 1840-1973 (Montreal, Quebec: McGill-Queen’s University Press, 1993), 36. 

[3]

productive claims were staked by prospectors already in the area or nearby. 8 Given the proximity of Bonanza Creek to the Han summer fishing village of Nuklako, as stampeders began to arrive Nuklako was seen as the ideal settlement location. The Han were forced out by the North-West Mounted Police (NWMP) so that Dawson City could be established at the former site of Nuklako. The Han ended up being resettled by Chief Isaac of the Han and Anglican Bishop William Bompas just downriver at a village they named Moosehide. 9 In July of 1897, the Seattle Post-Intelligencer wrote of seventy thousand dollars’ worth of gold that had just arrived in port via the steamer Portland from the Klondike, triggering the stampede. 10 The largest migration of people into the Yukon occurred in the spring and summer of 1898, with an informal census showing a population of approximately 30,000 people in Dawson City and the surrounding area. In June of 1898, the rapid population increase prompted the Canadian government to pass the Yukon Act, splitting the Yukon Territories from the Northwest Territories. 11 By 1899, the remainder trickled in from the further-flung areas of the country. Unfortunately, for most of those who arrived in the latter half of 1898 and 1899, little fortune remained that others had not already claimed. Finally, in 1899, the papers announced that gold had been found in Nome, Alaska, and the Yukon Gold Rush was over almost as soon as it had begun. Many of those who had no luck in the Yukon made their exodus to Alaska to chase new dreams. 12 In 1900, the White Pass & Yukon Railway was completed, and the rush was over for all intents and purposes. 13

Impact on & Treatment of Indigenous Populations 
The Yukon is the home territory of fourteen different First Nations whose ancestors have 
inhabited the region for at least 12,000 years. These fourteen nations are the Carcross/Tagish, 
Champagne and Aishihik, Na-Cho Nyäk Dun, Kluane, Kwanlin Dün, Liard, Little Salmon/Carmacks, 
Ross River Dena, Selkirk, Ta’an Kwäch’än, Teslin Tlingit, Tr’ondëk Hwëch’in, Vuntut Gwitchin and 
White River. The fourteen first nations fall within eight different language groups: Gwich'in, Hän, 
Kaska, Northern Tutchone, Southern Tutchone, Tagish, Tlingit and Upper Tanana, and are often 
broadly referred to by these language groups. Beyond this, there are another eight transboundary

Prior to settler populations entering the territory, the Indigenous populations maintained trade networks in the north, southwest, and eastern interior with the Alaskan Koyukon and Inuit people. They traded in goods such as hide, bark baskets, native copper and eulachon oil for bone and tusks. 15 In the 18th century, Russia established trade networks along the Yukon River, though not within the Yukon itself 16, and traded with the Tlingit, whose traditional territory spans the Yukon, Alaska and British Columbia. 17 In the 1840s, explorers, prospectors and fur traders began penetrating the Yukon; in the early 1860s, the first Anglican missionaries arrived. In the 1870s, private traders and prospectors began entering the territory, and the Fort Reliance trading post was established. In 1886, the first gold was discovered, and the community of Forty Mile was founded, triggering the first wave of permanent settlement and expansion in the region. 18

In general, the 1840s-1890s saw a tense coexistence between Indigenous and settler communities as they began to penetrate the territory more and more. There was a trading post established in 1848 in Fort Selkirk by Robert Campbell that was initially tolerated but eventually destroyed when it began to impact the Chilkat's (Tlingit) trade too much. The lands and animal populations were ravaged, and, on occasion, as with the Tagish in 1888, stores that had been collected to see a community through the winter were traded away for items like tobacco, tea and blankets, leaving the community with little to survive the cold seasons. 19 Beyond this, alcohol abuse and disease became major concerns among Indigenous populations. Over time, they would see epidemics of smallpox, typhoid, whooping cough, tuberculosis, polio, influenza and diphtheria. 20 One example of the devastating impact of these diseases is an estimate by Cornelius Osgood, who first studied the Han, that there were approximately 1,000 Han in the Yukon in the 1840s. However, by the 1901 census, only 81 Indigenous people lived in Moosehide. 21

The impacts of colonialism were mitigated somewhat by the Tlingit's control over the mountain passes, the most straightforward access points to the territory's interior, and their continual refusal to grant access to outsiders. However, in February of 1880, after some infighting and violence between the younger Tlingit, who wanted to maintain control, and elders, who saw value in opening the passes to outsiders, the Tlingit and Americans reached an agreement. "The blockade of the mountain passes would be lifted on the following three conditions: prospectors would be accompanied by Tlingit guides to ensure no trading took place, they would hire Tlingit slaves as packers, and they would use the less important route, the Chilkoot, rather than the Chilkat." 22

After 1880, as more outsiders began to filter in, the segregation of Indigenous people from newcomers increased. Though more accepted in the beginning as a beneficial reciprocal relationship, relationships between Indigenous individuals and outsiders were frowned upon, particularly during the KGR when greater numbers of non-Indigenous women began to enter the Yukon. 23 White men who had relationships with Indigenous women and accepted Indigenous communities, like George Carmack, were referred to as “squaw men.” Such men were shunned and made to feel inferior by their peers, and children of these unions were sometimes abandoned by both communities. 24

When gold was discovered in 1896, and the rush began, many Indigenous communities made accommodations and shifts to their ways of life. They helped those coming in while finding ways to benefit from this influx of strangers. Many Tlingit and Tagish, sometimes whole families, including women and girls, offered their services as navigators and packers to stampeders for a fee. 25 Despite their willingness to transport the heavy packs and gear that stampeders balked at, packers were often the subject of derision in writings by stampeders, seen as lazy and untrustworthy. The reality is that the packers understood their worth and the leverage they held;

While the Tlingit, Tagish and Tutchone did their best to adapt to this new way of life, the Han, who were arguably the most affected by the KGR, stayed on the periphery as much as they could. The communities were segregated at Forty Mile, at the forts, and would be in Dawson City as well. 30 With the founding of Dawson as a white settlement the Han were forced to move, giving up all claims to their former village of Nuklako. Going over the heads of Commissioner Ogilvie and the NWMP Commander Charles Constantine, Bishop Bompas and Chief Isaac of the Han managed to secure the parcel of land that would become Moosehide. Bishop Bompas, who first arrived in the Yukon in 1865, consistently fought for the benefit of the Indigenous population through an Anglican lens. He felt that the settlers were a bad influence on the Indigenous peoples, and preferred their company to that of the white miners. Throughout his time in the north he encouraged the segregation of Indigenous communities for their own protection, consistently fighting for their benefit, while at the same time infantilizing them.

Despite Bompas’ efforts, as Charlene Porsild notes in her work Gamblers and Dreamers, "more than thirty Han families were removed to a plot of land precisely the same size as a single homestead offered to prospective farmers on the Canadian prairies at this time, an irony that seemed lost on government officials." 31 This was certainly not an ideal situation, and Commander Constantine, who held a strong dislike for the Indigenous population and an almost equal dislike for Bompas because of his regard for them, would never offer the slightest help when it was asked for, considering them a lazy, dirty nuisance, and stating: "When I came to this country [my instructions were] that the Indians were not to be recognized in any way which would lead them to believe that the Government would do anything for them as Indians." 32

The mother of Pierre Burton, Laura, who had visited Dawson City just ten years after the rush, described "half-breeds and Indians," as the lowest rung of Dawson society. 33 In spite of that, it is said quite often that Chief Isaac, who had received his name from Bishop Bompas, had quite a good relationship with those in Dawson City. Still, Chief Isaac was by no means a pushover, he often fought for the rights of his people, even writing articles for the local newspapers in an attempt to combat misunderstanding and bring to light inequality:

“Long time ago before the white man came along, Yukon Indian was happy. Indian had plenty game, no trouble and was fat. White man comes and Indian go out and kill meat to feed him. Indian gives white man clothes to wear and warm him by Indian fire. Byemby ... million white man come and cut down Indian’s wood, kill Indian’s game, take Indian’s gold out of the ground, give Indian nothing. Game all gone, wood all gone, Indian cold and hungry, white man no care.” 35

As people flooded in, Chief Isaac (figure 2) saw the threat to his culture and gave the songs of his people to their Alaskan relatives for safekeeping, songs that were finally returned to them in 1990. The name Klondike itself came as a mishearing and a corruption of the word that the Han used to refer to themselves, "Tr'ondëk." 36 The Indigenous people have remained steadfast, the one consistent population in the region. This legacy is reflected today through their sovereignty and governance of much of the territory.

This number comes from Pierre Burton's work "Klondike: The Life and Death of the Last Great Gold Rush," which does not include a citation for the figure and has been repeated by virtually everyone else since then. 38 However, thanks to luck and the help of kind strangers on the internet, in the last few months I have encountered two primary documents referencing the number. One is a Seattle Post Intelligencer article from 1898 estimating 100,000 have headed north, and the other is a letter from an NWMP officer, Z.T. Most of those we see in photos and hear about in stories of the Klondike Gold Rush are white men, people with nothing to their name, looking to make a new start. Though white men were undoubtedly a majority, the individuals who set out for the Klondike, or who inevitably became embroiled in it, were from all walks of life - they represented all genders, ages, races and economic backgrounds. They were not all American and Canadian either; this was a worldwide phenomenon, with at least twenty percent of the stampeders coming from dozens of countries overseas, including Russia, Japan, Australia and France. 40 It is unlikely that many of the stampeders fit into the stereotype of the down-on-his-luck drifter (Figure 3). There were inevitably many people looking to start over; however, more than one source have suggested that at least some wealth was an absolute requirement for any stampeder looking to set out for the goldfields. This is reinforced by the 1898 NWMP law that all stampeders needed to bring a year's worth of supplies with them. 41 Still, we do have to consider that many would have given up all they had to attain the requisite outfit for the journey. The stampeders all had different levels of fitness and expertise, which impacted their success levels in forging their paths to the gold fields; many underestimated the difficulties they would face along the way, to terrible consequences. Others saw these failures and scoffed at the hubris of others while confidently walking into their own nightmares. 43 Those who reached Dawson first discovered the sourdoughs, worldly men who had been there long before the rush began and understood how the Yukon worked. To the sourdoughs, those newcomers were referred to as tenderfoot or cheechako and, though they had overcome many trials already, were only welcomed into the fold once they had proven they had what it took to survive a Yukon winter. 44

Society in Dawson at the turn of the 20th century was as stratified as any other community at the time, with a social elite and ranking based on respectability. Dr. Barrett, a physician at St. Mary's Hospital, noted that "the growing community soon featured a social elite, which drew membership from the ranks of the professional and business class and almost completely excluded mining and labouring people. Barrett called them 'the nucleus of 400' among whom 'hospitality and good fellowship flourished to a degree unthought of in older Canadian communities." 45

People would connect and gather with those who shared a place of origin or similar economic, religious, or cultural background. 46 The Anglican Church, Presbyterian Church, and Catholic Church established themselves in 1897, and the Methodist Church followed a year later. "Almost all Dawson's Scandinavians reported themselves Lutherans, for example, while all Russians professed Judaism. Similarly, the French, Irish, and French Canadians were overwhelmingly Catholic." 47 The community was dominated by Protestants, who counted themselves in the highest circles of Dawson society; however, there was little competition between the churches and even cooperation - as was the case when the Protestants sought to raise money for their new Good Samaritan Hospital after seeing that the Catholic's St. Mary's Hospital was unable to keep up with the numbers of the sick. 48

Women, Indigenous people and other non-white participants in the KGR faced discrimination. Even those Indigenous individuals tied to wealthy and respectable white families were not immune: Sadie Stringer, the wife of Isaac Stringer, the bishop; Mrs. Robert McDonald, the Indigenous wife of the Metis missionary Reverend Robert McDonald, and Reverend Totty and his Indigenous wife were all shunned from polite society at one point or another, excluded from parties and other social events because of their race or association with Indigenous people. 55 As mentioned, racism and discrimination were not limited to Indigenous peoples. There was no known Chinese population in Dawson City during the KGR despite the overseas Chinese participating in all prior gold rushes in the 19th century along the Pacific. Before the KGR, in 1894 or 5, sourdoughs already in the Yukon area met with Chinese prospectors who had just arrived at the port in Dyea and banned them from the north. 56

Though I have seen little published on children of the KGR, children were present in the Klondike and must be considered in our discussions of mortuary practices. We know that during the Victorian era, the perception of children shifted drastically. Given the rapid industrialization of the time and less need for the labour that children provided, adults began to see children in a separate sphere to themselves. Children began to be viewed as innocent and dependent rather than miniature adults. We can speculate that, as with many frontier communities, children still would have had to grow up fast, assisting their families with what was required to survive. Geography & Environment of the Klondike The American side of the Chilkoot and White Pass trails is characterized as a damp, temperate coastal forest. On the other hand, the Canadian side is a subarctic plateau, much drier but more subject to permafrost and ice. 68

Most significant settlements along these routes, including Dyea, Skagway, Carcross, Whitehorse and Dawson City, and the various camps, were founded along major river systems. With rivers being the primary mode of maintaining direction and transporting goods once stampeders arrived in Bennett Lake, this was necessary. The unfortunate consequence is that most are placed right within the floodplains of these rivers. 69 For Dawson City the frost-free season is only between ninety and one hundred and eighty days. Even within the frost-free season, a layer of permafrost

all presenting different challenges to those who chose to use them. 
1. The All-Water Route 
The all-water route consisted of travellers brought by steamship up the Pacific coast to 
St. Michael, Alaska. In St. Michael, they would then take a riverboat to Dawson City up the Yukon 
River. The entire length of this route was approximately 6,759 kilometers and was the safest and 
most luxurious of all the options. However, it was not an option for most; the exorbitant cost of 
passage meant that the all-water route was reserved for only the wealthiest of individuals, and, 
though it was the safest choice, it still presented its share of danger. The long trip could only be 
undertaken in the summer when the rivers were not frozen. Those wealthy individuals used to a 
cushy lifestyle onboard, who were unlucky and got stranded along the route when the rivers

2. The Glacier Routes Though travelling over a glacier seems like a startlingly poor choice, it was a choice that more than a few made. Outside the all-water route, groups of stampeders were punished for willingly choosing to travel over the Malaspina and Yakutat glaciers just to the south and the Valdez Glacier to the northwest. The Stikine Route The Stikine route was more convoluted. Like the all-water route, it required one to take a steamship up the Pacific coast; however, in this case, individuals would disembark in Wrangell, Alaska. Next, a paddle-wheeler would transport Stampeders up the Stikine River to Glenora, British Columbia. Individuals would then hike 150 miles to Teslin, board a boat that took them along the Teslin River to Fort Selkirk and then down the Yukon River, finally, to Dawson City. 76

Given the number of boats involved, the Stikine option would have been the second most expensive option, but certainly not without its share of danger, as highlighted in the poem at the beginning of this study. Unlike the Chilkoot and White Pass trails, the hike between Glenora and Teslin was not well-defined and was significantly longer and swampier, leading to individuals getting lost or sick. 77

5. The Chilkoot Trail The Chilkoot Trail was one of the two most popular overland routes. Stampeders would take a steamer up the Pacific coast to Dyea in southern Alaska and, from Dyea, hike over the Chilkoot Pass to Lake Lindeman in the Yukon. Once at Lake Lindeman, they would either construct a boat or use one they had brought to continue down the Yukon River to Dawson City. Alternately, for those wanting to avoid the rapids between Lake Lindeman and Lake Bennett, some would hike between the two and board their craft in Bennett. The Chilkoot trail was only thirty-three miles in length, with another five hundred and sixty miles down the Yukon River. Just the trail itself was challenging, as it is high-elevation and rugged, with the last handful of miles over the pass at a nearly forty-five-degree incline with an elevation of over eleven hundred meters. 80

With both the Chilkoot and White Pass trails, a requirement was put in place by the NWMP that each stampeder was to have a year's worth of supplies with them on the trek. 81 It was realized early on that starvation, scurvy, and the inability to easily attain supplies once one reached Dawson posed a real danger, so, in the end, the NWMP put this rule in place to try and mitigate risks. Unfortunately for those hiking the Chilkoot, sleds and horses were only usable for a short time. Toting a year's worth of supplies over the pass meant that instead of hiking all thirty three miles once, stampeders would often have to make multiple, sometimes dozens, of trips along the severely congested trail, bringing a portion of their supplies at a time. 82 By attempting to eliminate some risks, the NWMP opened up these individuals to other risks, such as exhaustion and exposure.

The Victorian era was the era of the "beautification of death," with North America seeing the height of memorial opulence less than two decades before the KGR began. Picking up inspiration from Classical and Gothic revival stylings, using expensive materials such as marble and granite and incorporating a range of elaborate symbology. The Industrial Revolution had led to a sharp increase in consumer culture, and the burial landscapes became competition grounds, with mausoleums, obelisks, statuary, fences and curbs all taking their turns in popularity. 87 During the time of the KGR, in the latter half of the 19th century, the lawn cemetery rose in popularity with its neat and orderly rows and maintained grounds. Though trends were delayed across America from east to west, as a whole, by the 1890s, this styling had been firmly established and only moderately toned down. Both simple and complex memorials became the standard of the time, with a noted preference for complex and highly decorated. 88

There are several ways that burials during the Klondike Gold Rush differ from what one might call the "standard" Victorian burial of the time, that is to say, burials within long-established areas of North America with easy access to materials and open lines of communication with other communities. There were none of these luxuries in the Yukon and Alaska, in towns like Skagway and Dawson City, which were only developed out of necessity alongside the gold rush. Building materials were limited to what the surrounding environment had to offer, and communication between communities was a lengthy process that, at least in the case of Dawson, ceased entirely in the winter months. 89 The fundamental nature of the gold rush undoubtedly impacted burial and commemoration in the Klondike. In the Klondike, elaborate commemoration with marble and granite was, for the most part, not possible. Though skilled craftspeople certainly settled in the north, there was no easy way of getting such materials to such locations. The standard Klondike grave marker was made of wood in the shape of a cross or half-round with simple inscriptions in black. Though the topic of gold rush cemeteries has seen relatively little academic study, I wanted to present a small discussion about how the landscapes of death might have been similar or different

#### CHAPTER 2 Methods & Theory

MORTUARY ARCHAEOLOGY & AGENCY

This study is rooted in the subdiscipline of mortuary archaeology, considering, among other things, the intertwining relationship between agency and identity. Mortuary archaeology focuses on burial landscapes, contexts, associated material culture and, sometimes, human remains. Everything from the broader burying ground to the hardware on the coffin, if there was a coffin, can tell us something about an individual's socio-cultural and spiritual interactions in life and how others interacted with them in death. 96 I place these mortuary remains within the framework of a materialist approach to the past. For Daisy Turnbull this is:

“An approach to archaeology that focuses on the relationship between humans and the materials they interact with. It is not only concerned with the physical attributes of objects but rather, the compelling notion that materials are shaped and given a conscious agency when humans engage with them.” 97

My own work is embedded in the concept of "secondary agency" as proposed by Alfred Gell. Secondary agency is an approach to materiality that rejects the ability of materials to control human actions or alter the life course of humans. Material objects do, however, have the ability to invoke feelings in humans or affect another's actions. 98 Objects can create an emotional pull on an individual based on their historical relationship to that object. Using a personal example, I am deeply attached to my parent’s house because it has been in our family for two generations. It is the house I lived in for the majority of my life, and it is a house that I have spent many hours restoring alongside my parents and sister. To another person, my parent's house is just a house,

In considering mortuary remains, we realize that the dead themselves cannot physically or vocally express agency through traditional means. The body has been transformed into an object, but expresses agency by eliciting emotional responses from those who knew them, mediated by the time, proximity and personal history of living individuals with the dead. These can be positive or negative emotions, and these emotions will impact the treatment of the dead and their representation within death. For those who did not know the deceased during life, there is still the potential for preconceived notions to create emotional impacts. In this case, the categorization of a body by race, gender, age, social class or even cause of death may effect the ways the living give mortuary treatment to a body in death.

COMMEMORATION & MEMORIALIZATION

As commemoration and memorialization play a large role in the act of remembrance, and within this study, it is best to highlight the distinction between the two.

Many define commemoration as an actively occurring observance or ceremony; however, I find the definition provided by the Australian War Memorial to be more in line with my own views: “Commemoration means to remember, honour, or show respect to a person or event. This can be done through a special action like a ceremony or celebration, but commemoration can also occur through the creation of an object, work of art, writing, music, or a memorial.” 99 I would add to this that the person or event need not have a positive association to receive commemoration. Often, commemoration is extended as a remembrance of the great atrocities of the world, as a rebellion against erasure and as a reminder of the fallibility of human nature.

Memorialization then falls under the umbrella of commemoration as one of the various forms that commemoration can take. It is the physical, material manifestation of remembrance seen

through features such as graves, statues, dedicated park benches or memorial gardens. Simply, all memorialization is commemoration, but not all commemoration is memorialization.

I must emphasize that I am considering this topic from the perspective of religious traditions and values as seen in North America. Throughout the world, the same religious organizations can and do exhibit vastly different behaviours regarding mortuary practice; treatment is dependent on how mortuary spaces are owned and operated within that country in concert with the beliefs of the organization and the history of the organization within that country.

“In North America, cemeteries may be owned by religious organizations, municipalities, private corporations that may be either non-profit or for-profit or private family plots on private land.” 100 Additionally, “most […] cemeteries burial concessions give the family holding a plot the right to keep the remains there in perpetuity.” 101 Thus, in the case of historic cemeteries, that is cemeteries that are no longer in use, regardless of ownership, there is typically very little in the way of funds for care, and much of the upkeep in these cases is undertaken by volunteers. Generally, this means that cemeteries like these, regardless of ownership, fall to the stewardship of those that are in some way tied to or invested in the space, hence why the cemeteries associated with organizations tend to see more consistent care when compared with public cemeteries.

There are some distinct differences between Catholics, Protestants and Jews in terms of cemetery development and care in North America. Jewish cemeteries are steeped in ritual and follow specific rules regarding their creation and care. They are always separate and consecrated spaces bordered by a surround, be it a fence, wall or hedge. Early on, Protestant groups would occasionally establish their cemeteries on consecrated grounds; however, more often than not, you will now see those of different Protestant denominations grouped in separate sections of the same cemetery. In opposition, occasionally you will see designated sections for Catholics in public cemeteries; however, based on the dictates of their faith, it is far more common to see designated Catholic cemeteries, provided as both “sanctified ground for the dead as well as places of prayer

Religion Map (Dordrecht, NE: Springer, 2015), 623–647, 624. 
101 Gade, “Cemeteries as a Template,” 624.

and remembrance for the living.” 102 Generally, most places where there is a Catholic church, there will be an associated cemetery.

Catholic and Jewish cemeteries fall under the ownership of a church, synagogue or private institution, and the care shown toward these spaces can be seen as an extension of the belief systems behind the creation of the spaces themselves. Generally, they are tended to by the church and/or congregation or family members out of a sense of responsibility toward the dead and their fate after death. In Protestantism, where there exist fewer concerns about what happens after death, caring for the dead is less of a priority. Still, as with anyone else, the potential for secondary agency to act upon the living exists, creating a need to care for those who were loved in life despite religious doctrine.

THE LIMITS OF THIS STUDY

Temporally, this study includes only those who died between August 1896 and January 1900. 1896 was chosen, rather than the "traditional" date of 1898, as August 1896 was when the initial discovery of gold occurred, triggering the KGR. Though in a much smaller quantity than in 1898, stampeders began filtering into the region relatively soon after this discovery. Those already in the region took advantage and staked claims early. 1900 was chosen to bookend this range, as midway through 1899, the Nome Gold Rush pulled many of those that had come to the Klondike away, and midway through 1900, the White Pass & Yukon Railway was finally completed, entirely changing the socio-cultural dynamic though the greater mobility it provided.

Spatially (Figure 6), this study encompasses the two main routes into the Klondike, the Chilkoot and White Pass Trails, several key locations in British Columbia, including Lake Laberge, Bennett Lake and Atlin, and a large swath of the Yukon extending from Carcross to Forty Mile.

ARCHIVAL RESEARCH

The first part of this study consisted of archival and database research. This type of study would usually rely upon government death records; however, as the Yukon did not begin formally recording deaths until 1898, and Alaska did not until 1913, this has left significant gaps in the historical record. Thus, alongside death records, we referenced burial records, mortuary records, newspapers, personal diaries, court records, census data, former research in this region, online cemetery databases such as Find a Grave, and genealogy platforms such as Ancestry. The main sources that I utilized are as follows: The Yukon Territorial Records, 1898-1903 (Library and Archives Canada (LAC)) A microfilm of the original handwritten document. In 1898, Superintendent Steele mandated by law that all deaths in the Yukon Territory be reported to and registered with the NWMP stationed in Dawson City. The registrar should record as much detail as possible about the deceased; that way, the NWMP could inform the next of kin, and the deceased's estate could be settled. During this process, when possible, Steele also required that a medical certificate be provided to the NWMP. 103

Baptemes, Mariages, Sepultures de Ste-Marie de Dawson City, Yukon 1898-1956 (Library and Archives Canada; Yukon Archives; Dawson City Museum) I had access to two versions of this record. The original handwritten copy in English and French on microfilm from Library and Archives Canada and a typed and bound version published in 1976 are available at LAC, Yukon Archives and Dawson City Museum. As the title suggests, these were records of all baptisms, marriages, and funerals St. Mary's church ministered to from 1898-1957.

Anglican Church Records – Dawson City Funerals 1897-1931 & Moosehide Burials 1897-1929 (Copies of older registers - Yukon Archives) We treated these copies as facsimiles in terms of their interpretive value because the original documents are still extant, just not viewable. These documents were not open access,

Overall, sources were broken down into three tiers:

Tier 1: Primary sources were the most valuable and the most reliable. That said, even primary sources can have their fallibility; newspapers, for instance, sometimes print incorrect, misleading or exaggerated information. In this case, the main limitations of the primary documents are the limits to their accessibility, my ability to interpret handwritten notes, the nuances of translating from one language to another and interpreting various forms of shorthand. Transcripts of original documents were of equal value if I had access to the original document or if the existence of the original document could be confirmed. Access to both the original document and transcript was beneficial as the transcripts could be used to verify my interpretations of the primary documents. Similarly, the primary could be used to detect transcription errors in the transcript.

Tier 2: Research conducted by other researchers that included their information sources. With a list of sources, you can confirm the quality of the sources and ensure that the information is not coming from a void. In this case, much of the prior research relied on written/archival sources, interviews, and on-the-ground research, which was done over a significant time, increasing its reliability. These documents' limitations centred around not knowing what kind of systems and checks others had used when compiling their information.

[34]

Tier 3: Finally, sites like Find a Grave and FamilySearch were invaluable to this research. However, as anyone can contribute to sites such as these without documentation of where they get their information, it is important that information gathered from these sites (excluding primary documents) was treated more as jumping-off points and supplementary or confirmatory.

As is the nature of human error, all three of these tiers, even the primary documents, were potentially subject to transcription errors, including spelling errors, translation errors or missing/incorrect information. Beyond transcription errors, Tiers 2 and 3 also risked echoing misinformation from source to source. These issues highlight the importance of correction and verification through as many sources as possible.

Before arriving in the North, I also intended to collect GPS information for each burial; however, a lack of clear understanding of how accurate GPS information is in the North led me to abandon this upon testing my equipment and realizing that I was not adequately prepared to collect accurate enough readings. The survey form was modified from a cemetery maintenance survey form and is included here as Appendix Two. The sections included on the survey form were chosen for their ability to answer several questions. Inscriptions and decorations can say a lot about an individual's identity - their age, date of death, sometimes their cause of death, birthplace, religion, who commissioned the marker or associated organizations. The condition of a marker, whether it is the original marker and the presence of more than one marker for the same individual can say a lot about cemetery care as well as degradation and loss created by the surrounding environment. The form, material and type of surround can say a lot about an individual's affluence; in some cases, you can infer religion or other associated organizations from the shape. The marker's orientation (N, S, E, W) and placement within the broader mortuary space can give clues about an individual's religion or social status. If for no other reason, the results of these surveys were valuable as they allowed me to maintain a record of these burials for posterity. The cemeteries in and around Dawson, in particular, were virtually ignored until the 1970s, and, as such, many burials have been subject to change or lost entirely. Thus, maintaining a record amidst the changing nature of these mortuary spaces is crucial for the continued remembrance of those lost.

Community Meeting & Cleanup While in Dawson City, I arranged a community gathering at the Dawson City Museum with the assistance of the museum director and staff. The goal of this gathering was to share the work that I was doing in the community and what I was finding with those who were interested, but also to provide a space for dialogue and community members to share with me anything they might know or have experienced relating to death and commemoration during the KGR, including details an outsider might be unaware of, like cemetery preservation initiatives or obscure burials. Following this gathering and discussions regarding the 3rd Avenue Typhoid Cemetery, its condition, and management, the museum director conceived a community cleanup initiative for

[36]

the cemetery, scheduled to take place during the city's Discovery Days celebrations on August 
15th-19th, 2025. Eleven volunteers, including the museum director and myself, showed up on the 
community cleanup day. We cleared vegetation from all remaining visible gravesites and the 
pathways in between and located two previously concealed gravesites. Interestingly, seven of the 
11 volunteers were not community members but were seasonal workers employed at one of 
Dawson's many hotels. 
DATABASE 
This research resulted in a database of individuals who died during the KGR. Over 20 
pieces of information relating to various aspects of identity were collected for each individual. 
These include several demographic points, i.e. age, sex, race, and religion, and aspects such as the 
location of birth, cause of death, location of death, location of burial, burial and marker type, 
associated organizations (e.g., Freemasons, NWMP, Yukon Order of Pioneers, etc.), and 
profession. As much of this information was gathered as possible using the terminology of the 
source material as a reflection of socio-cultural norms. The quality of the data was determined by 
several yes/no acknowledgements that have been put in place when we have confirmed aspects 
such as identity, death (including location) and burial (including location) through a primary 
source, and all sources referenced were tracked and noted alongside the respective individual 
within the database. 
When it came to data cleansing and choosing whom to include and not include within the dataset 
for this thesis, we began by removing duplicates. Often, an individual could be recorded across 
multiple records under slightly varying names. This error can be a byproduct of the original 
recorder mishearing or not knowing how to spell a name or a transcription error further down the 
line. Generally, we noticed this occurring in real-time and added all name variations into a singular 
entry. However, sometimes, we ended up with two or three entries for the same individual – 
these were combined and removed. 

Beyond removing duplicates, decisions about who was included were based primarily on the range of this study. If it was shown through the data acquired that an individual died within the geographic region of this study between 1896-1900, they were included. There are some individuals in the dataset for which we have no known date and/or location of death. In these instances, we relied upon other context clues. For instance, if an individual was buried in 1899,

[37]

the chances are they died in 1899 or earlier - but likely not more than three years earlier, as that would be irregular in this context. Similarly, if an individual was buried in a location in the study area, the likelihood is high that they died somewhere within the study area, so they were allowed. If an individual had no known location of death or burial but the information came from a record directly associated with the area of study, such as the Anglican Church records for Dawson City, they were deemed acceptable. Though we have located just over 1,100 individuals total; for analysis, based on the range outlined above, I will be referencing a database of 955 individuals. 104 Of these 955 individuals, 625 were located or confirmed through a primary source and 330 from, typically, several secondary sources.

## CHAPTER 3 Findings

INDIGENEITY

After compiling my initial database of the KGR dead, I noticed that there were very few known Indigenous individuals listed, suggesting that Indigenous individuals were not equally accounted for in the written record. This trend continued during my exploration of primary materials and records. Most contemporary death records that I encountered only had the names of one or two known Indigenous individuals, if they had any at all.

I would be remiss if I did not note that the Indigenous individuals I found referenced most often were the Nantuck Brothers. These four brothers were arrested for the murder of William Meehan and the theft of his belongings. They were all found guilty; two of the brothers died in jail of tuberculosis, while the remaining two were hanged in August of 1899. Interestingly, after their deaths, despite having been found guilty of murder, I learned through a conversation with Susan Mooney and the acquisition of a photograph from Yukon Archives that the two brothers who had died of tuberculosis had been buried in Hillside Cemetery. 105 In contrast, upon execution, the other two were buried in a lime pit near the Fort Herchmer barracks, the location of which was unrecorded and unknown until the pit was accidentally uncovered during the construction of Dawson City's new sewage treatment plant in 2010. 106

Soon after, Carcross Tagish First Nation members began to seek a proper burial for the Nantuck brothers. In 2011, they were reburied in Dawson City with a small ceremony organized and attended by representatives from the Carcross Tagish, Kwanlin Dün, and Ta’an Kwäch’än First Nations, among whom the Nantuck brothers had descendants. 107

Indeed, where I encountered the best records of Indigenous individuals who had died during the KGR was in the research the Trʼondëk Hwëchʼin had conducted to try and determine who was buried within the Moosehide cemetery. However, as it turned out, the majority of KGR-associated individuals uncovered by that project were found through the Anglican Church records, which contained records of burials that had taken place both in Dawson City and in Moosehide. The Anglican Church burial records proved to be the only primary document providing information on a subset of Indigenous deaths at the time of the KGR.

There are now 44 Indigenous individuals within the dataset, with six others assumed to be Indigenous. Of these individuals, 40 are recorded within primary documents, 38 in the Anglican Church burial records for Moosehide and Dawson City. These records can only be accessed in person at the Yukon Archives in Whitehorse with written permission from the Bishop of Yukon, and cannot be photographed. A single individual, presumed to be Metis, was located within the St. Mary's Catholic Church burial records, and the last, referred to as a "half-breed youth," was located within NWMP documents.

The Anglican Church burial documents consisted of a record for Moosehide burials and a record for Dawson City burials. The list of Moosehide burials contained all Indigenous individuals, and the Dawson City burials contained a majority of settler burials with a handful of Indigenous individuals who had died at Fort Herchmer. Between these two documents was an observable difference in record keeping. Individuals on the Dawson City burial list had far more identifying information than those on the Moosehide list; where they could be determined by the individuals recording the deaths, aspects of identity such as profession, age, place of birth, last known location, time ill, doctor, specific death date, cause of death and informant of death were all included. However, for those on the Moosehide list, only the year of death, approximate age, name of kin, and a notation of "Indian" in the profession category were recorded. Additionally, Indigenous individuals were typically only referred to by their "English" first name, given upon conversion to the faith, though, in place of a last name was sometimes a reference to their place of birth/people, for instance, Tagish Charlie. The use of English names with place names was also a phenomenon I witnessed in grave inscriptions at the relocated Dyea cemetery, though for individuals outside the range of this study.

Beyond archival research, as noted above, as part of the permitting process, I was granted

permission and intended to visit two separate semi-restricted locations within the Trʼondëk Hwëchʼin traditional territory—the Moosehide Cemetery and Forty Mile, which contains several cemeteries. Given the nature of these sites, I had little information before visiting them.

Moosehide Cemetery (Moosehide, Yukon)

Moosehide Cemetery is located in the Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in village of Moosehide, only accessible by river, or a trail from Dawson City. The first known burials 108 took place in 1898, and though the village has no current full-time residents, the Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in continue to bury family there today. Access to Moosehide and the cemetery is completely controlled by the Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in. People who are not of the nation and wish to visit the site must attain prior permission via permit except during Moosehide Gathering, held every other year, where all are welcome to attend. 109

Moosehide Cemetery covers a large swath of land, the area is irregularly shaped and partially fenced off on two sides, with a gate at the main entrance. Directly to the south is a ravine, and to the east, behind the cemetery, is forest. Just inside the main gate was what appeared to be the newer section of the cemetery with more recent burials; community members regularly maintain this section. To the north and parallel with the maintained portion, a larger section of the cemetery is completely overgrown and contains, I believe, the oldest of the burials. Walking through this area was difficult, with much of the vegetation well over my head; however, in the area I could cover, no markers or structures appeared to remain. After visiting the cemetery, I suspect it carries on further to the east than indicated by the cleared space.

Though there were no visible remaining burials dating to the time period of this study, I did observe a row of new stake markers made of metal lined up along the inside of the fence directly to the right of the entrance. These appeared to be displaced from the named individuals' true burial locations and their actual intended location. They appeared to be meant to serve more as

Forty Mile First Nation Cemeteries (Forty Mile, Yukon)

My intent to visit what I understood to be two Indigenous cemeteries in Forty Mile stemmed partially from a misunderstanding of the limited literature I had regarding the Forty Mile Cemeteries in general, of which there were apparently five active during the Gold Rush. 110 From a report put together in 2007, I was under the impression that there were two Indigenous cemeteries, one across the Yukon River from Forty Mile that I likely would not be able to access and one along the main trail from the fish camp to the townsite. 111 Once there, I discovered that what I thought to be a cemetery along the fish camp/townsite trail was, instead, a single burial thought to belong to a First Nations individual. Though the single trailside burial was easy enough to locate, the exact locations for the remainder of the cemeteries in Forty Mile, save one, the Historic Cemetery, are currently unknown to me. While there, Zack Yeager, a community member who had accompanied us to Forty Mile, flew his drone over the river to the suspected area of the second Indigenous cemetery; however, we could not see anything that resembled a cemetery in the explored location.

While scanning through documents supplied to me by Karl Gurcke of the National Park Service, I learned that there had also previously been a small First Nation cemetery in Dyea referred to as the "Native Cemetery," which had been established nearly 10 years prior to the KGR but was, apparently, still in use at the time. However, no photographs of the cemetery or records about those buried there remain. Like the Dyea Cemetery, this cemetery is thought to have been washed away by the Taiya River. Confusingly, Dyea Cemetery was also referred to as the Native Cemetery at one point, perhaps because both Indigenous individuals and settlers were allowed to be buried within this cemetery, though still segregated. 112

Despite being unable to observe Indigenous mortuary practices dating back to the KGR, from a sign that was placed just inside Moosehide Cemetery, I was able to learn that, at least in the case of the Trʼondëk Hwëchʼin, after contact with settlers' mortuary practices shifted somewhat, and spirit houses were used to house the remains of the dead. Through archival photographs shared with me by the Trʼondëk Hwëchʼin Heritage Department, I was able to confirm that such spirit houses were still visible in Moosehide Cemetery in 1917. The use of Spirit Houses was not limited to the Trʼondëk Hwëchʼin. Though it appears to be a tradition that was introduced to these communities; these are, regardless, mortuary practices that were common to many Indigenous communities in 19 th-century Alaska, Yukon, and northern British Columbia . 113 Several Indigenous communities across the Yukon have been conducting their own research into mortuary records and cemetery preservation. Aside from the Trʼondëk Hwëchʼin’s own Moosehide Cemetery research project in 2011, another example of this work is the 1970s grant funded effort by the Mundessa Club, headed by George Dawson K’alazhaw, the grandson of Chief Mundessa, “to work with Elders and youth on maintaining traditional First Nations cemeteries at Whitehorse, Marsh Lake and Lake Laberge.” 114

There are many reasons why the memory of Indigenous individuals who died during the KGR has not persisted through time despite the knowledge that so many died. We can, of course, first acknowledge the very present racism that existed toward Indigenous peoples, as explored in the background chapter of this work. We have learned that Indigenous peoples were regarded among the lowest in society, often misused, mistrusted and considered lazy by stampeders and officials alike, even while they were carrying their equipment and trying to help them survive. That said, the mistrust surely went both ways, particularly after having been forced from the Dawson area by the NWMP and government. Yes, the NWMP had a law in place that all deaths were to be reported to them in Dawson City, but did Indigenous peoples feel that they were subject to this law, and, given the relationship we see between Constantine and the Han, did the NWMP care if Indigenous deaths went unreported? We know that, at least in Alaska, Indigenous people and

children were often not given death certificates. 115

Our only historic documentation of Indigenous burials during the KGR are the Anglican records of burials at Moosehide. This was an Anglican mission community, and the vast majority of Indigenous people in the region lived elsewhere. This suggests that, even though these are the most complete documents concerning Indigenous deaths during the KGR, they are a small subset. We have learned that all individuals in Moosehide were nominally members of the Church of England by 1901, but it is unclear whether conversion to the Church was a necessary precursor to burial at Moosehide during the KGR.

Additionally, it is the case that the individuals recorded were not recorded under their birth name, which essentially strips them of their identity and the ability to differentiate individuality. With no last name and new first names taken from scripture, you are left with several individuals who share a first name, and there is often no way of differentiating between them beyond their kin connections. Also, English names do not necessarily seem to be a product solely of conversion to the faith, with some settlers calling some Indigenous individuals by English names to ease communication on their end.

Even now, that there are so many hurdles in place that need to be overcome to access the single primary document that contains the majority of information about Indigenous deaths during the KGR and beyond, says a lot about why these individuals have been forgotten. Not everyone has the privilege of being able to take a trip to Whitehorse, to an archive that has terrible hours, to physically view documents, and then the ability to copy the significant amount of information contained within those documents by hand. This can be attested to by the researcher who had initially been working on the Moosehide Cemetery project and did not have the time or resources to go to Whitehorse. 116

When it comes to physical burial spaces, First Nations then, as now, have their own ways of taking care of their dead. What appears to be a lack of maintained KGR-era burials could be directly tied to these cultural ways of understanding and approaching the dead, which have changed through time. Though I cannot say if this is the case here, spirit houses were purposefully left to deteriorate

They are not to be rebuilt, no matter how dilapidated. The tradition is to let them go back to the earth, along with the personal items placed within." 117 As mentioned, within the last few decades, communities have begun to make efforts to compile records of their ancestors and restore their traditional burial spaces. However, this very Eurocentric type of perpetual care of the dead can likely be attributed to acculturation, at least in part.

That said, there are several explanations for why I was less successful in locating KGR Indigenous burial spaces when compared with settler burial spaces. This is not simply a matter of the deterioration of burial markers. Firstly, the locations of Indigenous burial spaces are not for me to know. I am grateful for being given the opportunity to look for and explore them, but their specific locations remained undisclosed for a reason. The reason that I was able to survey Moosehide at all is that it was established as part of the Anglican parish and thus recorded in the record by the Anglican Church, and because the Trʼondëk Hwëchʼin are open about its existence. Another reason is environmental deterioration; as mentioned, the "Native" and Dyea Cemeteries, which both contained Indigenous burials, have both been washed out by the Taiya River. This fate may have also befallen the First Nations Cemetery in Forty Mile. Prior to going to Forty Mile, it was a concern of mine that at least two of the cemeteries for which I knew an approximate location, including the First Nations cemetery, might have been destroyed, given their proximity to the river. However, the First Nations cemetery in Forty Mile was described as being "on a high bank," which hopefully will have protected it. 118 We might have also just been looking for it in the wrong location, given the vague description of its location.

Thus, Indigenous deaths during the KGR remaining unrecorded or forgotten over time can likely be attributed to and summed up as a combination of historical racism, cultural practices, lack of accessibility to historical records and environmental degradation. Those who have been recorded and persistently remembered are so, in part, because of a renunciation of their culture, a level of notoriety based on their actions in life, or because they were able to “pass” as not Indigenous and, thus, were more readily accepted into and included within HGR society.

FAMILY & FRIENDS

For stampeders coming into the region, connection to family and friends, or lack of it, was important to their experience of the north. Some stampeders travelled to the north alone or with like-minded people they barely knew; others travelled with friends or family. In this data, we can see a trend where those who travelled with friends or family or even maintained a good connection with friends and family in the "outside world" received a different level of treatment in death.

I was fortunate in my research to come across a record from Lowe’s Mortuary in Dawson City, which was active during the KGR. This document was a book in which employees of Lowe’s tracked orders for funeral arrangements, including preparation of the body, style of casket/coffin, transportation to the cemetery, and even transportation out of the territory if required. Additionally, it recorded who ordered and paid for these services. Out of the minimal number of applicable entries recorded in Lowe’s Mortuary records (39), 6 of the individuals had their burial or burial preparations paid for by a person I identified as family; however, the actual number is likely much higher. Additionally, we have records of 110 individuals who were transported out for burial, some of whom were accompanied by a friend or family member to ensure they reached their destination safely—one individual even travelled all the way back to England! Typically, the friend or family member accompanying the deceased would have already been in the region, but in some cases, a family member would travel to the area to undertake the task. The number of individuals sent out for burial (12%) is astounding given how much it would have cost, which, thanks to the Lowe's Mortuary records, we can say, at least in some cases, was $360, quite a sum in the 1890s. Similarly, several individuals were initially buried in the north but were later disinterred and sent out for reburial. Of the 110 individuals known to have been shipped out for burial, 12 were reburials, and two are speculated to be reburials. To put this into perspective, in the Klondike during the KGR, a standard laborers’ salary, for miners, hoist operators, etcetera, was around $6 per day, and not much more than that for any except the highest-paid

[46]

professionals. Thus the costs of sending a body out of the Klondike for return “home” would have been three to six months’ salary. 119

Sometimes, friends and family would provide higher-quality memorials. In some casesthese were paid for to be placed on the grave in the north. Unmarked graves, or those with wooden markers, were sometimes later replaced with more permanent ones by friends and family. Finally, permanent memorial markers were at times placed in secondary locations, such as family plots in hometowns, in addition to original markers in the north. I have noted 70 individuals with stone markers in this study. Of those, 23 markers were placed on the graves of individuals buried in the north and the remaining 45 are located in cemeteries outside of the Klondike, where individuals had been transported out for burial, usually to their hometowns. Those receiving a stone marker outside of the Klondike are probably much more common than represented in this study, as graves of Klondikers outside the Yukon have not been the main focus of this study. Of the 23 recorded stone markers belonging to individuals buried in the north, we believe four were placed near the time of burial, 12 were placed at a later date, and seven have an unknown provenience. Additionally, we know that at least 10 of the 23 markers, regardless of when they were placed, were paid for and erected by friends, family members or an associated organization.

Beyond the physical treatment of the dead, family and friends have had a significant impact on the persistent memory of these individuals through the historical record. In general, a death was much more likely to be reported in Dawson if someone who knew the individual witnessed the death. You will often see in death/burial records of this time period a section where the informant of death is noted; sometimes, this will be a physician, but often, it is an acquaintance. From time to time, families would put out ads in the newspaper looking for information about family members who had gone missing or died in the north. When this occurs, it suggests that the missing individual did not already have a family member or friend with them; if they had, the accompanying individual would likely have written home. Similarly, the death of a family member in the north was sometimes reported in the family’s local paper, either by the family itself or the community, out of respect for the loss of a valued member. Let us also consider the impact of family beyond direct involvement with the treatment of the KGR dead. Historical record-keeping was also influenced by friends and family through publicly available genealogy sites. For the most

119 Porsild, Gamblers and Dreamers, 41,68,96,151,168,184-185; Gray, Gold Diggers, 18.

[47]

part, these sites work through continued research and input by family members, people invested in learning about and maintaining their family’s history. During this process, we were able to locate information on 318 of the deceased through one or more ancestry sites.

There are several ways that the involvement of family and friends, past and present, have impacted the remembrance of the KGR dead, beginning with those individuals shipped out for burial. Being shipped out for burial to more populated areas assists with an individual being perpetually remembered in that markers outside of the north at this time tended to be higher quality (not wood) and in locations/environments where they will deteriorate more slowly and have a higher likelihood of being taken care of on a more regular basis. Similarly, placing a higher quality marker in the north provides a much higher likelihood that it will persist in the harsh northern environment than the standard wooden marker, even if persistent care within the cemetery space is lacking.

Travelling with family or friends likely also increased the likelihood that those who died on the trails were taken for burial in nearby towns if the body could be recovered. However, this cannot easily be confirmed through our current data. Even in cases where burial had to occur at the location of death, we see evidence of great care being taken in the treatment of family members who had died on trail, as we can see in this excerpt from the journal of Amos Entheus Ball describing the burial of his friend Theodore's brother:

"We burned the frozen ground and dug a grave about three feet deep. With small round poles we built his coffin and lined it with moss, then rolled him in his blankets, placed him in and laid the top over with short sticks. Then we covered all with moss and placed the ground over his grave. I never saw a brother weep as Theodore did, and he wanted to turn back. He was a Frenchman and talked so broken, I could scarcely understand. "Don't weep, Theodore," I pleaded, "I'll be a brother to you the best I can." – Amos Entheus Ball 120

What we can also see from this quote is an example of a wilderness burial that has not been marked by wood or cairn. This burial, covered over by sticks, moss and dirt, almost certainly became indistinguishable from the surrounding area within a short time and lost forever.

120 Ball and Procter, Tenderfoot to Sourdough, 14.

[48]

Whether in the wilderness or in town, I believe that it can reasonably be assumed that if an individual had family and friends present, and those individuals had the means, the likelihood of a somewhat more elaborate treatment of the body, funeral and burial is much higher. Though we do not know how closely the benefactors are related to the dead, we can see several funeral/burial arrangements in the Lowe's Mortuary records that exceed 400 dollars.

The historical record is clearly biased. Unusual occurrences witnessed by large numbers of people or that required the coordination of many services were much more likely to be documented in some way; this included extravagant funerals/burials and the transportation of bodies. From the significant number of individuals recorded on genealogy sites, it is also clear that a familial connection has resulted in much better historical documentation and preservation. Genealogy sites are often connected to online cemetery databases, with interested parties contributing to both. In the same way, those interested in genealogy tend to be interested in ensuring their family history, including any associated gravesite, is maintained. In one case, in the Typhoid Cemetery, we can see a marker placed as recently as 2008 by a family member to replace one that had long since disappeared. This family member also donated to the Dawson City Museum and made a notation in the Typhoid Cemetery documents recording her contribution to the museum and the cemetery.

In general, having friends or family, an emotional bond, whether those people were present or far afield, meant you were much more likely to be cared for pre and post-burial, whether that be transportation, funeral arrangements, making others aware of your death or a lasting memorial. It also means there was a much greater likelihood of being persistently remembered with said memorial maintained.

SOCIAL ORGANIZATIONS

As discussed earlier, a big draw for joining fraternal organizations were the benefits afforded to members. As part of a life insurance plan taken out through the organization, assistance after death was often provided with the costs of burial and commemoration. An example of this may be seen with Irol Totten (Figure 8), buried in the 3rd Avenue Typhoid Cemetery in Dawson; the life insurance policy that he had taken out with the Woodsmen of the

[49]

World included a monument rider, which covered the cost of his grave marker, the only stone marker in the 3rd Avenue cemetery. 121 Depending on the organization, this arrangement of support may be much less formal, the YOOP is interesting in this regard as, even among fraternal orders. The first lodge of the YOOP was founded in Forty Mile in 1894 with the main purpose of the organization being mutual protection. The requirements to join were restrictive, to be considered for membership within the YOOP you had to a) be a male and b) to have been in the territory prior to 1882, requirements that really only applied to the original sourdoughs. As the population of the Yukon grew, more lodges opened up and the YOOP became a more formalized organization with more responsibilities toward their members. However, even today, you can only join if you are a male and have been in the territory for at least 20 years. These requirements would have significantly limited membership; in fact, of the 58 individuals we know to be associated with a fraternal order, only 12 are in the YOOP, and, interestingly, none of those individuals are associated with a second fraternity. Such limited membership within the YOOP would, naturally, mean limited funds being brought into the order by the membership, which would have impacted their ability to financially support those within (and outside) of the group who required it.

While going through the 1963 YOOP meeting minutes, I noticed a lot of discourse concerning the care of YOOP cemetery spaces and members after death, which supports the above argument. The first was regarding the payment of a bill sent to the lodge from Wark's Funeral Parlor for $200 to cover the cost of the funerals of two Pioneers. The YOOP decided not to pay this bill, and it was an ongoing issue throughout the year, with the owner of the funeral parlour threatening to sue and the YOOP continuing to ignore the payment request. 122 The second revolved around two discussions about whether wreaths should be supplied for each Pioneer burial. Early in 1963, it was decided by the YOOP that wreaths would, indeed, be supplied at each pioneer burial; however, later in the year, the topic was brought up again, and it was decided that the Lodge could not afford the expense. Interestingly, the secretary at the time of the meeting noted that the Lodge was at one time financially broken by the cost of funerals and that an attempt was made to start a burial fund with no success. He believed "the Lodge should have sufficient funds before committing themselves to any funeral outlay." 123 Beyond this, any discussions of the dead revolved around cemetery and marker upkeep. At the very least, the YOOP provided burial space for their dead and maintained distinctive headboards related to the order. Even those buried outside of the designated YOOP cemeteries, of which there are 5 individuals, are easily distinguishable as members of the order.

In the same way, members of military organizations such as the NWMP or Yukon Field Force, as today, would very likely have been given assistance in death, and both military organizations and fraternal organizations had their own elaborate funeral services that would be given to members of their organizations. These types of special treatment were not limited to just fraternal and military organizations; if an individual was part of a workers' union or other similar "brotherhood," such as a firefighter, they could expect to have some assistance or special service. This was also the case for those employed on claims; it was not uncommon for the owner of a claim to cover funeral and burial expenses for any individuals who died working under them. 124 There are many individuals whose records indicate they were given special ceremonies. Two in particular stand out in that they highlight just how extravagant these special services could be: the funerals of Harry G. Spencer and F. Henry Donnelly. Harry G. Spencer's funeral took place at the Pioneer Hall.

The dead man’s horse, with bridle draped in black and white, followed the sled led by Constable Lindbladt. The empty saddle with boots fastened in the stirrups, toes to the rear, told the story plainly to the bystanders.

A detachment of the Yukon field forces of the Canadian military followed behind the horse in double column, 30 strong. Colonel Steele and Captain Harper, Starnes and Scurth, of the N.W.M.P., and Captain Burstall of the military, brought up the rear.

The impressive ceremony of bugling and volley firing over the grave was the last respect the boys could show their dead comrade, and the silent procession then wended its way to the barracks.” 126
