Unlike fraternal or military organizations, religious organizations did not necessarily assist with funerals or burials beyond services. However, as discussed before, we know that the Catholic church did not record those buried in unconsecrated ground, and we also know that those who were not part of the church, who were unbaptized, committed suicide, or were murderers, were not allowed burial in consecrated ground. However, all three types of organizations tended to have their own cemeteries or sections within larger cemeteries. As outlined in the overview of cemeteries I surveyed, the YOOP, Catholic Church and NWMP had their own cemeteries. Jewish individuals, Masons, Elks, and other fraternal organizations had designated sections within the Old Public Hillside Cemetery. There is also a Masonic Cemetery at Windy Arm and a Yukon Field Force section of the cemetery at Fort Selkirk. According to the database, 61 individuals were buried or commemorated in their associated organizations' cemeteries. We see seven individuals buried and two commemorated in the YOOP 8th Avenue Cemetery, seven individuals buried in the Police Cemetery, four individuals buried in the Yukon Field Force Cemetery, one individual commemorated in Bet Chaim, one individual buried in the Windy Arm Masonic Cemetery, and 38 individuals were buried in the Catholic cemetery or in the case of Father Judge, in the church.

Another similarity between these types of organizations is that they have a specific, uniform style of grave marker afforded to most members. For those buried in the Catholic Cemetery, it was a cross; for those in the NWMP cemetery, it became cathedral window style headboards with name and rank; and for the fraternal organizations, typically a shape specific to that individual organization but, even if not a specific shape, almost always with the organization's symbol included. That said, it is unclear if this was the case initially. Many of the original markers in the Catholic cemetery remain and confirm that, indeed, most were likely crosses. However, contemporary photos of the Police Cemetery and the remains of original YOOP markers suggest that they were much less standardized than the ones they were replaced with later.

Which brings us to perpetual care; there is evidence that all of these organization-associated spaces have seen continued care since the KGR, though in varying degrees. In Dawson City, many cemeteries fall into a grey area where they are the responsibility of whoever wants to take responsibility for them. Indeed, those associated with the KGR have some heritage protections.

[53]

However, heritage funding in the Yukon is stretched thin, particularly when maintaining KGR-era properties, given the significant area impacted by the event and the sheer quantity of artifacts and features left behind. As mentioned in the beginning, based on religious beliefs, there is a certain amount of moral obligation felt or expected by members of certain organizations toward the care of the dead. In the case of fraternal and government organizations, the obligation is often part and parcel of the organization's duties, and by becoming a member of such an organization, you are agreeing to such duties.

Police Cemetery (Dawson City, Yukon) 127

The Police Cemetery is located in a cordoned-off section of the Hillside Old Public Cemetery. The first recorded burials in the Police Cemetery occurred in 1898, with the last in 2001. Though there were diligently kept records relating to the cemetery and where individuals were buried within, the cemetery was somewhat neglected until the mid-1960s. In 1964 RCMP officer Frank Dunn, with the help of a prisoner named Henry, took charge of refurbishing the cemetery. At this time, the entrance sign and gate were placed, all headboards in the cemetery were replaced and made uniform, and white wooden cribbing filled with white gravel was placed in front of each grave. 128 Since then, the cemetery has been well-maintained, with a rededication ceremony in 2002, complete with 50 officers from across Canada, a memorial service and a regimental ball. 129

In the case of KGR-associated cemeteries, the NWMP cemetery is undoubtedly the most diligently cared for. A chain fence surround and arch at the entryway clearly delineates the space. The burials are in organized rows, in an approximately southeast-northwest direction, each topped with wooden cribbing filled with crushed stone. Not all of the grave markers in this cemetery are the same, as one might expect of a police or military cemetery; three, for individuals outside of the range of this study, are stone, while the rest are wooden markers that have been replaced and standardized at some point in time. Not all individuals buried within the cemetery now were placed there upon their death; records show that at least one individual who had been buried

St. Mary's Catholic Cemetery (Dawson City, Yukon)

In 1898, Father Gedreau requested land from Commissioner Ogilvie to be used for a parish cemetery. Despite the request not having been granted and the cemetery not officially established until mid-1899, the first burials in St. Mary's Cemetery still occurred in 1898. 131 The cemetery appears to have been relatively maintained until the 1940s and probably until it reached capacity in 1959. However, in 1998, when Ed and Star Jones began mapping, documenting and researching this cemetery, it was overgrown, and many of the original markers had fallen. 132

The Catholic cemetery is a sprawling space delineated by a white picket fence with a small sign just inside the entrance. Though all of the oldest and missing markers have been replaced at some point by white crosses and the old markers handily left behind the new as seen in figure 9, while I was there, I was dismayed at the lack of maintenance of the cemetery space. The grasses and weeds were above my head, and I struggled to get from one grave to the next to document what I was seeing. Overall, the replacement markers were still in relatively good condition; however, a few were beginning to lose paint, and if the cemetery is continuously left to grow wild as it was, the markers will begin to degrade more quickly, particularly what remains of the originals.

For the most part, the cemetery is organized in the standard fashion of neat rows with 12 graves per row, all facing the direction of the cemetery northeast-southwest. The cemetery appears to have been narrower in the beginning and expanded shortly after the turn of the century. Each of the first several rows has burials from 1896-1899 for about the first quarter of the row, and burials dating from 1900 onward make up the remainder. Unusually, at the left side of each row, up against the fence, are markers placed northwest-southeast; it is difficult to say if this was the

Yukon Order of Pioneers 8th Avenue Cemetery (Dawson City, Yukon)

The Yukon Order of Pioneers Cemetery is located on 8th Avenue in Dawson City. The older of two YOOP cemeteries in Dawson City, the land for the cemetery was purchased by the Pioneers in 1896, and the first recorded burial occurred in 1897. In 1898, the Pioneers paid to have the cemetery cleared of brush and to have a fence surround constructed. In 1924, the cemetery nearly reached capacity but was expanded through the purchase of adjacent land. Despite these efforts, the cemetery reached capacity only a decade later. In the 1970s, the entrance arch was replaced, and several headboards were taken to the Pioneer Lodge to be re-lettered. A series of circumstances led to those headboards being stored in the shed of a Pioneer until 1999, when they were rediscovered, re-lettered and returned during cemetery upgrades. In 2001, a shelter was built at the entrance just inside the fence by a high school shop class, and the following year, the wooden entry arch was replaced with one of steel, produced by a machine shop operator named Hank Behrends. 133

The YOOP cemetery is somewhat odd in that, like the Typhoid Cemetery, it is located directly next to residences in Dawson City proper rather than up on the hillside with the rest of Dawson’s cemeteries. The YOOP cemetery is bordered by a white picket fence with a large metal arch at the entrance. Directly inside and up a handful of steps is a small shelter containing laminated notes about those buried within the cemetery. All of the graves are in an east-west orientation, and there seemed to have been an attempt made to organize the burials into rows; however, owing to the landscape and shape of the cemetery, things ended up a little misaligned from right to left with the occasional single grave placed in seemingly random locations. While there was some overgrowth, it was clear that the cemetery had likely seen some clearing earlier in the summer; in addition, there was written and physical evidence of markers being replaced over time. Unfortunately, about 30% of the markers remained either completely illegible or displaced from their original position/context and lying on the ground, and even the fence surround was beginning to collapse in places.

Bet Chaim Jewish Cemetery (Dawson City, Yukon)

Though there is some confusion as to when the Bet Chaim Cemetery was officially established, a request was made by the Baron de Hirsch congregation for land in 1902 that was not revisited until 1913. Despite this later date, it is believed that the first burial occurred in the Bet Chaim Cemetery in 1902, prior to the formal designation of the land for use. 134 It is undetermined who is buried in this location, with only one physical marker remaining or potentially ever erected. Despite this, a plaque was created, including the names of all the Jewish individuals who had died and been buried outside of Bet Chaim prior to this time, as well as those who had, theoretically, been buried there afterwards. Before Bet Chaim, the Jewish population was buried in a section of the Old Hillside Cemetery in a designated section, which, interestingly, does not seem as if it was fenced or otherwise contained as is typical of Jewish cemeteries. 135 At the very least, I have seen no reference to such a feature, and certainly no remnant of one remains in Hillside Cemetery now.

In 1998, after some challenges locating the cemetery again, a significant refurbishment of the cemetery took place in which a new fence surround and entry arch were installed, the old plaque remounted, and a new brass plaque with a more accurate list of Jewish individuals buried within and outside the cemetery was placed. 136

Surprisingly, given that Dawson City does not have a Jewish congregation to care for it, besides the police cemetery, the Jewish cemetery appeared to be in the best shape. That said, the cemetery seems to see relatively consistent care from a small but dedicated group of individuals. The entire cemetery was restored and re-fenced in 1998 by the Jewish Historical Society of the Yukon, which had formed upon the rediscovery of the cemetery in 1997. 137 Moreover, the day I left Dawson City, I was informed that a small team of individuals would be heading up to Dawson from Whitehorse the next week to perform maintenance on the space. One cannot deny that there is certainly a connection between social organizations and being persistently remembered after death. The segregation of specific cemetery spaces, financial assistance, and level of care given to funeral, burial, commemoration and persistent care all contribute to an individual's history and memory traversing time. As noted before, while discussing the impact of family and friends, the quality of a marker and funeral that an individual is given can play an important role in remembrance. Not only did the markers of these individuals see perpetual care, but, as with Irol Totten, some were provided with durable stone markers inside and outside the north. William Cornell Ostrander is an example of an individual who was shipped out, and his stone monument paid for by the Woodsmen of the World in his home cemetery in Portland, Oregon. In a very short time, given what I have seen and if something is not done, Irol Totten's marker may be the only visible remnant remaining in the Typhoid Cemetery. When we consider the elaborate funerals bestowed on many of these individuals by organizations with their own complex funerary practices, we can see, given the spectacle, how these events are more likely to be recorded in historical text, as might be seen with the funerals of Spencer and Donnelly.

Given the nature of the military being a governmental branch, and the way they are viewed and largely respected in this country, those who have died will never be forgotten. The records and cemeteries for these deaths and individuals will always remain pristine, barring extreme circumstances. [59]

Despite all the good they do for their dead, fraternal organizations clearly face some challenges. While certain records about fraternal organizations are almost certainly rigorously maintained, as I witnessed with the meeting minutes, there would be some variance in the quality of other records across organizations, such as membership and associated deaths. Additionally, as seen within those meeting minutes, smaller organizations in more remote areas clearly struggled to fund post-death care for their members. Again, this would have varied from organization to organization, with older, more prominent and well-established fraternities like the Masons and Woodsmen undoubtedly being better funded and their modus operandi well-established.

When considering perpetual care, being part of a religious organization affords many of the same benefits as fraternal or military organizations. However, when we begin to explore burial, commemoration and record keeping, the role that religious organizations play is somewhat more complicated. The Catholic Church was the overseeing organization for the original hospital in Dawson City, St. Mary’s. I believe that St. Mary’s would not have made distinctions about the religion of the individuals they were treating and would have, theoretically, recorded all deaths that took place within the hospital records. However, despite not making distinctions in terms of care, the Catholic Church did not allow specific individuals to be buried within consecrated ground, and those buried in unconsecrated ground by the Catholic Church were not recorded within the church burial records. Unlike Catholic individuals, Protestant individuals did not have a specific burial location. Though I cannot speak to the Anglican view of murders and how they should be treated in death, the Anglican records include several individuals who were tried for murder and executed. Still, the records omit that they were murderers who had been executed, and, as noted in the section on Indigeneity, if you were an Indigenous individual and you were not a member of the Church of England, you likely were not receiving Anglican burial services or being included in their records; the same can be implied for the Catholic church. All that to say that, sadly, some religious organizations play a role in specific individuals being remembered and others being forgotten.

[60]

OTHER INFLUENCING FACTORS

Alongside the above social variables, four others appear to have impacted remembrance in death, though more discreetly. These are gender, age, notoriety and social currency/affluence.

Age/Sex

Within the dataset, we see 60 individuals that are 18 or younger. Of these, 37 are between the ages of one and 18, half of which have an unknown cause of death. Additionally, there are 22 children under the age of one, with 11 referred to merely as "infant," and 16 with cause of death listed as unknown. It is not uncommon for some children in official records not to have a name or their first and/or last name recorded. Several are referred to as "infant" or "baby," followed by the surname of the parents. In the case of children under one, there are eight with no known first name, three with no known last name and one with no known first or last name. Because cause of death is so often unrecorded among children, none of the causes of death that are recorded present particularly high numbers; however, in the under one category, of the six infants we know cause of death for, four are directly related to childbirth and complications in early development. In terms of sex, of those 59 individuals 18 or younger, 39 are male, four are unknown, and 16 are

[61]

female. Interestingly, the number of male (11) vs. female (9) infants under the age of one is quite close, considering there are more than double the number of males that died than females in the 1-18 bracket.

When comparing all known males and females of all age groups, of the 86 known females, 13 (15.12%) have no known first name, with 3 being infants and 8 referred to purely by marital status in lieu of a first name. Additionally, the cause of death for 37 of the 86 known females is unknown; however, where the cause of death is known, murder and typhoid fever tie for most prevalent, with 6 instances each. In comparison, of the 761 known males, 16 (2%) have no known first name, and five of those are infants or children. The cause of death for 234 of the known males is unknown, 31% verses 43% among females. In terms of burial location, there are only 12 females with no known burial location, half of which are individuals with no known first name. This is a much lower number at 14% than among the males where 151, or 19.8%, have an unknown location of burial.

Without a doubt, the women most frequently discussed and celebrated when it comes to the KGR are the dance hall girls, sex workers and entrepreneurs. There are even a few instances of dance hall girls/sex workers getting very fine and widely attended funerals despite their relative lack of influence/respectability within the broader society. 138 Is this because they are women, and it is tragic when a woman dies in a community where there are so few – or is this because of their paramours, the male following they have amassed in the course of their profession? Or, could it be a third option, could it be the case that these women are actually very well respected in society because of the invaluable services that they offer - and it's merely the derision seen by Superintendent Steele and his efforts to bring prostitution under control that makes them appear to be less respected by broader society?

Notoriety/Social Currency/Affluence

The cost of living in Dawson City during the KGR was significantly higher than other more established and accessible towns or cities of the time. Where a household of five in Toronto could get by on $38 a month, just to rent a property in Dawson could cost as much as $125 a month. 139

138 Funeral Records Ledger, 1898-1905, Uncatalogued, Dawson City Museum, Dawson City, YT. 
139 Porsild, Gamblers and Dreamers, 96. 

[62]

Highet states, “The cost of living in the Klondike was high, forcing many to sell off the year's supply of food, tools and other essentials contained in the outfit that they had been required to carry along with them on their journey to the goldfields in order to make ends meet or procure enough money for the return passage.” 140 That being the case, having money did not necessarily afford you a more opulent funeral, a better grave marker, or a trip home. In some instances, particularly toward the beginning of the KGR, when resources were especially scarce, individuals capitalized on that scarcity, and the cost of even the most basic burial shot sky-high. The reason being, of course, location and environment. As noted earlier, once the rivers froze up, nothing was getting in or out of Dawson. This, of course, led to food scarcity, which led to death, disease and the NWMP’s rules about supplies, but it also meant that whatever supplies were brought in throughout the summer and any specialized goods or services that people could offer became subject to price gouging in the winter through necessity and competition. That said, goods and services were not necessarily a whole lot cheaper in the summer months; even if the rivers were not frozen and there was open access to Dawson, it was still a remote area that required a lot of time, effort and risk to bring supplies to. Particularly at this point in time when the railroad had yet to be completed:

"Two men died on Clarence Berry's claim that winter, and the price of their funeral was astronomical. It cost two thousand dollars to hire a team of six malemutes to take the bodies into town. The nails for the coffins cost eight dollars and fifty cents a pound and the lumber forty cents a foot. Two workmen took six days to hack the graves out of the frozen ground and were paid two hundred dollars in wages." 141

Regarding notoriety and social capital, at least three individuals were so well respected or notorious within their respective societies that their deaths and funerals were heavily reported on at the time. They will inevitably appear in almost every text you read regarding the history of the KGR. These three individuals are Frank Reid, Jefferson "Soapy" Smith, and Father William Judge. Father Judge, “The Saint of Dawson,” was and still is praised for his love and devotion to the community of Dawson City. Buried under the gospel side of the altar in St. Mary’s, his funeral saw massive attendance, some sources saying the entirety of Dawson, and “two years after his

Whether it is accurate or not, Frank Reid was praised as the saviour of Skagway for the vigilante justice he served Jefferson Smith. Like Father Judge, Reid's funeral saw significant attendance, and he was given a large stone obelisk surrounded by a stone wall that still has pride of place in Skagway's Gold Rush Cemetery. 143 Smith's grave marker is less noticeable, off to the side and wooden like most of the rest and has seen at least five variations over time due to vandalism and other factors. 144 Still, Smith's family and the town of Skagway have kept the memory of this colourful con artist and gangster alive. For a long time, from 1974 until the late 80s or early 90s, the family would visit his grave annually, have a party with champagne, and piss on the grave of Frank Reid. Eventually, this tradition was deemed inappropriate and was put to a stop. 145

One can also see the effects of poverty, with the burden of care for those considered indigent falling to the authorities. There are at least two examples in the Lowe's Mortuary records of individuals given the most basic pauper burials at a cost of $60 or less, to support this. That said, though it cannot be picked out from the data I currently have, indigents must have been a notable issue within the north, considering Superintendent Steele tried to introduce a law barring all indigents (individuals not prepared to support themselves) from entering the territory. 146 We can only speculate how many friendless paupers went unaccounted for.

As with notable people, it can be seen within the data that if the cause of one's death is particularly unusual or sensational, it is more likely to be recorded and remembered. This, of course, applies to individuals like Frank Reid and Jefferson Smith, but it also applies to situations like suicide, murder, and the ever-discussed Palm Sunday Avalanche, which was reported in at least 13 different newspapers at the time. On the other hand, deaths due to typhoid fever were so common as to cause little comment.

The Palm Sunday Avalanche plays an interesting part in this discussion because, though it was widely reported and has been continuously discussed within the mythology of the KGR, we have very little understanding of exactly how many people died and who they were. Any newspapers writing about the event relayed lists of names of the dead, but these were names collected

Slide Cemetery (Dyea, Alaska)

The Slide Cemetery is located at the north end of what was once the town of Dyea, Alaska, now no more than a ghost town. Colonel Thomas M. Anderson established this cemetery to accommodate the victims of the Palm Sunday Avalanche that occurred on April 3rd, 1898. 149

Though this cemetery houses a handful of individuals not associated with this event, there are no known burials in this cemetery after 1898. Unfortunately, the way that we see women and children being overlooked in the historical record, here and elsewhere, is very much a product of the times. Where women are discussed at least some of the time, sometimes in a very positive and complimentary light when compared with men, it has been only once or twice that I have seen children discussed in contemporary literature about the KGR. Part of the reason for this, at least in terms of official documentation, is that, as mentioned earlier, children, like Indigenous people, were sometimes not issued death certificates. Furthermore, for women, their exclusion from fraternal orders meant that they did not necessarily see the level of attention or care in death afforded to many men associated with these organizations beyond the potential for a widower's pension.

As for the rippling effects of affluence and notoriety, situations and people like those discussed above are far more likely to be recorded in death records, newspapers, history books, and stone. Those who commit murder share an unusual middle ground with those who died in the Palm Sunday Avalanche. The circumstances surrounding both were widely reported at the time; however, the way that murder is viewed culturally means that while the act itself is widely

[69]

discussed, the funeral and burial arrangements of those executed for murder is far less so. For the Palm Sunday Avalanche, it was the panic surrounding the situation and the potential interference of Jefferson Smith and his gang that have left this event as, all at once, the most widely reported event in the KGR, but also one with immense uncertainty regarding the number and names of those who died in the event.

CAUSE OF DEATH & ENVIRONMENTAL CHALLENGES

Within the KGR, when we combine the most commonly seen causes of death with the environment and the conditions stampeders often faced, we end up with a unique and interesting set of circumstances. These circumstances create challenges that had the potential to, and often did, impact burial and commemoration across all demographics and social groupings.

The most common causes of death seen in the KGR (see table one below) database are typhoid fever (137), avalanche (89), drowning (84), pneumonia (46), and industrial/domestic accidents (46); all of which can be attributed in some way to the environment and circumstances these individuals found themselves in. As discussed earlier, the KGR was a fast-paced and transient phenomenon; it was over almost as soon as it began, and the routes the stampeders used were

Figure 13: A map showing the location of the Gold Rush Cemetery, 2025, Nicole Simon

[70]

often fraught with danger. These conditions, combined with a lack of experience, understanding and preparedness, can explain most of these conditions.

Tuberculosis, typhoid fever and cerebrospinal meningitis are all conditions that can be more rapidly spread through and are associated with unclean living conditions and close contact within these spaces. The KGR led to a significant population boom in both Skagway and Dawson City, and those living in Dawson were essentially living in their own filth. The tents and cabins in which people lived were small and not particularly watertight, and there was not an adequate disposal system for garbage and human waste, with most being tossed right outside one's front door or into the rivers. While the rivers did provide a working means of disposal if adequately utilized, most did not place their waste far enough into the current. So it sat freezing, thawing and rotting on the banks, contaminating the river water and groundwater. 155 Even when garbage was “properly” disposed of, it would then be carried downriver to pollute Moosehide and its inhabitants, aiding the spread of disease among the community. 156 Beyond this, it is noted that the men did not have much regard for their hygiene in general, being obsessed with their search for gold. 157 Though the small cabins that the miners lived in were not watertight, they were mostly airtight and often had no windows, as glass was an expensive commodity. Two, three and four men often shared these small cabins, and the cabins and tents were crowded together in limited space. Confined spaces and limited ventilation meant that contagious diseases such as typhoid and tuberculosis spread quickly among the population, when combined with the yearly flooding that Dawson City faced, these were not ideal living conditions to avoid disease. 158

Drowning, avalanche and the types of accidents seen in the database, primarily asphyxiation and trauma, are modes of death directly related to the environments the stampeders were travelling and working within. Most routes included some form of water transportation, often on rough waters and with handmade watercraft. Death, or the risk of death on the water was so significant that in 1898 the NWMP started to require that all individuals leaving Bennett register their watercraft. 159 When traversing the Chilkoot or White Passes, the avalanche risk was ever-present, particularly in the spring when the ground and snowpack were beginning to thaw. Though recorded avalanches during this time are few, the ones that did occur claimed many lives, with the Palm Sunday Avalanche of 1898 taking an undetermined number of souls, estimated to be between 60 and 90, and making up the majority of the individuals that died from avalanche (Figure 14) in this study at 80 individuals. 160 Most accidents occurred after the stampeders reached their final destination, with 26 being work-related and 21 specifically mining-related. Placer mining posed the most risk when tunnelling occurred; individuals often operated in tight quarters without ventilation, and while the risk of a cave-in was less because of the permafrost, it was not zero, especially when the miners employed methods to defrost the ground and make digging easier. 161 That said, half of the individuals who died in work-related accidents died in the mine shafts, either smothered by dirt, overcome by gas or after a fall leading to catastrophic injury.

Scurvy, exposure and pneumonia are, for the most part, examples of death caused by a lack of understanding and preparedness on the part of the stampeders, many of whom did not know anything about the north before beginning their journey and, therefore, did not know how long it would take or what they would need to survive. Most modes of transportation relied on the rivers, so when winter set in there was no way to get supplies into the north; there are many news articles from the winters of 1897 and 1898 that speak of the challenges faced by those in Dawson, and particularly the potential for starvation, without ready access to supplies. As noted earlier, many of these individuals were giving up the entirety of their savings to purchase their kit in hopes of striking it rich or, at the very least, starting a new life in some form. It was difficult for those who had risked everything and left their lives behind to arrive in Dawson and not find the success they had dreamed of. The murders recorded here occurred primarily within communities. Of the 36 murders we are aware of, 23 took place in populated areas, with 21 murders in Alaska and 14 in the Yukon, overall. Several sources of the time suggest that Skagway was a particularly lawless town and that Dawson City, in comparison, was a much safer place to be, particularly when Major Sam Steele arrived. 163 Whether this is the truth or Canadian propaganda, in February of 1898, Steele did write to Ottawa to inquire about the possibility of enforcing a restriction on the importation of firearms into the Yukon, and the NWMP strictly maintained order at the summits of the Chilkoot and White Passes, ensuring that no unsavory or unprepared individuals were entering Canada. 164 Though this did not entirely prevent murder from happening on the Canadian side, it does appear to have made it somewhat safer, particularly given the disparity in population size, with 8,000 – 10,000 in Skagway, and approximately 30,000 in Dawson and the surrounding area in 1898. 165

Beyond being a contributor to the most common causes of death seen during the KGR, the environment produced several difficulties when it came to the burial and commemoration of the dead. In the Klondike, elaborate commemoration with marble and granite was often impossible because of the limited transportation. The standard KGR grave marker was made of wood in the shape of a cross or half-round with simple inscriptions in black. Sometimes, a fence would be constructed surrounding the grave; whether this would have been for decorative purposes or to keep wild animals from disturbing the burial depends on location. 169 Aside from the transportation of materials, there was the movement of the bodies themselves. When deaths occurred on the trails, there were two options: bury them where they lay, or transport the body off trail to the nearest town where they would be buried or shipped out. Often, as is the case with up to 48 of the 84 drowning victims, the body could not be recovered for burial at all. The only actual methods for transporting the dead off-trail would have been dogsled or sledge. Indeed, there are written accounts of bodies transported off the trails in this manner:

"[Gene Allen] found a throb of pity gripping at his heart as he watched the dog-drawn sleds come mournfully back down the trail, bearing their shrouded burdens, frozen stiff in the bitter Northern winter temperature." 170

However, there were some routes where dog sleds were inaccessible or where the closest town could be days away and, in cases like these, or with rockslides and other similar circumstances; it was more prudent to bury the dead en route rather than worrying about how to transport a body alongside the hundreds of pounds of supplies one would be transporting. When it comes to commemoration in these cases, with so many other things to worry about, the main goal would have been to ensure the body was buried as best it could, which provided challenges of its own. A burial had to be deep enough to try and deter a wild animal from digging up the remains; however, the nature of the landscape is that the ground is frozen by permafrost not far below the surface. Sometimes, in a weakened state and with limited time, all that one could manage was a

Often, because of the struggle presented just by burying the bodies, these wilderness graves would not have been marked or, because of the nature of wooden markers, any marker would have quickly disappeared. However, some accounts, particularly from those travelling the All Canadian or Glacier routes, noted how stampeders were left so despondent by the challenges they had faced that they no longer cared for much else beyond themselves.

"Since the accident of several days before when my brother-in-law lost his life, a great change had come over the men. The first laws of nature, "self preservation," began to assert itself. We were so weary in body and mind that we were not responsible for our actions; we had very little feeling left. The humanity that was in us ebbing away and nothing was left but the animal. Each man was a world in himself and a very narrow world at that." – Arthur Dietz 173

Out of the 955 individuals in the database, 280 are known to be wilderness deaths, not including the 30 individuals that died on mining claims. Of those 280, 158 were transported from their location of death for burial. However, in this case, we must remember that 77 of those were victims of the Palm Sunday Avalanche. As can be seen in table 2 above, there are 199 individuals with no known location of burial, and 89 of those, nearly 45%, are individuals who died in the wilderness. In contrast, only 72 of the 459 who we know died in a populated area have no known burial location. In general, wilderness graves are more prone to being unknown, unrecorded and, eventually, lost; still, all of the factors discussed above can significantly impact the socio-cultural aspects of how the dead are treated and remembered, which I explore below.

3rd Avenue Typhoid Cemetery (Dawson City, Yukon)

The 3rd Avenue Typhoid Cemetery is located on a steep, forested hillside just off 3rd Avenue in Dawson City. Originally called Prospect Hill, after outbreaks of typhoid in the summers of 1897 and 1898, it received its current moniker. The Typhoid Cemetery was the first cemetery in Dawson City, with burials dating to 1897; however, the cemetery rapidly filled and was not used after 1899. 175 In 1912, while undertaking roadwork on 3rd Avenue, several burials were rediscovered, exhumed and reinterred further back within the cemetery. The cemetery was also cleaned during this process, and the fence surrounds were replaced. Despite several cleanup efforts since then, the cemetery has largely been abandoned to neglect. 176

The Typhoid Cemetery has a location right on Google Maps, so one might think it would be easy to locate; unfortunately, the given location is incorrect. In my search, I eventually resorted to knocking on doors and asking neighbours if they knew where it might be. Even then, the cemetery is so overgrown and concealed that an individual living less than 30 meters away did not even know there was a cemetery there. Once there, I was dismayed by the state of the cemetery. It was hard to tell, but my impression was that the cemetery had not been laid out in any typical fashion. What burials remained visible wound their way up a steep hillside with only a little spread to the left or right. That said, this is based on what graves are remaining; there are certainly graves that have long since disappeared, and the extent of the cemetery is likely much more significant than I could observe. My database accounts for as many as 133 individuals buried in this cemetery, more than any other cemetery I visited. However, the remains of only 20 or so burials are visible today.

When going through the records for Baptemes, Mariages, Sepultures de Ste-Marie de Dawson City, we did notice one individual who was recorded as placed “dans le charnier;” however,

Bennett Lake Cemetery (Bennett Lake, British Columbia)

As seen in Figure 15, Bennett Lake is located approximately 1 km along the Chilkoot Trail from its trailhead in Bennett, BC. Little is known about the history of this cemetery, though the earliest burials appear to have occurred in 1898, and interments did not continue after 1899. From 2006-2008 as part of the Parks Canada Yukon Field Unit, Michael Gates put together a management plan and headed a major restoration project of both the Bennett Lake and Lake Lindeman Cemeteries. This project consisted of "placing new fences around the graves, removing the encroaching vegetation, replacing some badly decayed wooden markers, and preserving the originals for future reference." 178

Unfortunately, I did not have as much time in Bennett Lake Cemetery as I would have liked. The cemetery is not located on Google Maps, and I had not found any good descriptions about where it was located prior to reaching Bennett. Luckily for me, one of the White Pass & Yukon Train employees had visited the cemetery before and could point me in the proper direction.

The Bennett Lake Cemetery is located just off the Chilkoot Trail in a nicely elevated position with lovely mountain views. There is no fence bounding the cemetery, and the only vegetation is the trees surrounding the hill; the cemetery is sandy and dry, which is a benefit to preservation. There are only two rows of graves and, in an odd juxtaposition, most of what remains are old wooden surrounds in various stages of degradation with no indication remaining of who might have been there and three nearly pristine stone markers. There are so many stone markers in such a small cemetery because, during the restoration project, the Masons and the McCue family were consulted regarding the new markers that would be placed. Aside from the stone markers, five other wooden markers remain at this location, though only three are still legible. Though the first recorded burials took place in 1898, after the 3rd Avenue Cemetery had reached capacity, the cemetery was not formally established

It was hard to know precisely where this cemetery began and ended. Hillside Old Public Cemetery is an absolutely sprawling and completely unmaintained space that takes up the entirety of the southwest side of the Dawson City cemetery complex. Most of the space was bounded by trees except for an opening on the south corner of the cemetery, which led to the oldest burials. The condition of this cemetery was appalling; once again, the vegetation was well over my head in spots and made it difficult to navigate; there were collapsed markers of all materials, trees growing out from the middle of grave surrounds, obvious unmarked graves and dozens of entirely illegible markers. From what I could tell, the more recent burials had been organized in rows, with the graves approximately oriented east-west. I could also perceive sections set aside for children and for the Order of Elks. The oldest part of the cemetery was located virtually on the hillside; when they said, "extending down the hill as far as it can be utilized," I believe they did just that. When I read the Joneses' notes on this cemetery, they speculated that many of the hillside burials had eroded out with time, and I would have to agree with that assessment. At the very least, from the photograph I had found in Yukon Archives, I could tell that the two Nantuck brothers had been buried on this hillside just behind Robert Colquhoun and, while I was able to locate Colquhoun's, which had, somewhere along the line, been given a stone marker and wooden surround, the Nantuck brothers were nowhere to be seen. Beyond graved likely having deteriorated out of the hillside, I believe the cemetery likely encompasses a larger area than has currently been "cleared."

In general, Forty Mile is a difficult location to navigate. Formerly a campsite and tourist spot, in 2023, ice jams upriver broke and flooded the townsite, moving entire buildings with the force. Since then, the area has been closed to visitors as cleanup and restructuring occur. Knowing this and the proximity of at least two of the cemeteries to the river, as mentioned above, I had concerns before going to Forty Mile that the cemeteries did not survive the flood. While I cannot comment on the state of the First Nations cemetery across the river, I did manage to navigate to the historic cemetery.

I cannot speak to the ease of access the cemetery might have enjoyed before the flooding; however, it’s clear to see in Figure 16 just how remote this cemetery is. Today access is hindered by overgrown trails with sections of standing water and thick mud. Beyond this, once pointed in the right direction, locating the actual cemetery was not as difficult as I would have expected. The cemetery, marked only by a simple sign leaning up against the base of a tree, is in a somewhat elevated space some distance from the townsite. Given the number of fence surrounds still upright and that most things appeared to be in their proper locations, it happily seemed to have escaped the forceful flood that ravaged the rest of Forty Mile.

While it appeared that there had been some maintenance to the cemetery by clearing the brush, many of the markers and surrounds were in poor condition. There were 36 burials still identifiable by the presence of marker, fence, or the remains of either. That said, of those 36 burials, only six markers had even partially legible inscriptions, and only about half of the burial spaces were intact, with an upright fence and marker. Within the cemetery, the graves were oriented in approximate rows in the standard east-west manner; however, unusually, between rows, the burials alternated from a head-to-head and foot-to-foot placement. Given the organization style, the space between some burials and the visible sinking, I believe there were once 13-17 more burials than are currently recognizable.

181 Forty Mile, Uncatalogued, Dawson City Museum.

[83]

What all of these cemeteries share is that, due to a combination of the environment, their (sometimes quite remote) locations and lack of association with any one organization, they have been much more subject to unchecked degradation and loss over time. Indeed, in Hillside Cemetery, Typhoid Cemetery and Bennett Lake Cemetery, without intervention in the next decade, the only markers that will still be standing are the stone ones that were placed by family and organizations.

Given the number of individuals with no known cause of death and location of burial (89) and those with no known location of death and burial (35), I would suggest a strong relationship between cause/location of death and remembrance post-mortem. Playing off the common causes of death and environmental challenges explored above, I have a few suggestions about who the majority of the missing/unknown dead might be. To restate, the most common causes of death seen are typhoid fever, avalanche, drowning, pneumonia, and accidents. To begin, let us once again consider that, of the 93 drowning victims, 62 were either not knowingly recovered or have no known burial location. That is not to say that they have/had no burial location or that they were never recovered. Indeed, there were many circumstances during the KGR where individuals were recovered months after their deaths and never identified; I have read examples of both drowned individuals recovered downstream, and individuals who died in the Palm Sunday

Figure 16: Map showing the location of Forty Mile Historic Cemetery, 2025, Nicole Simon.

[84]

Avalanche but were never found until the snow thawed. 182 Though likely hyperbole, I have also read an account of crosses lining the riverbank. 183 Still, as discussed, there are many examples of burials, even whole cemeteries, as in the case of Dyea Cemetery, that have been completely erased by the meandering Yukon rivers and the ever-changing northern environment.Moreover, other deaths, including, again, those in the Dyea Cemetery, were never properly recorded. Included in this category are individuals who committed suicide and were not allowed to be buried in consecrated ground. In Dawson City, the churches did not keep a record of those buried in unconsecrated ground, and, in this database, eight of the individuals known to have committed suicide have no known burial location.

Similarly, given the fear of communicable disease, those who died from such afflictions were often buried in a separate, more convenient location, as appears to be the case here with the Typhoid cemetery. Generally, these deaths and burials would happen so quickly that there would not be time for proper record-keeping or commemoration. Though not the same type of death, the same can be seen in the case of the Palm Sunday Avalanche victims and the Slide Cemetery; so many people died and were buried so rapidly that there was no proper effort made to correctly identify or record the dead.

Other undocumented deaths might include murders. Given the number of recorded murders that took place in towns with witnesses (19 of the 32 known murders), it is likely that many murders were well concealed and never discovered. The area the KGR took place within is vast and remote, with many individuals who travelled alone or in pairs, and could have easily been killed without witnesses to the act.

#### CHAPTER 4 Discussion & Conclusion

One could say that the Klondike Dead influenced me to begin this project, so, in a way, the theory aspects of this project did not influence data collection so much as the theory influenced me. Agency is something I always consider and believe should always be considered by those undertaking any mortuary studies, as it has a significant bearing on the image that mortuary spaces present and what you are made to believe of a person's life. How much of what you are seeing is reality, and how much does someone else's will shape that image?

In the case of this study, because data collection began in the course of my honours research, we were trying to collect as much information about each individual as possible as a means of confirming their identity and to keep a future record of those people and their identity. While working on this thesis, those aspects of identity came into play and, alongside what I was seeing in my cemetery surveys, influenced the categories of analysis. When considering secondary agency in relation to who has been remembered and forgotten in death, as we have discussed, time, proximity and personal history are directly proportional to the amount of influence exerted by an object on a person. Considering this, the categories of Family and Friends emerged from a recognizable pattern I was seeing in the data of Family and Friends playing a significant contribution to the remembrance of their loved ones; that category was given. Social Organizations were chosen because of a) the natural separation between social organizations in death that you see in North America and b) because such organizations bring like-minded people together in ways that create friendship, certainly, but in ways that can also create bonds as strong as a family. Indigeneity, Age, Sex and Affluence are all more nuanced; individuals in these categories can all, of course, be affected by the bonds of time, proximity and personal history, but those in these categories also have the ability to exert the second type of influence I discussed, influence based on preconceptions. Cause of death could have an impact on an individual in this way as well, but environment was chosen not for the influences I saw it creating within agency but for the unique and overarching problems that it caused which had the potential to override all of the natural instincts brought about by time, proximity and personal history between people.

Compared to other 19th-century gold rushes in the Pacific, the KGR was an event that never had

[86]

been and never will be seen again.

The topic of death in the Klondike has received little attention in the past. When reading about the KGR, there are frequent acknowledgements that many people died, but the discussion tends to stop there. The types of danger and death stampeders faced are often only highlighted as a measure of the success of those who survived and made lives for themselves. Discussions concerning what happened to those who died, if and how they were buried or commemorated, and what mechanisms influenced those choices are, sadly, sorely lacking. That said, historical research into representation and writings highlighting the lesser-known stories, contributions, personages, and communities who took part in or whose lives were unavoidably drawn into the phenomenon that was the KGR have become much more common in the past 25 years. The closest relevant studies to my own have been related to illness, disease and death. One was conducted by M.K. Lux in 1997, who analyzed disease as precipitated by the rapid growth of Dawson City, and the other by Megan Highet, who analyzed the various forms of illness and disease in her 2009 work Rushing to the Grave: Death and Disease During the Klondike Gold Rush, 1898-1904.

Unfortunately, and surprisingly, given the popularity of mortuary studies, the deaths of other gold rushes seem to have seen the same neglect, with only two studies that I am aware of. On that note, let us return briefly to the earlier topic of death and commemoration during the California, Australian and New Zealand gold rushes.

Based on what we have observed throughout the course of this project, it is safe to assume that the same general mechanisms explored here can be applied to other gold rushes. The dead exerting agency on the living relative to the relationship between the two or preconceptions that are easily seen through analysis based on the same social groupings - this is the baseline, the standard operating procedure. However, every gold rush then becomes its own unique and special occurrence based on the combination of people involved, the environment they are travelling, living and working within, and the trials and tribulations that come from both.

Where the stampeders of the KGR had to cross mountains, those of the Australian and New Zealand goldfields had to traverse oceans. Having to bury your dead at sea is something that would not have occurred in the KGR, but it is another example of a situation where people might

[87]

be forced to abandon their natural instincts to care for and commemorate dead loved ones or companions. In this case, for the greater good of the living. Were records kept for these individuals? Did their memory and history survive? The importance of physical mortuary spaces to the persistence of memory and identity suggests that their chances were significantly diminished.

As Chinese individuals were barred from the Yukon, we did not have the chance to see how that particular brand of racism, which was rampant at this time, might have interfered with their treatment in death. However, the fact that it was racism that kept them out of the North says something in and of itself and gives us a clue. I imagine, as in the case of Petchey's study, that the environment and circumstances would have adversely affected the pattern of burial, exhumation and repatriation typically seen at this time among Chinese populations. Costs that were already inflated would almost certainly have been worse for Chinese individuals, and, with limited community, friends and family except among their own, it would have been exceedingly challenging to plan and orchestrate the shipping of remains out of the North.

In Oroville, California, we see a Jewish Cemetery of the gold rush era, now designated as a California Point of Historical Interest; in the past, it was maintained by a private group called the Commission for the Preservation of Jewish Cemeteries and Landmarks of the Magnes Memorial Museum. 184 All of the markers that date back to the time of the California Gold Rush are stone and still in excellent condition. Whether they were placed when these individuals died or replaced later, this is not like any commemoration that one would see in the KGR. This tiny slice of information says so much about this one small community. It tells a story about the kind of access to materials they might have had, the persistence of Jewish values in the face of the gold rush and beyond, and the need to adhere to a Victorian standard of death when that would have been so much more difficult to do.

There is one great overarching theme that draws all of these events together. These individuals were willing to risk everything, even their lives, for the chance at something new and extraordinary. I do not say this to romanticize the situation, far from it. I say it to highlight just how many people died in any one of these events and just how little we know about who they

were or their motivations.

CONCLUSION

Many deaths that occurred during the KGR have been completely lost to time. It is difficult to estimate the number of people whose bodies were lost because their deaths occurred in the wilderness. It does not matter if you are a member of an order, if your family is there with you, if you are wealthy or well respected, or whether you are male or female. If you died in a manner in which your body could not be located; if you died in a disgraceful or abhorrent manner; or if you were buried in a manner or location which has resulted in your grave being lost then your background is irrelevant to your commemoration. If any one of these things occurred, you may, if you are lucky, be recorded in a death record, but by the very nature of these situations, you are not receiving the typical treatment, continual care and remembrance in death normally afforded to those of your station in life.

That said, though the environment and cause of death in this circumstance can act as levelers in many situations, we cannot overlook the influence of sociocultural factors. Having friends and family who care, being affluent or a member of a social organization, being Indigenous, man, woman or child - none of these things exerted influence independently. These can and are complexly interwoven, creating a wholly unique experience for each individual. A person always exists within several spheres of influence that can profoundly affect how they are treated in both life and death. Throughout this study, we can see the effects of established relationships based on time, proximity, and personal history, as well as the results of pre-conceptions. These complex and sometimes nuanced relationships, how people interact with the world and those around them, affect how an individual is perceived and treated after death.

There is bias in the subset of society that experiences representation and persistent remembrance after death. There is a privilege in remembrance during and outside the KGR, whether that be a privilege afforded by wealth, sex, community or the colour of one's skin. We need to acknowledge and remain cognizant of the fact that much of the tourism and heritage work related to the KGR is tied to existing historical records and remaining material culture, including those pertaining to the dead. The individual sociocultural spheres above have actively contributed to an overrepresentation of certain individuals over others, which has shaped the

[89]

iconic vision of the KGR that persists today throughout much of Canada.

This dataset has many gaps, but that is precisely the point. Every gap in our knowledge represents someone who was relegated to a lesser status in history, the ones who got left behind 125 years ago. Studies like this one help shed light on inaccuracies and misrepresentations in popular history and help us understand how they exist and persist. The more we are forced to acknowledge such biased and romanticized views of history and the mechanics surrounding how these histories come to be formed, the closer we come to the truth and work toward correcting a sometimes harmful legacy.

citations.title: The Tr’ondëk Hwëch’in and the Great Upheaval: Mining, Colonialism, and Environmental Change in the Klondike, 1890-1940
citations.text:
The Tr’ondëk Hwëch’in and the Great Upheaval: Mining, Colonialism, and Environmental Change in the Klondike, 1890-1940

by

Heather Green

A thesis submitted in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the degree of

Doctor of Philosophy

In

History

Department of History and Classics

University of Alberta ©Heather Green, 2018

ii

## Abstract

This study examines the colonial history of gold mining in the Klondike region of the central Yukon from 1890 to 1940. The Klondike Gold Rush (1897-1900) marked the beginning of major transition in the lives of the Tr’ondëk Hwëch’in that lasted well into the

20 th century. Mining worked to reorganize and disassemble the local Klondike environment through both placer mining and industrial dredge mining. Along with direct environmental impacts, gold mining had indirect impacts on the Tr’ondëk Hwëch’in people such creating competition for resources and conflicts over access to resources, and the emergence of a new industrial economy to the Yukon.

Throughout this period the state imposed southern colonial bureaucracies and administration in the Yukon that favoured colonial ideologies and practises of land use over local Indigenous practises that led to the displacement and relocation of Tr’ondëk

Hwëch’in peoples from previously used areas. State imposition often clashed with colonial authority on the ground, creating a complicated history of colonization of environment and humans in the Yukon. This study also examines the various ways in which Indigenous

Yukoners shaped the structure of colonialism in the Yukon through a variety of responses.

This dissertation argues that the Klondike Gold Rush began a pattern of long-term systemic alienation of Yukon First Nations from traditionally used resources and areas; in part this resulted from the physical impacts that mining had on the environment of the central Yukon, but Indigenous displacement also resulted from the role of colonial bureaucracies and state extension into the Klondike. The colonial structure of the Yukon was complicated and contested, creating conflicts between colonizers over how best to administer to the realities of the Yukon; it was also shaped by the responses and

iii

contributions of Indigenous Yukoners who frequently challenged their loss of access to resources and the outside imposed changes mining brought to their lives.

iv

The research project, of which this thesis is a part, received research ethics approval from the University of Alberta Research Ethics Board, Project Name “Historical Investigations into Tr’ondëk Hwëch’in Experiences During and After the Klondike Gold Rush, 1890-1950”, No. Pro00049921, 2015 (renewals in 2016, 2017). This research has also received Yukon Scientists and Explorers Research License (No. 6800-20-984) approval and has been carried out according to an agreement with the Tr’ondëk Hwëch’in Heritage Department’s Protocol for Conducting Traditional Knowledge Research and/or Accessing Traditional Knowledge, 2014.

The time it takes to complete a dissertation is not an insignificant commitment and

I have been lucky to meet some fantastic friends who became family along the way. There are too many to list here, but some individuals who have gone above and beyond in their support and encouragement over the years include Gino Canlas, Heather Kerr, and

My many research trips would not have been possible without the financial support from Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, Northern Scientific Training

Program, UAlberta North, and the Department of History and Classics. I am also grateful for the research assistant and teaching opportunities that I have had along the way from the

material. Staff at the Yukon Archives, especially Donna Darbyshire and Chelsea Jeffery, over the past several years have fostered a creative and supportive research environment.
