- /ʕadˤːrˤ/ > [ʕadˤːərˤ] ('to meet')

However note that word-initial initial /j, w/ are realized as /i, u/ before consonants. In word-medial or -final position [əj], [əʝ], and [əw] are realized as [ij], [ij], and [uw] respectively, and may become [i] and [u] in rapid speech. [68] 

Tamazight in fact has numerous words without phonemic vowels, and those consisting entirely of voiceless consonants will not phonetically contain voiced vowels. [nb 7] 

[ə] is written as ⟨ⴻ⟩ in neo-Tifinagh and as ⟨ e⟩ in the Berber Latin alphabet. French publications tended to include [ə] in their transcriptions of Berber forms despite their predictability, perhaps due to the French vowel system. This can cause problems because alternations such as /iʁ(ə)rs/ 'he slaughtered' – /uriʁris/ 'he did not slaughter' would then have to be morphologically conditioned. [70] 

### Stress

Word stress is non-contrastive and predictable, and falls on the last vowel in a word (including schwa). [71] [72] 

Examples:

- /sal/ > [ˈsal] ('to ask')
- /dajtːħadˤarˤ/ > [dajtːəħaˈdˤarˤ] ('he is present')
- /fsːr/ > [fəsːˈər] ('to explain')
- /tfsːrnt/ > [təfəsːəˈrənt] ('you (fp) explained')

## Grammar

Central Atlas Tamazight grammar has many features typical of Afro-Asiatic languages, including extensive apophony in both the derivational and inflectional morphology, gender, possessive suffixes, VSO typology, the causative morpheme /s/, and the use of the status constructus.

### Morphology

Tamazight nouns are inflected for gender, number, and state. Singular masculine nouns usually have the prefix /a-/, and singular feminines the circumfix /t...t. [73] Plurals may either involve a regular change ("sound plurals"), internal vowel change ("broken plurals"), or a combination of the two. [74] Masculine plurals usually take the prefix /i-/, feminines /ti-/, and sound plurals also take the suffix /-n/ in the masculine and /-in/} in the feminine, but many other plural patterns are found. [75] 

Examples: [76] 

: / a xam/ → / i xam n/ 'big tent(s)' (m)
: / a maziɣ/ → / i maziɣ n/ 'Berber(s)' (m)
: / a daʃu/ → / i d uʃ a/ 'sandal(s)' (m)
: / a srdun/ → / i srd a n/ 'mule(s)' (m)
: / ta xam t/ → / ti xam in/ 'tent(s)' (f)
: / ta funas t/ → / ti funas in/ 'cow(s)' (f)
: / taɡrtil t/ → / tiɡrt a l/ 'mat(s)' (f)
: / ta mazir t/ → / ti m i z a r/ 'property(ies)' (f)

Nouns may be put into the construct state (contrasting with free state) to indicate possession or when the subject of a verb follows the verb. This is also used for nouns after numerals and some prepositions, as well as the conjunction /d-/ ('and'). [77] The construct state is formed as follows: in masculines, initial /a/ becomes /u, wː, wa/, initial /i/ becomes /i, j, ji/, and initial /u/ becomes /wu/. In feminines, initial /ta/ usually becomes /t/, initial /ti/ usually becomes /t/, and initial /tu/ remains unchanged. [78] 

Examples (in Ayt Ayache): [78] 

: /babuxam/ ( ← /axam/) 'head of the house'
: /ijːs ntslit/ ( ← /tislit/) 'the horse of the bride'

Central Atlas Tamazight's personal pronouns distinguish three persons and two genders. Pronouns appear in three forms: an independent form used in the subject position, a possessive suffix (and a derived independent possessive pronoun), and an object form affixed [nb 8] to the controlling verb.

Demonstrative pronouns distinguish between proximate and remote. When they occur independently, they inflect for number. They may also be suffixed to nouns: /tabardaja/ 'this pack-saddle'. [79]

Central Atlas Tamazight verbs are heavily inflected and are marked for tense, aspect, mode, voice, person, and polarity. Tamazight verbs have at their core a stem, modified by prefixes, suffixes, moveable affixes, circumfixes, and ablaut. The prefixes indicate voice, tense, aspect, and polarity, while the suffixes indicate mood (normal, horatory, or imperative). Subject markers are circumfixed to the verb, and object marking and satellite framing are accomplished via either prefixing or suffixing depending on environment [82] Some verb forms are accompanied by ablaut, and sometimes metathesis. [83] 

Pronominal complement markers cliticize to the verb, with the indirect object preceding the direct object:/iznz-as-t/ "he sold it to him". [84] 

Attributive adjectives occur after the noun they modify and are inflected for number and gender. [85] [86] Adjectives may also occur alone in which case they become an NP. [86] Practically all adjectives also have a verbal form used for predicative purposes, which behaves just like a normal verb. [86] 

: /argaz amʕdur/ 'the foolish man' (lit. 'man foolish')
: /tamtˤut tamʕdur/ 'the foolish woman'
: /irgzen imʕdar/ 'the foolish men'
: /tajtʃin timʕdar/ 'the foolish women'
: /i-mmuʕdr urgaz/ 'the man is foolish' (lit. '3ps–foolish man')
: /argaz i-mmuʕdr-n/ 'the foolish man' [using a non-finite verb]

Prepositions include /xf/ ('on'), /qbl/ ('before'), /ɣr/ ('to'), and the proclitics /n/ ('of') and /d/ ('with, and'). [nb 9] They may take pronominal suffixes. Some prepositions require the following noun to be in the construct state, but others do not. [87] 

### Syntax

Word order is usually VSO (with the subject in construct state) but is sometimes SVO (with the subject in free state), e.g. (/ifːɣ umaziɣ/ vs. /amaziɣ ifːɣ/ 'the Berber went out'). [4] Tamazight also exhibits pro-drop behavior. [88] 

Tamazight may use a null copula, [89] but the word /ɡ/ 'to be, to do' may function as a copula in Ayt Ayache, especially in structures preceded by /aj/ 'who, which, what'. [90] 

wh- questions are always clefts, and multiple wh-questions [nb 10] do not occur. [91] Consequently, Tamazight's clefting, relativisation, and wh-interrogation contribute to anti-agreement effects, [nb 11] similar to Shilha, [91] and causes deletion of the verbal person marker in certain situations. [92] 

## Vocabulary

As a result of relatively intense language contact, Central Atlas Tamazight has a large stratum of Arabic loans. Many borrowed words in Berber also have native synonyms (/ lbab/ or /tiflut/ 'door'), with the latter being used more in rural areas. [93] The contact was unequal, as Moroccan Arabic has not borrowed as much from Berber languages, [94] but Berber has contributed to the very reduced vowel systems of Moroccan and Algerian Arabic. [95] 

Arabic loans span a wide range of lexical clasees. Many nouns begin with /l-/, from the Arabic definite prefix, and some Arabic feminines may acquire the native Berber feminine ending /-t/, e.g. /lʕafit/ for /lʕafia/ 'fire'. [96] Many Arabic loans have been integrated into the Tamazight verb lexicon. They adhere fully to inflectional patterns of native stems, and may even undergo ablaut. [5] [6] Even function words are borrowed: / blli/ or / billa/ 'that', / waxxa/ 'although', /ɣir/ 'just', etc. [93] 

The first few (1–3 in Ayt Ayache and Ayt Ndhir) cardinal numerals have native Berber and borrowed Arabic forms. [nb 12] [97] All higher cardinals are borrowed from Arabic, consistent with the linguistic universals that the numbers 1–3 are much more likely to be retained, and that a borrowed number generally implies that numbers greater than it are also borrowed. The retention of one is also motivated by the fact that Berber languages nearly universally use unity as a determiner. [98] 

Central Atlas Tamazight uses a bipartite negative construction (e.g. /uriffiɣ ʃa/ 'he did not go out'), which was apparently modelled after proximate |Arabic varieties, in a common development known as Jespersen's Cycle. [99] It is present in multiple Berber varieties and is argued to have originated in neighbouring Arabic varieties and to have been adopted by contact. [100]

Languages of Morocco

| Languages of Morocco | |
| --- | --- |
| | |
| Official | Modern Standard Arabic Standard Moroccan Amazigh |
| Vernacular | Arabic dialects (92.7%) [1] Moroccan Arabic: (91.9%) [1] Hassaniya: (0.8%) [1] Berber languages (24.8%) [1] Tashelhit (14.2%) [1] Central Atlas Tamazight (7.4%) [1] Tarifit (3.2%) [1] |
| Foreign | French (36%) [2] English (14%) [3] Spanish (4.5%) [4] |
| Signed | Moroccan Sign Language |
| Keyboard layout | Arabic keyboard |

Sign in Arabic, Berber and French in Agadir

The official languages of Morocco are Modern Standard Arabic and Standard Moroccan Amazigh. [5] Moroccan Arabic (known as Darija) is the primary spoken vernacular and lingua franca, [6] but a number of regional and foreign languages are also spoken. According to the 2024 Moroccan census, 92.7% of the population (including second-language speakers) spoke Arabic, whereas 24.8% spoke Berber languages. [1] 

The languages of prestige in Morocco are Arabic in its Classical and Modern Standard forms and sometimes French, the latter of which serves as a second language for approximately 33% of Moroccans. [7] According to the 2024 census, 99.2% or almost the entire literate population of Morocco could read and write in Arabic, whereas only 1.5% of the population could read and write in Berber. When it comes to foreign languages, this figure rises to 57.7% in French, 20.5% in English, and 1.2% in Spanish. [8] The census also reveals that 80.6% of Moroccans consider Arabic to be their native language, while 18.9% regard any of the various Berber languages as their mother tongue. [1] [9] 

According to a 2000–2002 survey done by Moha Ennaji, author of Multilingualism, Cultural Identity, and Education in Morocco, "there is a general agreement that Standard Arabic, Moroccan Arabic, and Berber are the national languages." [10] Ennaji also concluded "This survey confirms the idea that multilingualism in Morocco is a vivid sociolinguistic phenomenon, which is favored by many people." [11] 

There are around 6 million Berber speakers in Morocco. [6] French retains a major place in Morocco, as it is taught universally and serves as Morocco's primary language of commerce and economics, culture, sciences and medicine; it is also widely used in education and government. Morocco is a member of the Francophonie. [12] Spanish is spoken by many Moroccans, particularly in the northern regions around Tetouan and Tangier, as well as in parts of the south, due to historic ties and business interactions with Spain. [13] 

## History

Mother tongues of Moroccans (per 2024 census)

1. Arabic (80.6%)
2. Berber languages (18.9%)
3. Others (0.50%)

Historically, languages such as Phoenician, [14] Punic, [15] and Berber languages have been spoken in Morocco. Juba II, king of Mauretania, wrote in Greek and Latin. [16] It is unclear how long African Romance was spoken, but its influence on Northwest African Arabic (particularly in the language of northwestern Morocco) indicates it must have had a significant presence in the early years after the Arab conquest. [17] [18] 

Arabic came with the Muslim conquest of the Maghreb; [19] Abdellah Guennoun cites the Friday sermon delivered by Tariq Ibn Ziad just before the conquest of al-Andalus in 711 as the first instance of Moroccan literature in Arabic. [20] However, the language spread much more slowly than the religion. [19] At first, Arabic was used only in urban areas, especially in cities in the north, while the rural areas remained the domain of Berber languages. [19] 

Under the Almohads, the khuṭbas (from خطبة, the Friday sermon) had to be delivered in Arabic and Berber, or as the Andalusi historian Ibn Ṣāḥib aṣ-Ṣalāt [ar] described it: " al-lisān al-gharbī" (اللسان الغربي 'the western tongue'). [21] The khaṭīb, or sermon-giver, of al-Qarawiyyīn Mosque in Fes, Mahdī b. ‘Īsā, was replaced under the Almohads by Abū l-Ḥasan b. ‘Aṭiyya khaṭīb because the latter was fluent in Berber. [21] 

The first recorded work in Darija or Moroccan Arabic is Al-Kafif az-Zarhuni's epic zajal poem " al-Mala'ba," dating back to the reign of Marinid Sultan Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Othman. [22] 

During the Middle Ages, sailors and traders in the Mediterranean, including the Barbary Coast, developed a contact language known as Mediterranean Lingua Franca or sabir. It was influenced by the languages of Italy, Catalan, Occitan, Berber, Arabic, Spanish and Portuguese. Its use declined after the European conquest.

### Language policy

After Morocco gained independence with the end of the French protectorate in 1956, it started a process of Arabization. For this task, the Institute for Studies and Research on Arabization was established by decree in 1960. [23] [24] The policy of Arabization was not applied in earnest until 17 years after independence. [25] An editorial in Lamalif in 1973 argued that, although French unified the elite and major sections of the economy, national unity could only be achieved based on Arabic—though Lamalif called for a new incarnation of the language, describing Standard Arabic as untenably prescriptive and Moroccan vernacular Arabic (Darija) as too poor to become in and of itself a language of culture and knowledge. [25] 

In the year 2000, after years of neglecting and ignoring the other languages present in Morocco, the Charter for Educational Reform recognized them and the necessity for them. [26] 

Until then the Berber languages were marginalized in the modern society and the number of monolingual speakers decreased. In recent years, the Berber culture has been gaining strength and some developments promise that these languages will not die. [27] 

Arabic, on the other hand, has been perceived as a prestigious language in Morocco for over a millennium. However, there are very distinctive varieties of Arabic used, not all equally prestigious, which are MSA (Modern Standard Arabic), the written form used in schools and ' Dialectal Arabic', the non-standardized spoken form. The difference between the two forms in terms of grammar, phonology and vocabulary is so great, it can be considered as diglossia. MSA is practically foreign to Moroccan schoolchildren, and this creates problems with reading and writing, consequently leading to a high level of illiteracy in Morocco. [27] 

The French language is also dominant in Morocco, especially in education and administration, therefore was initially learned by an elite and later on was learned by a great number of Moroccans for use in domains such as finance, science, technology and media. That is despite the government decision to implement a language policy of ignoring French after gaining independence, for the sake of creating a monolingual country. [27] 

From its independence until the year 2000, Morocco opted for Arabization as a policy, in an attempt of replacing French with Arabic. By the end of the 1980s, Arabic was the dominant language in education, although French was still in use in many important domains. The goals of Arabization were not met, in linguistic terms, therefore a change was needed. [27] By 2020, the country ended its policy of Arabization, with French reimplemented as the medium of instruction in core subjects such as science and math. [28] 

In 2000 the Charter of Educational Reform introduced a drastic change in language policy. From then on, Morocco has adopted a clear perpetual educational language policy with three main cores: improving and reinforcing the teaching of Arabic, using a variety of languages, such as English and French in teaching the fields of technology and science and acceptance of Berber. The state of Morocco still sees Arabic (MSA) as its national language, but acknowledges that not all Moroccans are Arabic speakers and that Arabization did not succeed in the area of science and technology. The aims of the charter seem to have been met faster than expected, probably since the conditions of the charter started to be implemented immediately. In the early twenty-first century the different minority languages are acknowledged in Morocco although Arabic is still dominant and is being promoted by the government. [27] [29] 

Berber was made an official language in 2011. In 2019, a law was enacted to implement the constitutional changes from 2011. [30] The government aims to generalize Berber education to all Moroccan schools. [31] However, as of 2023, only 10% of Moroccan pupils study Berber. [30] The government hired civil servants able to speak the three main dialects (Tachalhit, Tamazight and Tarifet) to help citizens in courts, hospitals, and other public services. [32] [33] According to a 2012 study by the Government of Spain, 98% of Moroccans spoke Moroccan Arabic, 63% spoke French, 26% Berber, 14% spoke English, and 10% spoke Spanish. [13] 

## Education

Literate population of Morocco (2024)

| | percent |
| --- | --- |
| Can read and write in Arabic | 99.2% |
| Can read and write in French | 57.7% |
| Can read and write in English | 20.5% |
| Can read and write in Berber languages | 1.5% |
| Can read and write in Spanish | 1.2% |
| Can read and write in other languages | 1% |

Framework Law 17:51 allowed scientific subjects to be taught in foreign languages—especially French—in public elementary schools. [34] 

In 2019, the Parliament voted to expand Berber classes to all Moroccan schools. [35] [36] [37] According to Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch, about 2,000 schools taught Amazigh in 2022 and the government was training more teachers to accelerate the roll out of Berber teaching. [38] As of 2023, this reform is still in progress. [39] 

In July 2023, the gradual generalization of learning English from secondary school was decided by the Ministry of Education. [40] 

## Arabic

Percentage of Arabic speakers in Morocco by subdivision

Arabic, along with Berber, is one of Morocco's two official languages, [5] although it is the Moroccan dialect of Arabic, namely Darija, meaning "everyday/colloquial language"; [41] that is spoken or understood, frequently as a second language, by the majority of the population (about 85% of the total population). Many native Berber speakers also speak the local Arabic variant as a second language. [42] Arabic in its Classical and Standard forms is one of the two prestige languages in Morocco. Aleya Rouchdy, editor of Language Contact and Language Conflict in Arabic, said that Classical/Modern Arabic and French are constantly in conflict with one another, but that most Moroccans believe that the bilingualism of Classical Arabic and French is the most optimal choice to allow for Morocco's development. [43] 

In 1995 the number of native Arabic speakers in Morocco was approximately 18.8 million (65% of the total population), and 21 million including the Moroccan diaspora. [44] 

As a member of the Maghrebi Arabic grouping of dialects, Moroccan Arabic is similar to the dialects spoken in Mauritania, Algeria, Tunisia, and Libya (and also Maltese). The so called Darija dialect of Morocco is quite different from its Middle Eastern counterparts but in general understandable to each other, it’s estimated that Darija shares 85%-90% of its vocabulary with Modern Standard Arabic. The country shows a marked difference in urban and rural dialects. This is due to the history of settlement. traditionally, Arabs established centers of power in only a few cities and ports in the region, with the effect that the other areas remained Berber-speaking. Then, in the 13th century, Bedouin tribes swept through many of the unsettled areas, spreading with them their distinct Arabic dialect in the non-urbanized areas and leaving speakers of Berber isolated in the mountainous regions. [citation needed] 

### Modern Standard and Classical Arabic

Moroccans learn Standard Arabic as a language. It is generally not spoken at home or on the streets. Standard Arabic is frequently used in administrative offices, mosques, and schools. [45] According to Rouchdy, within Morocco Classical Arabic is still only used in literary and cultural aspects, formal traditional speeches, and discussions about religion. [43] 

#### Moroccan Arabic

Moroccan Arabic, along with Berber, is one of two mother tongues acquired by Moroccan children and spoken in homes and on the street. [45] The language is not used in writing. [46] Abdelâli Bentahila, the author of the 1983 book Language Attitudes among Arabic–French Bilinguals in Morocco, said that Moroccans who were bilingual in both French and Arabic preferred to speak Arabic while discussing religion; while discussing matters in a grocery store or restaurant; and while discussing matters with family members, beggars, and maids. [47] Moroccan linguist Moha Ennaji said that Moroccan Arabic has connotations of informality, and that Moroccan Arabic tends to be used in casual conversations and spoken discourse. Ennaji added that bilingual Moroccans tend to use Moroccan Arabic while in the house. [48] Berbers generally learn Moroccan Arabic as a second language and use it as a lingua franca, since not all versions of Berber are mutually intelligible with one another. [46]

Hassānīya, is spoken by about 0.8% of the population, mainly in the territory of Western Sahara, claimed by both Morocco and the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic. Communities of speakers exist elsewhere in Morocco too.

## Berber

Berber-speaking areas in Morocco

The exact population of speakers of Berber languages is hard to ascertain, since most North African countries do not—traditionally—record language data in their censuses (An exception to this was the 2004 Morocco population census). The Ethnologue provides a useful academic starting point; however, its bibliographic references are inadequate, and it rates its own accuracy at only B-C for the area. Early colonial censuses may provide better documented figures for some countries; however, these are also very much out of date. The number for each Berber language is difficult to estimate. [citation needed] 

Berber serves as a vernacular language in many rural areas of Morocco. [46] Berber, along with Moroccan Arabic, is one of two languages spoken in homes and on the street. [45] The population does not use Berber in writing. Aleya Rouchdy, editor of Language Contact and Language Conflict in Arabic, said that Berber is mainly used in the contexts of family, friendship, and "street". [46] In his 2000–2002 research, Ennaji found that 52% of the interviewees placed Berber as a language inferior to Arabic because it did not have a prestigious status and because its domain was restricted. [49] Ennaji added that "[t]he dialectisation of Berber certainly reduces its power of communication and its spread." [10] 

Speakers of Riffian language were estimated to be around 1.5 million in 1990. [50] The language is spoken in the Rif area in the north of the country and is one of the three main Berber languages of Morocco.

The Tashelhit language is considered to be the most widely spoken as it covers the whole of the Region Souss-Massa-Drâa, and is also spoken in the Marrakech-Tensift-El Haouz and Tadla-Azilal regions. Studies done in 1990 show around 3 million people, concentrated in the south of Morocco, speak the language. [50] 

Central Morocco Tamazight is the second Berber language in Morocco. A 1998 study done by Ethnologue, shows that around 3 million people speak the language in Morocco. [51] The language is most used in the regions Middle Atlas, High Atlas and east High Atlas Mountains.

Other Berber languages are spoken in Morocco, as the Senhaja de Srair and the Ghomara dialects in the Rif mountains, the Oasis Tamazight and Eastern Zenati in eastern Morocco, and Eastern Middle Atlas dialects in central Morocco.

## French

French and Arabic (MSA) coexist in Moroccan administration and business.

Within Morocco, French, one of the country's two prestige languages, [43] is often used for business, diplomacy, and government; [53] and serves as a lingua franca. [54] Aleya Rouchdy, editor of Language Contact and Language Conflict in Arabic, said that "For all practical purposes, French is used as a second language." [46] Some Generation Z protest groups have called for French to be replaced by English as the second foreign language of Morocco. [55] 

Different figures of French speakers in Morocco are given. According to the OIF, 36% of Moroccans speak French overall, while 47% of students have French as their medium of instruction at schools. [2] According to the 2014 census, about 66% of literate people can read and write French, [56] that is, 66% of 68% = 45%. Other sources put the number of total French speakers at 64% as of 2014. [57] 

## Spanish

In a survey from 2005 by the CIDOB (Barcelona Centre for International Affairs), 21.9% of respondents from Morocco claimed to speak Spanish, with higher percentages in the northern regions. [58] By 2017, that figure had declined to about 4.5% of the population. [59] 

Spanish was used in northern Morocco and Western Sahara due to Spanish occupation of those areas and the incorporation of Spanish Sahara as a province. After Morocco declared independence in 1956, French and Arabic became the main languages of administration and education, causing the role of Spanish to decline. In northern Morocco, transmission of Spanish television is often available and there are interactions in Spanish on a daily basis in areas bordering the Spanish cities of Ceuta and Melilla. [43] 

Today, Spanish is still offered as one of the foreign languages in the educational system but has fallen well behind French and English. According to the Cervantes Institute, there were 11,409 students learning Spanish in Morocco in 2016, a large decline from about 50,000 in 2005. Demand for Spanish and overall competency in the language has fallen since the start of the 21st century. [60] 

### Judeo-Spanish

After the expulsion of the Jews from Spain in 1492, thousands of Sephardic Jews took refuge in Morocco. The Jews of Portugal were similarly expelled in 1496. They spoke Old Spanish, Portuguese, Judeo-Catalan, Judeo-Aragonese and other Romance languages. Mixing in Morocco and influenced by local Arabic, their language became Haketia (with an offshoot in Oran, now part of Algeria). Unlike other Judeo-Spanish dialects, Haketia did not develop a literature and, during colonization, North African Sephardim adopted Spanish and French. Emigration to Spain, the Americas, and Israel has significantly reduced the number of speakers of Haketia.

# Stylizing Tamazight (Berber)-Influenced Moroccan Arabic in a Moroccan Stand-Up Comedy

Languages. Published: 2025-09-24. 1 citation.

## Authors

- Atiqa Hachimi (University of Toronto): h-index 8; 312 citations; corresponding author
- Gareth Smail (College of Charleston): h-index 2; 27 citations; corresponding author

## Topics

- Language, Linguistics, Cultural Analysis
- Linguistic and Sociocultural Studies
- Hispanic-African Historical Relations

---

# Stylizing Tamazight (Berber)-Influenced Moroccan Arabic in a Moroccan Stand-Up Comedy

Article

Atiqa Hachimi 1,* and Gareth C. Smail 2,*

1 Department of Historical and Cultural Studies, University of Toronto Scarborough, 1256 Military Trail, Toronto, ON M1C 1A4, Canada 2 Department of International Studies, College of Charleston, 9 Glebe Street, Charleston, SC 29401, USA * Correspondence: atiqa.hachimi@utoronto.ca (A.H.); smailgc@cofc.edu (G.C.S.)

## Abstract

Elaborating on the concept of heteroglossic stylization, this paper examines how a Moroccan comedian—Zakaria Ouarssam—stylizes Tamazight (Berber)-influenced Moroccan Arabic (MA) in order to evoke comedic personae associated with the country’s Middle Atlas region. Our analysis focuses on Ouarssam’s on-stage performances to document the complex mul tilingual repertoire that allows him to (i) create contrasts between a supposedly unmarked MA and a stylized Tamazight-influenced MA and (ii) evoke comedic stances that associate the latter with stereotypes of his home region. Particular attention is given to Ouarssam’s use of code switching between Tamazight-influenced MA and untranslated Tamazight as a novel and potentially boundary-pushing practice when considered in the context of its live performance on national television. The paper argues that Ouarssam’s stylized performances contribute to the construction and valorization of an alternative expres sion of Amazigh and regional pride, even as they reproduce certain linguistic hierarchies and ideologies.

Keywords: heteroglossic stylization; performance; stance; code-switching; ethnic humor; mass media; Moroccan Arabic; Berber; Tamazight; language activism

## 1. Introduction

For centuries, Morocco has been a place of multilingual contact between Arabic and Tamazight1, but the 20th century has precipitated a long process of language shift toward Moroccan Arabic (MA), locally known as Darija. The most obvious driver of this shift ¯ has been urbanization, fueled by a combination of chronic rural drought, colonial and state expansion, and global economic integration (Boukous, 2011; Ennaji, 2005, pp. 77–78; Hoffman, 2006, 2008). Because MA functions as an urban lingua franca, urbanization has turned Moroccan cities into “the crucible of [Tamazight language] attrition” (Boukous, 2011, p. 84), and studies since the early 1990s have documented intergenerational language loss in urban areas, where younger generations speak progressively less Tamazight than their elders with stronger connections to the countryside (Bentahila & Davies, 1992; Boukous, 2011; El Aissati, 2001; Errihani, 2008). This process has been exacerbated by a history of popular language ideologies and state language policies that have discriminated against Tamazight, casting it as a relic of a premodern past and promoting Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and French as the languages of modern public life (Boum, 2007; Chakrani, 2013; Hoffman, 2006, 2008; Maddy-Weitzman, 2011). These dynamics are particularly salient in provincial capitals such as Khenifra, the city from which Zakaria Ouarssam, the young

Languages 2025, 10, 246 https://doi.org/10.3390/languages10100246 comedian under analysis, hails. The Khenifra region—once a site of stalwart Amazigh resistance to French colonialism—is widely associated with rural Central Atlas Tamazight language and culture, popularized by iconic late 20th century artists such as Mohammed Rouicha, Moha Oulhoucine Achibane, and Hadda Ouakki. However, the city itself has grown from a pre-colonial kasbah in 1912 to a sprawling urban center today of more than 100,000, where MA is the dominant language of young people, whether or not they identify as ethnically Amazigh. Against this backdrop of long-term language shift, ideologies around MA itself have also been changing. Beginning in the late 1990s, nationalist postcolonial ideologies that aspired to modernity through MSA have given way to a growing acceptance of MA as a medium of contemporary life, fueled in large part by new media technologies beyond the reach of the state, a trend which sociolinguists have termed Moroccanization (Caubet, 2017). This shift has led to an explosion of MA representation in the public sphere, ranging from music and television to writing in advertisements and online communication (Caubet, 2005, 2017; Elinson, 2013; Hickman, 2022; Miller, 2017). This expanding functionality of MA participates in a wider regional trend in which vernaculars are increasingly seen (and accepted by states) as legitimate mediums for and symbols of mediatized public life (Hachimi et al., 2022; cf. Coupland, 2014). Indeed, the fading authority of MSA has led to new “centripetal forces of language” (Bakhtin, 1981, p. 272), wherein supra-local varieties of MA associated with the urban educated elite have emerged as hegemonic. Ouarssam’s stylized regional variety is set against a backdrop of this normative MA, or h£d ĳra Qadijja “lit. normal speech”—a presumably unmarked register that is often defined “more by what it is not rather than by what it is” (Hachimi, 2007, pp. 116–117), i.e., one whose linguistic structures do not easily index a stigmatized regional, ethnolinguistic, or class identity. A parallel development has been the rising awareness of an Amazigh identity, what Lafkioui (2011, 2013) calls “Amazighness,” as a translocal form of belonging and heritage. Tamazight language has historically been excluded from public life in Morocco due to a confluence of explicit legal discrimination and socioeconomic marginalization. In the early 1990s, the long-suppressed Moroccan Amazigh Cultural Movement began organizing more vocally to document Tamazight linguistic and cultural practices, forge a new Tamazight literary culture, and advocate for linguistic and cultural rights (El Guabli, 2020; Maddy Weitzman, 2011). In response, the Moroccan state eventually began a process of overture to the Tamazight activists’ demands. Morocco’s political opening at the beginning of the 21st century has thus seen the flourishing of an “Amazigh renaissance” (Errihani, 2012), marked by both an explosion of cultural production in and about Tamazight as well as the creation of a state-led officialization project. In 2001, the government established the Royal Institute of Amazigh Culture (IRCAM), charged with the codification of a national standard language that united the country’s three major regional varieties (Boukous, 2011; Soulaimani, 2015, 2016) and paved the way for the language’s (halting) introduction into schools (Buckner, 2006; El Aissati et al., 2011; Errihani, 2006). A Tamazight television broadcast channel was introduced in 2010 (Belhiah et al., 2020; Boukous, 2011), and the language was constitutionally recognized as an official language second to Arabic in 2011. This Standard Tamazight, however, is not the same as the local varieties that people speak in their daily lives. These recent developments in media and public discourse have made the heteroglossic nature of Moroccan social life more apparent. Competition talent shows such as Stand Up are a microcosm of these dynamics, which expose the ways in which participants position themselves in relation to dominant sociolinguistic ideologies and hierarchies of Arabic, Tamazight, and French varieties. Our aim in this paper is to shine a light on the stylization of MA and its relationship with Tamazight by zeroing in on in-group parodying of Tamazight- influenced MA by Zakaria Ouarssam, a bilingual lower-class youth from Khenifra who won the 2019 season of the Moroccan Stand Up competition TV show. Building on recent theories of the sociolinguistics of performance and heteroglossic stylization (e.g., Bell & Gibson, 2011; Coupland, 2007; Higgins, 2015; Jaffe et al., 2015), we argue that the heightened reflexivity of stand-up comedy offers a rich sociolinguistic and metacommunicative context for understanding the creative and strategic uses of regional, social, and stylistic variation in contexts of Tamazight-MA language contact. The study of such heteroglossic performances provides a privileged site for “examining the dynamic relationships between ideologies, linguistic forms, and processes of identification” (Jaffe et al., 2015, p. 138). This paper draws on Ouarssam’s on-stage performances of five sketches in four episodes to situate his use of stylized Tamazight-influenced MA within broader processes of sociolinguistic and language ideological change in Morocco. Our analysis proceeds in two parts. First, a sociolinguistic analysis documents how Ouarssam mobilizes phonological, lexical, and morphosyntactic resources to create contrasts between his stylized voices and normative MA. We argue that in doing so, Ouarssam indexically links his performed characters (and their stylized speech) with well-worn comedic stereotypes of Tamazight speakers as rural-dwelling, naïve, and uneducated. Second, we conduct a stance-taking analysis (cf. Du Bois, 2007; Jaffe, 2009) of segments of Ouarssam’s on-stage performances, focusing on how he embodies his stylized personae, how he positions himself vis-à-vis his multilingual stylization, and how he aligns with and disaligns from those he is speaking to or about. Ultimately, we argue that stylized Tamazight-accented MA is a “social voice” (Bakhtin, 1981) that inhabits a particular positionality within Morocco’s recent history of urban ization, language shift, and vernacularization described above; its humor presupposes the perspective of MA-dominant youth poking fun at—whether lovingly or cruelly—an older Berber-dominant generation with roots in the countryside. Thus, Ouarssam’s abil ity to connect with his audience via stylized Tamazight-influenced MA participates in and capitalizes upon the evolution of Morocco’s sociolinguistic and language ideological landscape, and especially, a growing awareness and embrace of Amazigh identity among young Moroccans who are less likely to speak the language (cf. Lafkioui, 2024). Ouarssam’s successful comedic performance of Tamazight-influenced MA, moreover, sheds new light on the representation of a demographic and local identity that are marginalized both within the broader Moroccan national culture and the Amazigh cultural movement itself, even as it reproduces certain linguistic hierarchies and ideologies. More generally, our focus on stylization in multilingual discourse, which has not received the same attention as dialect stylization (Higgins, 2015), seeks to contribute to this growing body of research and illuminate the ways in which multilingual public performances portray and impact marginalized local identities. Specifically, we give particular attention to Ouarssam’s use of code switching between untranslated Tamazight and Tamazight-influenced MA as a novel and potentially boundary-pushing practice when considered in the context of its live performance on national television. Overall, the study has broader implications for the role of mediatized heteroglossic performances in ongoing sociolinguistic change in Morocco (Hachimi, 2022; Benítez-Fernández & Guerrero, 2022; Falchetta, 2022), insofar as it “provides a frame that invites critical reflection on communicative processes” (Bauman & Briggs, 1990, p. 61).

2. Tamazight-Influenced Moroccan Arabic

The proportion of Tamazight to MA speakers in Morocco is widely disputed due to difficulties in census taking, conceptual problems with the definition of a “speaker,” and ideological contests over the nature of Moroccan identity. Yet, even by the most conservative estimates, Morocco has the largest number of Tamazight speakers in the world. Morocco’s 2024 census estimates that 24.8% of the population (roughly 9.1 million) speak Tamazight in one of its regional varieties (Tarifit in the Rif region in the North, Tamazight in the Central Atlas areas, or Tachelhit (or Tashelhi(y)t)2 in the southern Souss area in the high Atlas) (HCP, 2024), not including those in the European diaspora.3 However, these figures do not capture the enormous diversity of (typically multilingual) linguistic practice among Tamazight speakers and households, ranging from isolated monolingual villages to mixed multigenerational households in large Moroccan cities (e.g., the second largest ethnolinguistic group in the Casablanca metropolis is made up of migrants from Morocco’s Tachelhit-dominant Souss region). Indeed, the same 2024 census estimates that 92% of Moroccans speak MA in their daily lives. This reflects the fact that most Tamazight speakers are also proficient in MA, whether it be their dominant language or one that they speak with some influence from Tamazight as their first language (L1).4 Despite this, the literature has paid scant attention to the range of regional, social, and stylistic variation that characterizes Tamazight-influenced MA, or the similarities and differences in the process of acquisition of MA among speakers of three major Moroccan Tamazight varieties. This is because, from structuralist and language acquisition perspectives, L1 influence on L2 tends to be conceptualized as “language transfer” (cf. Odlin, 1989), lacking the same community-level stability observable in typical L1 variation. From a sociolinguistic perspective, however, Tamazight-influenced MA has an undeniable social salience in Morocco as an object of reflexive attention, stereotyping, and even language prejudice.5In other words, we agree with Piller (2001) that there is no principled sociolinguistic reason “to regard variation between L1 and L2 users as in any way different from variation between speakers of different dialects and ethnolects” (p. 111). Such differentiation, she argues, implies that L2 users do not belong to the language community and risks constructing their way of speaking as deficient rather than simply different. Following from this, we emphasize that Tamazight-influenced MA—whether consciously or unconsciously produced—is an integral part of the Moroccan sociolinguistic repertoire, even as it is hardly discussed within the Arabic sociolinguistic literature. When scholars talk about “Berberized Arabic” (e.g., Chtatou, 1997, pp. 104–105), it is often in reference to MA as the outcome of the impact of Tamazight linguistic structures on Arabic over centuries of constant contact, to the extent that it is described as “relexified Berber” (Elmedlaoui, 2000, cited in Kossmann, 2017). While the influence of Tamazight on the historical development of MA is undeniable, the extent of this influence, however, remains debatable and controversial (see Kossmann (2017) for a recent review). For example, some Middle Eastern Arabic dialects turn out to have the same linguistic structures that were initially believed to have been borrowed from Berber (e.g., the vocalic system, see Aguadé (2010)). Overall, scholars seem to agree that although lexical borrowings are easy to discern, the similarities in the structures and constructions of the two languages make the task of ascertaining the direction of the influence more difficult, or as Lévy (2013) put it in relation to calquing: “who is calquing whom?” (p. ix). Less controversial linguistic features include the rounding of labial, velar and uvular consonants found in Tamazight, loss of vowel length contrast, sibilant harmony between /¬/ and /¶/, the borrowing of the Tamazight feminine circumfix /ta-. . .-t/ to form occupation nouns in MA, among others (see Lahrouchi, 2018; Bensoukas & Ech-Charfi, 2018). It is important to note, however, that the Tamazight influence on MA discussed in this literature operates below the level of reflexive awareness. In other words, contact features studied in this literature are not recognized as sociolinguistically significant generally, or even more specifically, in indexing Amazigh identity within the Moroccan sociolinguistic space.

Although “authentic speech” is not our primary goal in this paper, we believe that our focus on stylized Tamazight-influenced MA can shed some new light on the linguistic features and processes perceived as stereotypical from the perspective of a balanced bilingual youth. In doing so, we aim to contribute to a small but growing literature that has begun to document the dynamic multilingualism that has emerged from the processes of language contact and shift described at the outset of this paper. Typically using a code-switching paradigm, this literature has focused on the structural dimensions of MA-Tamazight code switching (Driouch & Elghazi, 2023; El Salman, 2007; Kossmann, 2012) and, to a lesser extent, on its functional dimensions (Driouch & Hermas, 2024). Meanwhile, the expressive functions of Tamazight code-switching have been examined in diasporic contexts (cf. Lafkioui, 2008, 2013, 2021); our attention to Moroccan national media illuminates the role of stylization and code-switching in the construction of regionalized identities within the domestic Moroccan sociolinguistic space. Before we turn to a detailed analysis of Ouarssam’s stylized performance, the next two sections give an overview of our conceptual and methodological approaches, respectively.

The concept of style has taken a central position in recent sociolinguistic theories to the point that the sociolinguistic analysis of identity has become synonymous with the study of style (Bucholtz, 2009). Critical of earlier unidimensional, static, and logocentric approaches to style, recent accounts adopt a semiotic approach capable of handling the multidimensional, reflexive and heteroglossic nature of stylistic practices which are key in the performance of identities (Bell, 1984; Bell & Gibson, 2011; Coupland, 2007; Eckert & Rickford, 2001; Mendoza-Denton, 2008; Rampton, 1995). To capture this dynamic nature of stylistic practices, scholars distinguish between style, styling, and stylization. Whereas a sociolinguistic style is understood as a cluster of distinctive and culturally recognizable linguistic and semiotic resources, styling refers to the active process of enacting stylistic meaning. Stylization, on the other hand, is a special type of styling understood as the self-conscious and mannered activation of styles and identities from well-known reper toires, which “brings into play stereotyped semiotic and ideological values associated with other groups, situations or times” and involves “strategic inauthenticity”, thus rendering deliberately ambiguous the “assessment of whether this utterance ‘is really mine’ rather than ‘me playing’ or ‘me subverting’” (Coupland, 2001, pp. 349–350). Acts of stylization can be put on or performed in everyday conversation, but they are integral to staged performance. Building on Bauman’s (1977, 1992, 2000) seminal work on performance, sociolinguists such as Coupland (2007) draw attention to the distinctive characteristics of staged (or high) performance, such as “preplanning, physical setup, venue, framing and social expectations” (Bell & Gibson, 2011, p. 557). Similarly, while the audience plays a key role in all performances, the expectation in staged performance is that the performer’s role is to entertain and display virtuosity. This “assumption of accountability to an audience” (Bauman, 2000, p. 1) is more pronounced with live audiences, and especially in stand-up comedy. Indeed, as Bell and Gibson (2011, p. 563) remind us, stand-up is “perhaps the most vulnerable of stage forms” because audience reactions, such as clapping or laughter (or lack thereof), can make or break the comedian’s act, for if the jokes fail, they can “literally be laughed off the stage”. Arguably, the stakes are even higher in a stand-up competition TV show, which is broadcast live to millions of viewers with the looming risk of being voted off the show with each new prime. As such, the stand-up contestants are accountable not only to a ratified co-present audience (the judges and the studio audience) but to the much wider non-ratified audiences whose votes allow them to proceed to the next rounds. That Ouarssam’s performance secured the most votes, allowing him to win the competition, invites scrutiny of his successful multilingual and heteroglossic stylization and its relationship with language ideologies, dominant and marginalized identities, and regional authenticity. Although dialect stylization has been a central focus of this literature, relatively less scholarly attention has been given to the type of heteroglossic stylization that includes multilingual and nonlinguistic semiotic resources that Ouarssam deploys in his comic performances. Building on this analytical perspective, we argue along with Jaffe et al. (2015, p. 135) that “while all performances are reflexive, heteroglossic performances particularly amplify that reflexivity with respect to their multiple frames, voices, and stances that they presuppose and establish.” Bearing in mind that multilingual stylization provides speakers with a much wider range of resources for enacting sociolinguistic differentiation and hierarchies (Vigouroux, 2015), our focus is on Ouarssam’s ability to use his entire linguistic repertoire to navigate different social voices, while orienting to what he is trying to achieve by combining linguistic and stylistic choices (viz., stylization and code-switching) in a particular way. From a heteroglossic perspective, stylization and code-switching both demonstrate how speakers draw on multiple linguistic and semiotic resources to express themselves, create and negotiate social meaning and identity within a diverse but unequal multilingual social context. The performance of mock linguistic varieties in multilingual discourse is a pristine example of heteroglossic stylization, tied in complex ways to language ideologies. It has long been argued that stylized mocking of linguistic varieties operate at different orders of indexicality, such that what may be construed as humorous and innocent at the level of direct indexicality, can be offensive and problematic at the level of indirect indexicality by virtue of the negative stereotypes that are evoked and reinforced in the stylized mocking of marginalized groups, such as the racializing styles of “mock Spanish” (Hill, 1999), “mock Ebonics” (Ronkin & Karn, 1999), and “mock Asian” (Chun, 2004). Our focus on stylized mocking of a stereotypical non-native representation of Tamazight-influenced MA in multilingual discourse is therefore meant to acknowledge this multilayered indexicality with its ideologically infused tension and ambiguity. Building on this work, we argue that the meanings and functions of stylized performances cannot be determined a priori, because they often depend on the social relations of the speakers and their interlocutors or audiences, whether stylized mocking is performed by in-group or outgroup members, as well as the nature of the stances projected through the stylization, whether they are sympathetic to or supportive of the individuals being stylized even if performed by the outgroup (Higgins, 2015). Heteroglossic performances therefore have a complicated relationship with dominant language ideologies and their association with identity. Evaluating the extent of oppressive or liberatory implications of heteroglossic performances in stand-up comedy, in particular, Jaffe et al. (2015) have argued that while “the act of putting a heteroglossic performance on stage is itself resistant, insofar as it presents as legitimate forms of linguistic, and by extension, cultural hybridity” (p. 137), the very ludic and humorous nature of comedy can undermine such claims to legitimacy (cf. Chun, 2004; Vigouroux, 2015). As we demonstrate below, stylized mocking of Tamazight-influenced MA is an important semiotic resource for Ouarssam, an emblem of regional identity within a program format that enacts a particular ideology of modern Moroccan pluralism: where a variety of ethnolinguistic identities are given representation, albeit primarily through a medium in dominant MA. Ouarssam’s performance both adheres to this format but also pushes its boundaries (for example, through bits of untranslated Tamazight) in a way that, for Moroccan audiences, is both funny and resonant with popular expressions of Amazigh identity.

## 4. Materials and Methods

This paper provides a sociolinguistic and stance-taking analysis of the performances of the Moroccan comedian Zakaria Ouarssam, which aired as part of the third season of the comedy competition Stand Up on Morocco’s Al Aoula TV from January to March 2019. The Stand Up show is widely popular and has been the second most-watched show on Al Aoula TV since it first aired. The finale was seen by 5.4 million viewers (not including reruns). Stand Up’s YouTube channel has close to 1 million followers and 245 million views, and Ouarssam’s sketches are among the most viewed on its channel, with two videos with over 10 million views. As a contestant, Ouarssam appeared on four of the show’s eight episodes (called “primes”), each lasting about 2.5 hours. The program used both judges’ feedback and audience voting to progressively eliminate contestants until the finale, where Ouarssam was declared the season’s champion. Our analysis specifically focuses on Ouarssam’s sketches across the four primes, summarized in Table 1 below.

Our linguistic analysis in Section 5.1 follows in the tradition of style-centric soci olinguistics to document some of the linguistic resources Ouarssam uses to create what Silverstein (2003) calls first-order and second-order indexical effects (cf. Eckert, 2008; Hachimi, 2007, 2018; Johnstone & Kiesling, 2008; Mendoza-Denton, 2008; Sharma, 2015; Zhang, 2005; among others). First-order indexicality, according to Silverstein, refers to the ideological link between specific linguistic features and some sociocultural model of personhood. To investigate this, we transcribed 35 minutes of audio and identified salient linguistic features across all levels of the grammar that, in our own analysis, are stereotypically associated with Tamazight-influenced MA within the broader Moroccan indexical field. We also identify examples of second-order indexical effects, where those same features come to be associated not only with a model of personhood, but also the characterological traits associated with that category of person. Our analysis here, informed by years of ethnographic and personal experience in the Middle Atlas and city of Khenifra specifically (cf. Smail, 2022), serves to establish a basis for understanding Ouarssam’s embodied performance (Section 5.2). Our analysis in no way lays claim to being a gen eralized account of Tamazight to MA language transfer. Indeed, we also show that the stylized register that Ouarssam adopts in his performance is not a singular “code,” but rather is deployed to varying degrees as a part of his effort to evoke a cast of comedic personae, including not only his own character as a narrator but also an ornery grandfather, a grandmother, a postmaster, a police officer, a romantic city guy, and many more.

Building on the view of stand-up comedy as interaction (Rutter, 1997), our analysis in Section 5.2 excerpts discourse from the openings and closings of each sketch and includes a longer interactional analysis of the opening acts of the Prime 2 sketch on “Ramadan” and Prime 8 Sketch 1 on “Problems”. Our approach to style emphasizes that style effects are achieved not only linguistically but also through the co-occurrence of linguistic, par alinguistic, and embodied resources of communication. Building on a long tradition of interactional sociolinguistics (cf. Gumperz, 1992, 2015; Bucholtz & Hall, 2005), we take these stylization resources as contextualization cues that index how Ouarssam means what he says within the playful frame of stand-up comedy. This interdisciplinary approach is key to demonstrating how these semiotic resources work together to achieve specific communicative and metacommunicative ends. Our discursive analysis then turns to the moment-by-moment multilingual realization of stance-taking by paying attention to the interplay of code-switching, style shifting, speech tempo, tone, gaze, facial expressions, and other embodied resources such as body language, song, and dance in the creation and negotiation of meanings and identities on stage.

## 5. Results: Heteroglossic Stylization and the Staged Performance of Khenifri Identity

The following analysis proceeds in two parts. Section 5.1 documents some of the linguistic features Ouarssam uses to index an Amazigh/Khenifri identity, as well as the second-order indexical effects associated with those characters. Section 5.2 is a discourse analysis of stance-taking during his embodied performance of those characters, and how he indexes not only characterological figures but relationships between himself as a performer and his voting audience. We show that Ouarssam deploys a heteroglossic repertoire, which includes linguistically marked Tamazight-influenced MA, Tamazight, MA-Tamazight code switching and mixing, regional Khenifra variety of MA, Standard Arabic, Moroccan French, including nativized French loans and catch phrases, and other visual and embodied re sources. This heteroglossic stylization, we argue, is an important semiotic resource as he attempts to authenticate his bilingual Khenifri identity, legitimate in-group mockery, and appeal to broader enthusiasm for Amazigh identity, all the while also indexing specific stances, activities, and characterological figures among other expressive and metaprag matic goals.

## Abstract
### 5.1. Linguistic Resources of Stylized Tamazight-Influenced MA
#### 5.1.1. Phonological Resources

At the phonological level, consonant gemination is by far the most dominant and most consistent linguistic resource for stylizing Tamazight-influenced MA in Ouarssam’s performance, but its exaggeration often depends on the social type being performed. Play ing with vowels comes a close second in terms of consistency, including nasalization of final vowels, lowering high front vowels (/i/ to /e/ or /¢/), vowel lengthening espe cially in final positions, a combination of nasalization and lowering, and/or lengthening. Other phonological processes include the lenition of stops to different degrees, such as /b/ > /β/; /k/ > /ç/, the release of stops, the backing of consonants, ¶-coloration of the sound /l/, degemination within and across word boundaries, e.g., dri for d£rri “boy”, l-qad ĳja for l-qad ĳijja “the issue”, wah¯ £d nuba for wah¯ £d n-nuba “once”. These phonological processes apply equally to MA words as well as French loans and expressions (e.g., the duplicate expression cinq cinq [sĩ:k sĩ:k] “lit. five (out of) five, i.e., perfect” is pronounced [ssĩ:ç ssĩ:ç] by geminating the sound /s/ and affricating the sound /k/. Together, these stylized resources show up most prominently when voicing the stereo typical country bumpkin with low proficiency in MA, which is epitomized by the charac terological figure of the grandfather, but by no means restricted to it. For example, in Prime 2, the constructed dialogue between Ouarssam’s voicing of his grandfather ideologically positions the latter as a lazy, binge eater who lacks piety for missing Ramadan evening prayers, known for requiring lots of energy and effort. Such second-order indexes semioti cally link Tamazight-influenced MA with a host of undesirable qualities and activities. At the same time, marked Tamazight-influenced MA is also used to directly index the come- dian’s own silly stances and absurd activities, such as his numerous irrational solutions to ensure that his own national identity card is used come hell or high water (e.g., sketch 2 in Prime 5).

#### 5.1.2. Morphosyntactic and Lexical Resources

Ouarssam made use of a few but highly marked morphosyntactic and lexical resources in his stylized performance to exaggerate the heaviness of Tamazight-influenced MA and index specific stances and characterological figures. For example, as shown in Table 2, he resorted to the insertion of the definite marker l- in positions when none is allowed in normative MA, e.g., with the indefinite particle ¬i-l, with the adverb l-bs ĳs ĳ£h¯ (treating an adverb as a noun), with the possessive pronoun “the my belly”, with double negative markers, and with the deictic particle rah which requires an indefinite nominal adjective, among others. From the language ideological perspective of normative MA, these are norm violations of the definite marker, which not only index incomplete acquisition of the system by Tamazight-dominant speakers of MA but also semiotically associate them with negative social meanings. Of great significance, while the stylization of the definite article was used predominantly to animate the persona of the grandfather as the quintessential old Tamazight-dominant country bumpkin, it was also deployed by Ouarssam to animate other voices, and specifically to index stances of laziness, foolishness, backwardness, and unreasonableness, to name a few. Furthermore, Ouarssam also resorted to stereotypical mispronunciations of French loanwords in MA, such as [lmonid ĳa] for normative MA [lmonad ĳa] (French [limªnad], which has come to mean all kinds of soft drinks in MA) or borrowed French words and phrases, such as his stylization of la carte nationale [la kaKt nasjªnal] “national identity card,” by substituting the sound [n] for [j] to render [nasjªnal] as [jasjonal]. It is impor tant to note that while trilling the /r/ in [la kart£] or varying between the trill and the standard French uvular pronunciation /K/ are common even among highly educated Moroccan francophones, pronouncing [n] as [j] provokes laughter because it indexes the incongruity between someone who does not know French but tries to sound educated and sophisticated—a nod to the multiple social meanings associated with non-standard pronunciations and to the language ideologies that underpin them. Other stigmatized styl ized forms include the stereotypical substitution of [b] for [p], denasalization of standard French vowels, and deletion of /w/ in [¬abban] for normative French [¬A˜pwE˜] “shampoo”. It must be clarified, however, that such highly marked lexical items are not limited to uneducated rural Tamazight speakers per se; rather, they can index speakers’ rurality, old age, lack of formal education, and unfamiliarity with the French language. Although Ouarssam deploys only a few stereotypical lexical variables, they are highly effective in semiotically associating unreasonable behavior and activities with Tamazight-accented MA and reasonableness and rationality with normative MA and/or relatively less marked MA dialect of Khenifra, which is represented and animated by voices of non-kin authority figures including, for example, the character of the policeman who pulls him aside to tell him to go home and stop his nonsense,6 or the employee at the post office who asks for his identity card. While our goal is not to hold performed speech accountable to actual speech, it is worth noting that, overall, Ouarssam’s dialect stylization of Tamazight-influenced MA approximates but does not account for the wide-ranging variation that exists in real people’s speech. Surprisingly missing in his stylization, for example, is the total absence of non normative use of gender and number agreement, which is common among L1 Tamazight speakers with little proficiency in MA. These features are well attested and frequently heard by the first author among her extended family members, especially those who are older and live in rural areas or towns where Tamazight is the dominant language in the family and the community at large (e.g., towns of Tounfit, Boumia, Bensmim, Ein Leuh, among others), and everyday in-group/familial stylization by the younger generation who are fully bilingual in Tamazight and MA. Why gender and number agreement fly below the radar of social awareness, whereas the definite article is ideologically salient in Ouarssam’s stylization of Tamazight-influenced MA, is an important question that is beyond the scope of this paper.7 What is relevant for our purposes here is that, as Bell and Gibson (2011) have noted, performers can undershoot as well as overshoot the target in stylized speech. These microlinguistic resources are important in understanding the ways in which Ouarssam’s performance positions normative MA as “neutral”, and Tamazight-influenced MA as backward, silly, and out of place. This language ideological positioning is con structed in the show itself, such that the “framing” talk by the show’s emcees and judges occurs in normative MA, and the show’s contestants—each labeled with their own city of origin—typically perform in more marked accents with varying degrees of stylization. This juxtaposition between locally marked MA varieties and their supra-local or normative counterpart is a staple in Moroccan comedy.8 We turn next to a close discourse analysis of stance-taking in Ouarssam’s performance to underscore the significance of his heteroglossic stylization in the co-construction of a specifically and unmistakably Khenifri identity.

### 5.2. Analysis of Stance-Taking in Performed Heteroglossic Stylization

Ouarssam’s comedy relies heavily on personal experience-based humor and story telling, which are well-known strategies used by comedians to establish rapport and connection with the audience. To this end, Ouarssam mobilizes his heteroglossic reper toire (i.e., Tamazight, Tamazight-influenced MA, normative MA, regional Khenifri MA dialect, French, and Standard Arabic as well as code-switching between these varieties in conjunction with other semiotic resources and cultural references). Most striking in Ouarssam’s comic acts is that he makes strategic use of “organizational” and “insertional” code-switching styles (cf. Bentahila & Davies, 2002). While the former refers to the sys tematic relationship code-switching has in organizing the structure of his opening and closing comic acts, as illustrated in Table 3, the latter refers to the occasional incorporation of Tamazight, French, and Standard Arabic nouns, loans, catch phrases, vocatives, and whole clauses, in discourse quantitatively dominated by different varieties and registers of MA. Importantly, the relative proportion of code-switching between MA and Tamazight is significantly higher than his MA-French and MA-Standard Arabic code switching (i.e., diglossic code switching), which are “unmarked” choices to use Myers-Scotton’s (2002) terminology. MA-Tamazight code switching, on the other hand, is the “marked” choice because it includes large chunks of information-bearing discourse in salient positions which can be presumed to be incomprehensible to much of his immediate and virtual MA-dominant audience. And while Ouarssam resorted to reiteration and paraphrasing— common strategies in code-switching to ensure comprehension (Gumperz, 1982)—delaying or altogether withholding translation of Tamazight is also a common strategic choice in his comic performances. For illustrative purposes, our analysis is structured around spe cific interactional moves that Ouarssam makes in select comedic performances, which are summarized in Table 3 below. Close discursive analysis reveals that Ouarssam deploys Tamazight and Tamazight Arabic code switching and mixing in significant and meaningful ways in structuring the openings and closings of his performances, which help enhance the distinctiveness and memorability of his comic acts. For example, as we illustrate in Table 3, Ouarssam followed a consistent format by opening four out of five sketches in Tamazight either by deploying a long stretch of untranslated Tamazight discourse as in his first sketches in Primes 2, 5, and 7 or by mixing Tamazight and MA catch phrases in opening Sketch 2 in Prime 5 and Sketch 1 in Prime 8. However, in the second and final sketch in Prime 8 (the finale), he opened his act in an iconic MA song, but opted to close it by bidding farewell to the audience in normative MA ssalamu Qalikum, immediately followed by a switch to the untranslated Tamazight word tanmmirt “thank you”, which closed not only the performance but his participation in the competition as a whole. It is important to note that in closing earlier acts, Ouarssam combined Tamazight-influenced MA catch phrases with the French merci “thank you”, which is pronounced [miGsi] rather than standard French [m¢K.si], i.e., substituting the vowel /¢/ with /i/, typical of some social varieties of Moroccan French considered sub-standard from dominant language ideologies. It is the tension between these hybrid communicative practices that is key in the construction of his comic style, his regional identity, and his audience as multilingual, multicultural, and plural (cf. Looking closely at Ouarssam’s first live performance, which aired on Prime 2 of the Stand Up competition show, is important because, as his first act on stage as a contestant, it was an opportunity to introduce himself and impress the ratified audience (i.e., the judges and studio audience) as well as the non-ratified voting Moroccan audience. As illustrated in Extract 1, Ouarssam’s Khenifri identity was on full display through a well-crafted multilingual and embodied performance. Specifically, he started speaking Tamazight before appearing on stage and came running while singing a well-known Amazigh joke “nt¬a nswa nkks Pazzar hajjax ddan ssara” repeating the refrain twice, while moving his upper body in unmistakable iconic Ahidous Berber dance, which is specific to the Middle Atlas region. The significance of these embodied and interdiscursive moves is that the joke itself is about an Amazigh man from the countryside who, upon visiting the city, was arrested, then taken to the police station, where his hair was cut, he was fed, and then he was taken in a police car. What is funny is that he unknowingly met all these unpleasant events with a happy-go-lucky attitude, saying when asked, “I ate, drank, cut my hair, and I am going for a ride”. This joke is part of the popular cultural repertoire of the Central Atlas region and is familiar to Tamazight and non-Tamazight speakers alike, which reproduces through its retellings the stereotype of the gullible Amazigh country bumpkin who cannot make obvious distinctions between a police arrest and a pleasant adventure and generosity. Ouarssam doubles down on indexing a Central Atlas Amazigh identity through the re entextualization of a joke in untranslated Tamazight and the performance of iconic Ahidous dance that Moroccan viewers, Amazighophone and Arabophone alike, can easily associate with the Central Atlas in view of the folklorization of Amazigh cultural identity discussed earlier.9 These multilingual resources and multimodal recontextualization play a key role in the construction and reconstruction of localized Amazigh identity (see Lafkioui (2008, 2013) for how this works in computer-mediated discourse).

In line 2, Ouarssam then gushes in rapid-fire in Tamazight, and after a brief pause, he switches to strongly marked Tamazight-accented MA to ask: “fhmtu ¬i h¯ a¶ã!?” “Did you understand anything?”. Not only does this metalinguistic question itself presuppose a lack of understanding of Tamazight by his co-nationals, but he used it in conjunction with humorous facial expressions, including raised eyebrows and eye stares, to deliver the punchline. The pretend serious tone of his metalinguistic question was immediately answered and demystified in a jovial tone in Tamazight-influenced MA: h¯it xxukom m£nn xnifr ĳa, Gir lkwippa lli djalkom “Because your brother is from Khenifra, only the cool haircut is yours”. In delivering this line, Ouarssam did not explicitly name the language he was speaking; instead, he simply disclosed his regional identity to justify his use of Tamazight, emphasizing the brotherly ties with the co-present studio audience of Casablanca where the show is held while also acknowledging having borrowed their fashionable haircut.10 The presupposition of this “we/they” dichotomy is that Tamazight-speaking people from Khenifra do not sport fashionable or cool haircuts. These simultaneous adequation and distinction intersubjective tactics, to use Bucholtz and Hall’s (2005) framework of identity in interaction, allow Ouarssam to position himself as a young, modern, urban Tamazight Arabic bilingual from Khenifra but with the same stroke to distinguish and distance himself from the figure of the rural Amazigh person whose low proficiency in MA is the object of humor (e.g., the grandfather). It is worth emphasizing that Ouarssam’s strategic use of untranslated Tamazight is not limited to opening and closing acts. In fact, bits of untranslated Tamazight expressions and phrases, vocatives, and discourse markers consistently peppered all his performances, including Pahiwawi “oh you (pl.)”, jah¯ijjana “what the hell”, ddifand ĳi used by Tamazight speakers to convey something is forbidden or bad, and to a lesser extent basic vocabulary such as tignni “food”, and Puhu “no”, and juh¯ nna “grandma”, which he used several times without translation, then decides to translate it for the audience later in the performance in more than one way, such as ¶dda “grandma”, and mrat dak ¶ddi “the wife of that grandpa” to enhance the humor. In other words, playful translation itself is the punchline. Other macaronic linguistic practices include calques such as drtu zzin from Tamazight expression tjam zzin “you look beautiful” when addressing the studio audience.

In this extract, Ouarssam started his narrative with a fully integrated Arabic loan in Tamazight, h¯mdas rbbi: n¬kras “thanks and praise be to God”, which may or may not be understood by his non-Tamazight speaking Moroccan audience, but his choice to close the narrative by switching to a Tamazight chant or lyrical poetry (known as Izlan in Tamazight) is interactionally significant. While this chant wa: jzzi:l uja jjix, ajarbbi ¬mm£l Gifi “What I have done is great. May God help me achieve my goal (i.e., win)” is well known in the Middle Atlas and is often sung by people at weddings and other festive celebrations, including by non-fluent speakers of Tamazight who may not fully know what they are saying, it is certainly not intelligible to the Arabic-speaking majority audience. Together, the content of his rhetorical question in Tamazight-influenced MA “Do you imagine if I go to and tell my father that I am not the only one left!? Can you imagine or not!?”, then his breaking into the performance of a Tamazight song bearing high information load complete with coordinated Amazigh dance moves (i.e., downward handclapping and a lowered posture), are strategic solidarity-seeking moves indexed as much by the implicature of his joke (i.e., the implication that he needs their help, i.e., their votes, to win the competition in order to make his father proud, or at the very least escape harsh treatment) as it is by varying patterns of code-switching and stylizing. To sum up, untranslated Tamazight, delayed translation of a Tamazight joke, a tradi tional Amazigh dance, and explicit talk about local Khenifra identity are constellations of semiotic resources used very early in Ouarssam’s heteroglossic performance in an attempt to authenticate his Middle Atlas Amazigh identity and solidify his in-group membership

## 6. Discussion

Our analysis has shown how Ouarssam brought together phonological, morphosyntac tic, and lexical features to draw a contrast between the stylized Tamazight-influenced MA of his staged personae and normative MA. At a discursive level, Ouarssam makes use of this contrast to multiple ends. On one level, Ouarssam’s stylization of Tamazight-influenced MA functions as an “icon” (Irvine & Gal, 2000) of the characterological traits that he makes the subject of his humor, such as naiveté, laziness, or lack of piety; for example, miscon struing an arrest for a joy ride is funny in large part because his narration is embodied and stylized—through accent, dance, and untranslated Tamazight—in a way that gives the impression of a naïve simpleton only concerned with a good time. Together, the accent and his performance play into well-worn stereotypes about Khenifra, rural Moroccans, and cer tain types of Tamazight speakers generally. On another level, legitimate mockery (cf. Chun, 2004) of these stereotypes depends on Ouarssam’s complex stance-taking in relation to his audience and the characters to which he gives voice. Stylization of Tamazight-influenced MA helps “transpose the origo” (Agha, 2007, p. 52) of his staged personae, making it obvious that Ouarssam-the-performer is not the same as the “social voice” (Bakhtin, 1981) he mobilizes; Ouarssam represents an urbanized and bilingual generation of Khenifris poking fun at an older, more monolingual and rural generation, a dynamic emblematic in Morocco’s recent history of urbanization and sociolinguistic change. At the same time, as an urban Khenifri youth, Ouarssam’s proximity to the subject that he mocks invites and seemingly authorizes the audience to do the same. We thus see Ouarssam’s performance as reinforcing dominant language ideologies in Morocco in at least two ways: by normalizing presumably socially and geographically unmarked MA as the medium of national public life (cf. Hachimi, 2007), and by associating Tamazight with a backward and bygone way of being located in the margins of Morocco’s modernity (cf. Boum, 2007; Chakrani, 2013; Hoffman, 2006, 2008; Maddy-Weitzman, 2011). With regard to the latter, imagining and articulating an Amazigh modernity for Morocco has been a central ideological project of the Moroccan Amazigh Cultural Movement and, since the creation of IRCAM, the Moroccan state as well. As a number of studies have documented, this has often involved “upscaling” (cf. Blommaert, 2007) Amazigh identity, from local to national or transnational imaginaries of belonging (Cornwall & Atia, 2012; Jay, 2016; Lafkioui, 2024; Silverstein, 2013), often tied to formal or informal projects of language standardization. Ouarssam’s representations, by contrast, run counter to this trend by insisting on a locally specific Khenifri figure. In this vein, we argue that Ouarssam’s performances, despite their rehearsal of prob lematic tropes, also push the envelope of Amazigh representation in the Moroccan national media space in ways that more high-brow and/or state-sanctioned discourses have not. Indeed, there is evidence that, as Kabel (2018) argues, the early 2000s Amazigh renaissance has given way to a state of “devitalization,” where monoglot language ideological com mitments to purity and standardization have alienated many Moroccans from language officialization, whether Tamazight-speaking or not. However, despite the limitations of state language officialization, popular interest in Amazigh identity beyond language has surged in Morocco (Lafkioui, 2024), and in this vein, Ouarssam’s use of heteroglossic stylization eschews ideologies of purity in favor of a repertoire that plays with and appeals to Moroccans’ everyday heteroglossic reality. In this sense, Ouarssam is able to present as authentic—despite his hyperbolized characters—in ways that standard language repre-

## 7. Conclusions

In using Tamazight-influenced MA on stage, Zakaria Ouarssam inserts himself within a specific and understudied social history within the sociolinguistics of Morocco: the multilingual dynamics of urbanization and intergenerational language shift. Our linguistic analysis documents the ways in which Ouarssam draws on phonological, morphosyntactic, and lexical resources to create contrasts between his seemingly “neutral” MA of everyday speech as a young urbanite and a stylized Tamazight-accented MA germane to his elders with rural roots. Our stance-taking analysis examines the performative significance of Ouarssam’s comedy and his success on the Stand Up show. We argue that rather than strictly mocking speakers of Tamazight-influenced MA, Ouarssam’s performance mobilizes his youth urbanite positionality to tap into surging interest in Amazigh identity among those most like him. Tamazight-influenced MA as a form is not new, but Ouarssam’s stylistic mobilization of it, along with untranslated Tamazight in MA-dominant spaces, and use of other heteroglossic linguistic resources, represents significant novelty in the Moroccan public media space.
