Behind-the-Scenes Facts About The Movie Titanic

# Behind-the-Scenes Facts About The Movie Titanic

 Dec 29 THINGS Miles Brucker 

> “Winning that ticket, Rose, was the best thing that ever happened to me... it brought me to you. And I'm thankful for that, Rose. I'm thankful. You must do me this honor. Promise me you'll survive. That you won't give up, no matter what happens, no matter how hopeless. Promise me now, Rose, and never let go of that promise.” – Jack, Titanic.

For years, the cinematic blockbuster, Titanic, held the record for highest grossing film of all time. There’s a reason for that: not only does the true-to-life story seem to naturally captivate our imagination, the more romantic and artistic elements which were added by James Cameron serve to elevate our emotional reaction and deepen the already tragic narrative. To this day, the story of the Titanic's maiden (and final) voyage, serves as a potent reminder of humanity's occasional hubris. And the film serves as a reminder that we're all suckers for a tragic love story (and a soundtrack from Celine).

Here are our favorite facts about the movie Titanic:

## 1. Whoops...

When Jack is preparing to draw Rose, he says to her, "Over on the bed...the couch." The line was scripted "Lie on that couch," but Leonardo DiCaprio made an honest mistake and James Cameron liked it so much he kept it in.

Paramount , Titanic (1997)

## 2. Well said, Kate.

Eager to get the role of Rose, Kate Winslet sent James Cameron daily notes from England. She also went to LA and kept phoning him until she got the part: "You don't understand! I am Rose! I don't know why you're even seeing anyone else!"

C Flanigan, Getty Images

## 3. A long time to sink.

The scenes set in 1912 (the whole movie except the present-day scenes and the opening and ending credits) have a total length of two hours and forty minutes, the exact time it took for Titanic to sink. Also, the collision with the iceberg reportedly lasted 37 seconds, which is how long the collision scene is in the movie.

Paramount, Titanic (1997)

## 4. A not-so-lonely grave.

When James Cameron was writing the movie, he intended for the main characters Rose DeWitt Bukater and Jack Dawson to be entirely fictitious. It was only after the script was finished that he discovered that there had been a real "J. Dawson" who passed aboard the Titanic. This "J. Dawson" was trimmer Joseph Dawson, who had been born September 1888 in Dublin, Ireland. His body was salvaged and buried at Fairview Lawn cemetery in Nova Scotia with many other Titanic victims. Today, his grave stone (#227) is the most widely visited in the cemetery.

Bigg(g)er, CC BY 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

## 5. A little wet on set.

Approximately 120 tons of water (triple what had been initially planned) were released for Eric Braeden's final scene. Braeden said that he has never been more terrified in his life than when he was preparing for it, as there was obviously no possible physical rehearsal.

Francois Durand, Getty Images

## 6. Great job, guys. How about some PCP?

On the final night of shooting, one or more pranksters mixed the dissociative hallucinogen PCP (angel dust) into the clam chowder served to the cast and crew. 80 people were taken ill, and more than 50 were hospitalized with hallucinations. When James Cameron realized what was happening, he forced himself to vomit before the drug took full effect. Bill Paxton felt listless for two weeks after the incident (although PCP's primary effects only last a few hours, the drug itself can take eight or more days to completely metabolize out of the body). The culprit(s) were never caught.

broddi, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

## 7. Fighting for Leo.

The studios wanted Matthew McConaughey to play Jack, but James Cameron insisted on Leonardo DiCaprio. He and Kate Winslet committed to the film even before the script was written, on the basis only of a 165-page outline James Cameron had written.

David Torcivia, Flickr

## 8. Real-life inspiration.

Many of the "core extras" used for the movie took on characteristics of actual survivors. One scene where two little girls are loaded onto a lifeboat and the man says, "It's only for a little while" is based on testimony from one of the girls who survived.

 Paramount ,Titanic (1997)

## 9. Recreating the Atlantic.

The post-sinking scenes were shot in a 350,000 gallon tank where the frozen corpses were created by applying a powder on the actors that then crystallized when exposed to water. Wax was applied to hair and clothes to create a wet look.

Paramount , Titanic (1997)

## 10. Improvised and awesome.

The movie's line "I'm the king of the world!" was ad-libbed by Leonardo DiCaprio. It was voted as the #4 of "The 100 Greatest Movie Lines" by Premiere in 2007.

Paramount ,Titanic (1997)

## 11. A right-sized raft.

The piece of wooden paneling that Rose floated on after the sinking is based upon a genuine artifact that survived the sinking and is on display at the Maritime Museum of the Atlantic in Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada, though it was scaled larger to provide sufficient buoyancy as a life-raft for Rose.

Phobophile~commonswiki, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

## 12. Isn't Rose lovable?

This was the first film to be nominated twice for an Academy Award for the portrayal of the same character: Kate Winslet received a Best Actress nomination for her role as Rose and Gloria Stuart received a Best Supporting Actress nomination for her portrayal of the older Rose. The next time this happened was with the movie Iris (2001), which also starred Winslet.

Alberto E. Rodriguez , Getty Images

## 13. Four-legged Phelps.

Rose, in her old age, owns a Pomeranian. A Pomeranian was one of only three dogs known to have survived the disaster. As the real ship sank, a passenger freed dogs from their kennels and a survivor later recalled a French bulldog swimming in the ocean. James Cameron filmed scenes portraying the doomed animals but cut them.

Paramount , Titanic (1997)

## 14. Winning Cameron's heart.

James Cameron was adamant about not including any songs in the film, even over the closing credits. Composer James Horner secretly arranged with lyricist Will Jennings and singer Céline Dion to write "My Heart Will Go On" and record a demo tape, which he then presented to Cameron, who responded very favorably and included the song over the closing credits. The song went on to win the Academy Award for Best Original Song.

Gareth Cattermole, Getty Images

## 15. Sneaky little buggers.

In the movie, Jack is a 3rd class passenger on the Titanic who sneaks his way up to first class with the hopes of never getting caught. In the real disaster in 1912, Third Class Passenger Hilda Maria Hellström really did sneak up to first class out of curiosity and never got caught. However, she was in her 3rd class cabin when the Titanic hit an iceberg, and she ended up surviving the sinking by boarding one of the last lifeboats to leave, Collapsible C.

Paramount , Titanic (1997)

## 16. Shameless self promotion.

James Cameron wrote the role of Lewis Bodine with his friend Lewis Abernathy in mind. When he couldn't find an actor to play the part, he went to Abernathy and asked, essentially, if he would play himself. Abernathy replied, "If you want to mess up your movie by casting me, buddy, alright."

Paramount , Titanic (1997)

## 17. Sweet, colorful sunshine.

During the part when Rose and Jack are at the bow of the ship (when Rose says "I'm flying, Jack!"), the sunset was real and not CGI. James Cameron knew that sunset was the perfect time to do that scene.

Paramount , Titanic (1997)

## 18. Sorry, Lindsay.

Lindsay Lohan auditioned for the role of Cora Cartmell. Lohan, who was then an unknown actress and was only 8 years old at the time casting took place, was the top choice for the role. However, James Cameron felt that Lohan's fiery red hair would confuse people into thinking she was related to the characters Rose and Ruth, who both had fiery red hair. Alexandrea Owens was cast instead.

Featureflash Photo Agency, Shutterstock

## 19. Just another few hundred million...

April 15, 2012 marked the 100th anniversary of the sinking of the Titanic. It was celebrated by the 3D special re-release of the 1997 James Cameron blockbuster Titanic, which earned the film an additional $343 million worldwide, pushing Titanic's worldwide total to an incredible $2.18 billion!

Paramount , Titanic (1997)

## 20. A nice dip in the pool.

Kate Winslet was one of the few actors who didn't want to wear a wetsuit during the water scenes. The water was so cold that when Rose gasps upon diving into the tank, it was the actress’s genuine reaction to the frigid water. As a result of not wearing a wetsuit, she got pneumonia.

Maggie (Maggiejumps), Wikimedia Commons

## 21. What can't James do?

James Cameron, not Leonardo DiCaprio, drew all of the pictures in Jack's sketchbook. This included the nude picture of Rose wearing the necklace that was drawn during the film. Thus, the hands seen sketching Rose during her nude scene were not Jack's but Cameron's. In post-production, Cameron, who is left-handed, actually went as far as to mirror-image the sketching shots so the artist would be appear to be right-handed, like DiCaprio!

Paramount , Titanic (1997)

## 22. Breaking the ice.

After finding out that she was going to be naked in front of Leonardo DiCaprio, Kate Winslet decided to break the ice by flashing him the first time they met! The nude sketch scene was actually one of the first scenes that was shot for the movie.

Paramount , Titanic (1997)

## 23. From Sweden with a potty mouth.

The Swedish phrases that Sven and his buddy exchange during the card game translate into the following: "I can't believe you bet our tickets! Shut up!" When grabbing Jack by the throat: "You damn weasel!" And after punching his buddy in the face: "You damn idiot! What the hell are we gonna do? I'm gonna kill you!"

Paramount , Titanic (1997)

## 24.

James Cameron infamously threatened to fire anyone who would dare get out of the tank for a bathroom break while shooting the lifeboat scenes, which lead to more than a few actors (including Kate Winslet) relieving themselves in the water.

Gage Skidmore, Flickr

## 25. Fake breath.

The scenes during which Thomas Andrews chastises Second Officer Charles Lightoller for sending the boats away without filling them to capacity is the only scene in the entire film in which the actors' breath was not digitally added in later.

Paramount , Titanic (1997)

## 26. A little over budget.

The film was initially budgeted at $135,000,000, but going two months over schedule required asking Paramount Pictures to contribute an additional $65,000,000 in exchange for U.S. distribution rights. But that is okay because it was the highest grossing film in box office history with a worldwide gross of US$1.8 billion until it was surpassed by Avatar (2009). Both films were directed by James Cameron.

Tinseltown, Shutterstock

## 27. Leave it to the imagination.

Jack's portrait of the one-legged prostitute is actually visible for two frames as he turns the page to his sketch of "Madam Bijoux." James Cameron decided not to show the portrait as he thought the audience would imagine something better.

Paramount , Titanic (1997)

## 28. Putting the work first.

James Cameron originally wanted Enya to compose the score for the film and even went so far as to assemble a rough edit using her music. When Enya declined, Cameron hired James Horner (who had composed the music for Cameron's previous film Aliens (1986)) to write the score. Horner stated that the tensions with Cameron were so high during post-production of "Aliens" that he assumed he and Cameron would never work together again. However, Cameron was so impressed with Horner's score from Braveheart (1995) that he contacted Horner, who was willing to forget the past.

FERT98, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

## 29. Real rooms.

The rooms that Caledon Hockley, Rose DeWitt Bukater and Ruth DeWitt Bukater occupied (B52, B54 and B56) were actual rooms on the real Titanic. They were originally booked by J.P. Morgan, but he canceled before the ship sailed. Morgan had a controlling interest in International Mercantile Marine, a conglomerate that owned the White Star Line. It was said that Bruce Ismay booked the rooms following Morgan's cancellation, but this was never proven.

Recuerdos de Pandora, Flickr

## 30. Reduce, reuse, recycle.

The scale model of the underwater wrecked ship was on display in the Titanic museum in Branson, MO for years. In August 2011, it was taken back to Hollywood and used to film the Titanic 3-D movie.

Roland Arhelger, CC BY-SA 4.0 , Wikimedia Commons

## 31. True love aboard.

Everyone know the romantic scenes between Jack and Rose, but most fans have no clue there was another love story featured in the film. The elderly couple seen hugging on the bed while water floods their room were the owners of Macy's department store in New York, Ida and Isidor Straus, both of whom died on the Titanic. Ida was offered a seat on a lifeboat but refused so that she could stay with her husband, saying, "As we have lived together, so we shall die together."

Paramount , Titanic (1997)

## 32. Really?

James Cameron, being a certified scuba diver, admitted that the reason why he wanted to make a movie about "a big ship that sinks" was because he wanted to dive to the real wreck of the Titanic.

NOAA/Institute for Exploration., Wikimedia Commons

S hare this with your friends by clicking below if you love this iconic movie. We hope you enjoyed these Titanic facts!

### Tragic Facts About Catherine of Aragon, Henry VIII’s First Wife 

 Jun 10 Christine Tran 

Dear reader,

Want to tell us to write facts on a topic? We’re always looking for your input! Please reach out to us to let us know what you’re interested in reading. Your suggestions can be as general or specific as you like, from “Life” to “Compact Cars and Trucks” to “A Subspecies of Capybara Called Hydrochoerus Isthmius.” We’ll get our writers on it because we want to create articles on the topics you’re interested in. Titanic Sinking: Timeline, Cause, Deaths and Rescue

# The Sinking of the Titanic: What Happened

Titanic struck an iceberg at about 11:40 p.m. on April 14, 1912, while crossing the North Atlantic on its maiden voyage. Flooding spread through more forward compartments than the ship could survive, and Titanic sank at about 2:20 a.m. on April 15. The disaster lasted roughly two hours and forty minutes, but the reasons so many people died extend beyond the collision itself.

Written and researched by Don St Germain Last reviewed: July 2026

 Collision About 11:40 p.m., April 14, 1912 

 Final sinking About 2:20 a.m., April 15, 1912 

 Time from collision to sinking About 2 hours 40 minutes 

 Rescue ship RMS Carpathia 

## Start with the four main questions

These guides explain the physical cause, the night’s sequence, the evacuation and the rescue in greater detail.

Cause

### Why did Titanic sink?

Understand the iceberg damage, progressive flooding, design limits and final breakup.

### What happened minute by minute?

Follow the collision, distress calls, lifeboat launches, final plunge and rescue.

Evacuation

### How were the lifeboats used?

Search all 20 boats and compare capacity, launch order, occupants and outcomes.

### How did Carpathia reach the survivors?

See how the responding ship prepared, crossed the ice field and recovered the boats.

## The sinking in plain language

- The iceberg collision opened Titanic to the sea across more forward compartments than the ship could remain afloat with.
- The ship sank gradually at first, which left many passengers unsure that entering a small open lifeboat was safer than staying aboard.
- The iceberg explains why Titanic was lost. Too few boat places, uneven loading, delayed access, cold water and distant rescue help explain why more than 1,500 people died.
- Titanic carried 20 lifeboats. Their total rated capacity was far below the number of passengers and crew aboard, and several boats left with empty seats.
- Carpathia reached the first lifeboat at about 4:10 a.m., nearly two hours after Titanic disappeared beneath the Atlantic.

## A concise timeline of the Titanic sinking

Times are approximate because witness watches, ship clocks and later reconstructions do not agree on every minute. The broad sequence is well established.

| Approximate time | What happened | Why it mattered |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Evening, April 14 | Titanic receives several reports of ice ahead on the North Atlantic route. | The messages establish that the ship was entering a region where ice had been reported. |
| 11:40 p.m. | The lookouts sight an iceberg and the bridge orders evasive action. Titanic strikes the ice along the starboard side. | Damage below the waterline allows seawater into several forward compartments. |
| Around midnight | Captain Edward Smith and shipbuilder Thomas Andrews review the flooding. | The emergency changes from damage control to preparing the boats and calling for help. |
| About 12:15 a.m. | Wireless operators Jack Phillips and Harold Bride begin sending CQD and SOS calls. | Carpathia and other ships learn that Titanic needs immediate assistance. |
| About 12:40–12:45 a.m. | The first lifeboat is lowered and distress rockets are being fired. | Several early boats leave before many passengers fully understand the danger. |
| About 1:00–1:40 a.m. | More boats leave from both sides as the bow settles lower. | Loading becomes faster, but practice and interpretation differ between officers. |
| About 1:40–2:05 a.m. | The final conventional boats and collapsibles are prepared or lowered. | The remaining evacuation window becomes extremely short. |
| About 2:18 a.m. | The lights fail and the hull breaks apart during the final descent. | The breakup, disputed in some early accounts, was later confirmed by the wreck. |
| About 2:20 a.m. | Titanic disappears beneath the Atlantic. | Hundreds of people are left in the water while the lifeboats remain scattered nearby. |
| About 4:10 a.m. | The first Titanic lifeboat reaches Carpathia. | The rescue begins and continues until the remaining boats are recovered. |

For a much more detailed reconstruction, see the Night of April 14, 1912 timeline.

## Titanic sinking at a glance

The exact passenger and casualty totals vary slightly among respected historical lists, so the broad figures below are presented honestly as approximations.

11:40 p.m.

### Iceberg collision

The lookouts sighted the iceberg shortly before the ship struck it on April 14.

2:20 a.m.

### Final sinking

Titanic disappeared beneath the sea during the early hours of April 15.

160 min

### Time to sink

About two hours and forty minutes passed between collision and final loss.

20

### Lifeboats carried

The boats had rated space for far fewer people than were aboard.

### People aboard

Passenger and crew totals differ slightly depending on the historical dataset.

### People survived

Specialist databases use nearby totals because a few records are classified differently.

More than 1,500

### People died

Most people left outside the boats entered lethally cold North Atlantic water.

Carpathia

### Rescue ship

The Cunard liner collected the survivors from Titanic’s lifeboats.

This site uses “about 705 survivors” and “more than 1,500 deaths” for broad summaries, then explains the underlying dataset on the detailed survivor and victim pages.

## Survival and loss overview

No single total is accepted by every database. The figures below are the clearest broad summary for readers, with links to the pages that explain the differences.

| Measure | Best broad answer | What readers should know |
| --- | --- | --- |
| People aboard | About 2,200 | Historical lists differ slightly over passenger, crew and special staff classifications. |
| People who survived | About 705 | Published specialist totals commonly range from about 705 to 712. |
| People who died | More than 1,500 | The death total changes slightly when the aboard and survivor lists change. |
| Overall survival | Fewer than one in three | Survival varied sharply by sex, age, class, deck location and crew duties. |

Use the survivor-count, death-toll and survival-rate pages for the site’s detailed treatment of competing totals and subgroup patterns.

## What is certain and what remains debated

Titanic history combines strong physical evidence with witness accounts that sometimes conflict. A trustworthy summary should show the difference.

| Question | Best-supported conclusion |
| --- | --- |
| Did Titanic strike an iceberg? | Yes. The collision and resulting flooding are established by testimony, damage analysis and the inquiry records. |
| Did the ship break apart? | Yes. Survivor accounts and the separated bow and stern on the seabed establish the breakup. |
| Was one person solely responsible? | No. The disaster resulted from connected navigation, design, regulatory, evacuation and rescue failures. |
| Were third-class passengers deliberately imprisoned? | A ship-wide order to keep third class below during the sinking has not been established. |
| Could Californian have saved everyone? | Its failure to investigate the rockets was strongly criticized, but the exact distance and possible arrival time remain debated. |
| What was the band’s final song? | The musicians continued playing, but survivor recollections do not establish one certain final selection. |

The Facts and Myths, Californian, third-class access and inquiry guides examine these questions in greater detail.

## Why did Titanic sink?

Titanic was designed to remain afloat with a limited number of watertight compartments flooded. The iceberg collision damaged the ship along the starboard side and allowed water to enter several forward compartments at once. The damage was not one enormous open gash. Inquiry testimony and later analysis support a series of openings and damaged seams spread along the hull.

As the bow settled deeper, water reached the tops of the internal bulkheads and spilled into compartments farther aft. The bulkheads slowed the flooding but did not extend high enough to stop this progressive movement once the forward angle became severe. Pumps could not remove water as quickly as it entered. The ship’s loss therefore resulted from the location and extent of the iceberg damage combined with the limits of its watertight subdivision.

Near the end, the increasing angle placed enormous stress on the hull. Titanic broke apart before both major sections descended separately. The 1985 wreck discovery confirmed the breakup and corrected decades of popular illustrations that had shown the ship sinking intact.

## Why did so many people die?

The physical damage explains why Titanic sank, but it does not by itself explain the scale of the death toll. Titanic carried only 20 lifeboats, with rated capacity for far fewer people than were aboard. The ship complied with the outdated legal minimum, yet legal compliance did not provide a place for everyone.

Several early boats left with empty seats. Some passengers hesitated because Titanic still appeared more secure than a small open boat in the dark. Officers did not all interpret “women and children first” in the same way, and uncertainty existed over how heavily boats could be loaded while hanging from the davits. Passengers also reached the Boat Deck at different times depending on cabin location, class routes, steward guidance, language, family groups and their own understanding of the danger.

The nearest ship known to respond by wireless, Carpathia, was hours away. Californian’s officers saw rockets but did not wake their wireless operator or make an immediate rescue attempt. Once Titanic sank, the water was so cold that most people who entered it had little chance of surviving until help arrived. These factors turned the loss of a ship into a mass-casualty disaster.

## What passengers and crew experienced

The collision did not feel equally violent in every part of the ship. Some people felt a long vibration or scraping sensation, while others noticed little at first. The engines stopped, doors opened, and passengers began asking what had happened. Because the ship remained lit and seemed stable during the early emergency, some returned to cabins, dressed slowly or resisted leaving for the cold Boat Deck.

Stewards moved through accommodation areas, waking passengers and directing them upward. The experience varied sharply. First-class passengers were generally closer to the upper decks and familiar public spaces. Many third-class passengers had longer routes through a ship they had known for only a few days. Crew members were not simply escaping: engineers, firemen, electricians, sailors, stewards, wireless operators and officers continued working while the evacuation progressed.

As the bow dropped lower, the danger became unmistakable. Boat loading accelerated, families were separated, and organized evacuation began to fail as water reached the forward Boat Deck. Survivor accounts from Jack Thayer, Lawrence Beesley, Eva Hart, Daniel Buckley, Charles Lightoller and Harold Bride preserve different viewpoints rather than one complete view of the night.

## The lifeboat evacuation was uneven

Titanic’s boats were arranged on the upper deck and included 14 standard wooden boats, two smaller emergency cutters and four collapsible boats. Their combined capacity exceeded the legal requirement but remained far below the number aboard. A full boat drill was not completed during the voyage, and the crew had limited time to uncover, swing out, load and lower every boat.

Early launches were cautious. Officers worried about the weight carried by boats suspended from the davits, and many passengers did not believe the ship would actually founder. Later boats were generally fuller as the sinking became obvious. Collapsibles A and B could not be launched normally and floated free or were washed away during the final minutes.

Most survivors escaped in lifeboats before Titanic disappeared. A small number survived after entering the water or reaching damaged collapsibles. The boat number attached to a biography can be useful, but occupant lists and launch times are not equally certain for every boat.

## Distress calls, Carpathia and the rescue

Wireless operators Jack Phillips and Harold Bride sent both CQD and SOS calls with Titanic’s position. Carpathia’s operator Harold Cottam heard the distress traffic and carried it to Captain Arthur Rostron. Rostron immediately changed course, ordered the ship prepared for survivors and drove toward Titanic’s reported position through an area where ice was present.

Carpathia could not arrive before Titanic sank. People in the boats first saw its rockets while they waited in darkness. The rescue ship reached the first boat at about 4:10 a.m. and recovered survivors one lifeboat at a time through the morning. Crew members prepared medical stations, hot drinks, blankets and spaces for people who had lost relatives, friends and nearly all their possessions.

The rescue ended the immediate struggle in the boats but not the disaster’s human consequences. Carpathia carried the survivors to New York, where families, reporters and officials waited. American hearings began almost immediately, followed by the British inquiry and international safety reforms.

## How historians know what happened

No one person witnessed every part of the sinking. Historians reconstruct the night by comparing passenger and crew testimony, wireless records, ship plans, lifeboat evidence, contemporary lists, newspaper interviews and the findings of the American and British inquiries. Each source has limits. Witnesses stood in different places, clocks differed, memories were recorded under stress, and some later recollections changed over time.

The wreck added physical evidence. Its separated bow and stern confirmed the breakup, while the debris field and condition of the sections helped researchers test structural reconstructions. The wreck cannot answer every question because impact damage, corrosion and decades underwater have altered it.

The strongest conclusion is often a careful one: state what multiple sources establish, identify where accounts conflict, and avoid turning an uncertain detail into a dramatic certainty. The site’s Sources and Research guide explains how testimony, official reports and later databases are used across these pages.

## Sources used for this overview

The page draws on the 1912 inquiry records and the site’s detailed evidence guides. Approximate wording is used where clocks, totals or witness recollections differ.

- British inquiry report: collision Lookout warning, bridge response and collision sequence.
- British inquiry report: findings Official conclusions on collision, speed, lifeboats and the Californian.
- British inquiry report: account of the boats Boat arrangement, capacity and evacuation findings.
- United States inquiry report: the rescue Contemporary summary of Carpathia and the lifeboat recovery.
- TitanicSurvivors.com survivor-count guide Why published survivor totals differ slightly.
- TitanicSurvivors.com sources and research guide How the site handles testimony, conflicting records and uncertainty.

## Explore the sinking in depth

Choose the part of the disaster you want to understand next. Each guide answers one focused question and links back to the wider sequence.

## Frequently asked questions

When did Titanic sink?

Titanic struck the iceberg late on April 14, 1912, and sank at about 2:20 a.m. on April 15.

How long did Titanic take to sink?

About two hours and forty minutes passed between the collision at roughly 11:40 p.m. and the final sinking at roughly 2:20 a.m.

Where did Titanic sink?

Titanic sank in the North Atlantic, south of Newfoundland. The wreck lies about 12,500 feet, or 3,800 metres, below the surface.

Why did Titanic sink?

Iceberg damage allowed water into more forward compartments than the ship could remain afloat with. Progressive flooding then moved farther aft as the bow settled.

How many people died in the Titanic sinking?

More than 1,500 people died. The exact total varies slightly because historical lists do not classify every passenger and crew record in the same way.

How many people survived Titanic?

About 705 people survived, although specialist databases use nearby totals such as 706 or 712.

Why were there not enough lifeboats?

Titanic met the outdated British legal requirement, but the rules had not kept pace with the size of the newest liners. The 20 boats could not hold everyone aboard.

Which ship rescued Titanic’s survivors?

RMS Carpathia responded to Titanic’s wireless distress calls and began recovering the lifeboats at about 4:10 a.m.

Did Titanic break in half?

Yes. Some survivors described a breakup in 1912, and the wreck discovery later confirmed that the bow and stern lie separately on the seabed.

# What year did the Titanic sink? How the movie stacks up the the facts of the famous wreck.

---

USA TODAY

Chances are you’ve heard the story of the RMS Titanic. On its voyage from the United Kingdom to New York City, the ocean liner hit an iceberg and sank. The wreck, famously dramatized in a 1997 movie, is a real-life event that made headlines in the early 1900s. The story gained renewed interest earlier this year when a submersible on its way to visit the wreckage imploded, killing all 5 passengers on board.

But what’s fact and what’s fiction?

Here’s everything you need to know about the Titanic’s sinking, from the year to the number of survivors to the size of the boat. Feel free to play Celine Dion’s "My Heart Will Go On" for added ambiance as you read.

## When did the Titanic sink?

The real-life Titanic sank at 2:20 a.m. April 15, 1912– only four days into it’s first-ever voyage.

## Where did the Titanic depart ?

The famed ocean liner took off from Southampton, England.

## How many people were on the Titanic?

The ship had just over 2,200 people aboard – a mix of passengers and crew.

## How many people died on the Titanic?

Over 1,500 people were killed in the sinking of the RMS Titanic. "RMS" stands for Royal Mail Ship.

## How many people survived the Titanic?

706 people in all survived the sinking, according to History.com. Notably, first-class passengers were 44% more likely to survive, while third-class passengers suffered much greater fatalities.

USA Today Network's Titanic coverage: The Titanic sank 110 years ago. An Indy newspaper got the story very wrong.

## Where did the Titanic sink?

The Titanic sank shortly after hitting an iceberg off the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, Canada.

## How big was the Titanic?

The Titanic was spectacularly large for its time, measuring 882 feet and 9 inches.

## How many Titanic survivors are still alive?

None. The youngest passenger onboard was Millvina Dean, who was only 2 months old at the time. She was the longest-living Titanic survivor and died in 2009.

## Is the Titanic still in the ocean?

Yes. Remnants of the Titanic wreck can still be found at the bottom of the Atlantic ocean, though a bacteria lives in the remains and will eventually consume them by eating at the iron in the ship’s hull.

## How long did the real Titanic sink?

It is approximated the Titanic took just over 2-and-a-half hours to sink fully.

## Were Jack and Rose on the real Titanic?

You may be familiar with the two romantic leads of the Oscar-winning James Cameron film – played by Leonardo DiCaprio and Kate Winslet. Or even the debate over whether they could have been saved at the movie’s end if Rose had just moved over a bit. In reality, these two people did not exist.

## Who is the ‘Unsinkable Molly Brown’?

Molly Brown was an American socialite and activist who survived the sinking of the Titanic. Her life story was made into a musical and then a feature film entitled “The Unsinkable Molly Brown” starring Debbie Reynolds. Kathy Bates played Brown in 1997's "Titanic."

## Just curious for more? We've got you covered

USA TODAY is exploring the questions you and others ask every day. From " How many people died on the Titanic?" to " Who was the Zodiac killer?" to " How many people are born a day?", we're striving to find answers to the most common questions you ask every day. Head to our Just Curious section to see what else we can answer for you.

Memorializing Titanic in Real Time : What exact time did Titanic sink?

 Contents 

## Titanica!

 by Samuel Halpern 

Each year, on the night of April 14th-15th, there are people who gather, both in person and virtually, to commemorate the anniversary of the sinking of the RMS Titanic. Many take part in what are called real-time simulations that show the ship from a few minutes before the collision with an iceberg to a few minutes after the time when she disappeared beneath the Atlantic. Others have taken cruises to the location of the now-known Titanic wreck site, where ceremonies were held at what was believed to be the right time to pay their respects to the 1496 people who lost their lives on that dark, cold night back in April of 1912. Others, observing by themselves, perhaps with a drink in hand and a favorite Titanic book close by, waiting for the right moment to honor those that were lost so many years ago.

But what exact moment do they all wait for? What exact time should that memorial wreath be thrown into the water over the Titanic wreck?

### The Historical Record

It has been well documented and accepted that Titanic struck an iceberg at about 11:40pm on April 14, 1912, and then sank 2 hours and 40 minutes later at about 2:20am on April 15, 1912. However, those times were by time kept on board Titanic, ship's time, not by some universally accepted time standard such as Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) that could easily be converted to any other time standard. So, what time in GMT did Titanic strike the iceberg, and what time in GMT did she sink?

The question of the difference between Titanic time and GMT came up during the US Senate investigation into the loss of Titanic back in 1912. On day 4 of the investigation, Titanic surviving officers Herbert Pitman and Charles Lightoller were asked if they knew what the time was in GMT when Titanic sank, and how that compared to ship's time:

> Senator SMITH. What was the Greenwich time compared with the ship's time? Mr. PITMAN. I can not say. Senator SMITH. Can you say, Mr. Lightoller? Mr. LIGHTOLLER. I can give you the Greenwich time. Senator SMITH. I wish you would. Mr. LIGHTOLLER. … 5:47 Greenwich mean time; 2:20 apparent time of ship.

According to Second Officer Lightoller, when it was 2:20am ship's time, it was 5:47am GMT. From the times that Lightoller gave, the difference between Greenwich time (5:47) and ship's time (2:20), was equal to 3 hours and 27 minutes. [1] Note: 5h 47m - 2h 20m = 3h 27m difference in times. Then, on day 10 of the inquiry, it was Titanic's Fourth Officer Joseph Boxhall's turn to answer a question about the time carried on board Titanic. The exchange was:

> Senator SMITH. Mr. Boxhall, you seem to be the one upon whom we must rely to give the difference between ship's time and New York time; or, rather, to give ship's time and give the New York time when this accident occurred.
> 
> Mr. BOXHALL. At 11:46pm, ship's time, it was 10:13 Washington time, or New York time.

From what Boxhall said, the difference between ship's time (11:46) and time in New York (10:13) when the accident happened was 1 hour and 33 minutes. [2] Note: 11h 46m - 10h 13m = 1h 33m difference in times. Boxhall used 11:46pm as the collision time in his workup when he derived his famous SOS distress position. Most eyewitnesses placed the collision at 11:40pm ship's time. Boxhall admitted that he did not know precisely what time the ship struck, citing 11:43 and 11:45 from what he heard from others. Using 11:46 rather than 11:40 would account for about a 2 mile overrun in his SOS position work up. It does not account for the full 13 miles that separate the SOS position from the location of the wreck site. In 1912, New York and Washington, DC were both keeping what is known as Eastern Standard Time (EST), a time that was, and still is, precisely 5 hours 0 minutes behind GMT. Therefore, a 1 hour 33 minute time difference between ship's time and New York time corresponds to a 3 hour and 27 minute time difference between GMT and ship's time. [3] Note: 1h 33m + 3h 27m = 5h 00m, the difference between GMT and EST. Thus we see that the information given by Boxhall supported the information given by Lightoller regarding the difference between ship's time and two recognized time standards, GMT and EST.

In addition to the testimonies of Lightoller and Boxhall at the US Senate inquiry, there is this interesting little tidbit of information extracted from an April 15th 1912 wireless message from Carpathia's Captain Rostron to Olympic's Captain Haddock that was received at 4:10pm NY time: [4] From a copy of detailed wireless log made by Olympic's operator E. J. Moore furnished to Senator William Alden Smith, May 25, 1912. (American Inquiry, p. 1138.)

> Capt. Haddock, Olympic: … Titanic foundered about 2.20am, 5.47 GMT, in 41.46 north 50.14 west; … – Rostron.

The reported foundering time, "about 2:20am, 5:47 GMT," implied that time carried on board Titanic was 3 hours 27 minutes behind GMT, or 1 hour 33 minutes ahead of time carried in New York, just as Lightoller and Boxhall had later testified about.

In the official report that came out of the US Senate investigation into the loss of the SS Titanic, it was written that an iceberg was sighted from Titanic "at 11:46pm ship's time, or 10:13pm New York time, Sunday evening, April 14." They also listed the foundering time "at 12:47am, New York time, April 15." Their conclusions were obviously based on the 1 hour 33 minute time difference between ship's time and EST, or 3 hour and 27 minute time difference between ship's time and GMT, that was offered up in the testimonies of Titanic's surviving officers Lightoller and Boxhall, and in the content of that April 15th wireless message from Captain Rostron to Captain Haddock.

### Questioning the Given Evidence

Despite the cited primary evidence given by Lightoller, Boxhall, and in that message from Rostron to Haddock, questions concerning the difference in time between what was carried on board Titanic and what was carried in places like New York or London have been raised over the years. This has come about when one takes a deep dive into how Titanic was navigated, and how clocks were set and adjusted during a westbound voyage to New York. Questions have come up such as why was the famous SOS position derived by Fourth Officer Boxhall nowhere close to the now known location of the Titanic wreck, and could Titanic's clocks have been partially put back some time before the accident actually happened?

Clocks on board Titanic, as with most other vessels that crossed the Atlantic back then, were adjusted each night around midnight so that when the sun reached its highest point in the sky the next day at Local Apparent Noon (LAN), the clocks would show 12:00 exactly. Having traveled 1549 nautical miles since taking departure off the Daunt's Rock Light Vessel outside Queenstown harbor on April 11, we know that Titanic had to be close to 43° 02'N, 44° 31'W when LAN occurred three days later on April 14. [5] S. W. Halpern, "Keeping Track of a Maiden Voyage", www.encyclopedia-titanica.org/keeping-track.html. For that location on that particular date, LAN, 12:00pm ship's time, came at 2:58pm GMT. That means that the difference between ship's time and GMT all that Sunday afternoon and evening would have remained at 2 hours and 58 minutes, a difference of nearly 3 hours. In terms of New York time, the difference was 2 hours and 2 minutes, or nearly 2 hours.

Confirmation of a 2-hour difference between NY time and the ship's time comes from Titanic's junior wireless operator, Harold Bride. Bride was asked about the time that was kept in Titanic's wireless cabin that Sunday, April 14:

> Senator SMITH. Did you have a watch or clock in your room? Mr. BRIDE. We had two clocks, sir. Senator SMITH. Were they both running? Mr. BRIDE. Yes, sir; one was keeping New York time and the other was keeping ship's time. Senator FLETCHER. The difference was about 1 hour and 55 minutes? Mr. BRIDE. There was about 2 hours difference between the two.

Notice that when Senator Fletcher asked if the difference between New York time and ship's time was 1 hour and 55 minutes, Bride immediately corrected him by saying the difference was about 2 hours. If the difference was really 1 hour and 33 minutes, Bride most likely would have said that there was about an hour and a half difference, not about a two hours difference.

So if the navigational data suggests a difference between ship's time and New York time of 2 hours and 2 minutes, which is apparently supported by Bride's testimony, how is it that the evidence from Lightoller, Boxhall, and Rostron suggest a time difference of 1 hour and 33 minutes?

A few people have proposed that Titanic's master clocks may have been put back some time before the accident happened, thereby extending the actual time duration between noon and the time when she struck an iceberg. As pointed out before, clocks were adjusted each night around midnight so they would show 12:00 when LAN occurred the following day. [6] If needed a small correction would be added or subtracted the next day in the forenoon. On the night of April 14th 1912, the westbound Titanic was to have had her clocks put back a total of 47 minutes. [7] (American Inquiry, p. 451.) This 47 minute adjustment was to have been carried out in two steps. The first adjustment, putting the clock back 23 minutes, was to have taken place just before or at midnight, thereby delaying the striking of 8-bells by 23 minutes, and delaying the official end of Sunday, April 14th on Titanic. The second adjustment, putting the clock back by 24 minutes, was to take place after the striking of 8-bells thus adding 24 minutes right after the start of Monday, April 15th 1912. The result of both of those planned clock adjustments would have been to increase the interval from LAN Sunday to LAN Monday from 24 hours to 24 hours 47 minutes. (This is somewhat analogous to putting your clock back by an hour when switching from summertime [daylight time] to standard time, thereby increasing the length of that particular day from 24 hours to 25 hours.) But was that planned clock adjustment ever carried out?

When asked at the US Senate investigation about the clocks being put back the night of April 14th 1912, Third Officer Pitman had this to say:

> Senator SMITH. When were the ship's clocks set; do you know? Mr. PITMAN. They are set at midnight every night. Senator SMITH. They were set at midnight? Mr. PITMAN. Every night. Senator SMITH. And were they set at midnight Sunday night? Mr. PITMAN. No; we had something else to think of.

In addition to Third Officer Pitman, Boatswain's Mate Albert Haines, who was on duty at the time of the collision, was asked about his activities and observations around the time that Titanic struck the iceberg. He was also asked about the time:

> Senator SMITH. What time was that? Mr. HAINES. The right time, without putting the clock back, was 20 minutes to 12.

It seems clear from these two eyewitnesses, that the clocks had not been put back prior to the accident that Sunday the night. Furthermore, putting time back on the two Magneta master clocks in the officer's chart room did not put the time back on the electrically controlled slave clocks that were located throughout the ship. These Magneta slaves clocks could only move in one direction, and that was forward.

When a master clock was put back, as they were each night on a westbound voyage, the slave clocks that it controlled would remain set to the time that was showing on the master clock when it was put back. That time would remain showing on the slave clocks until the hands of the master clock returned to the time that was showing when it was put back. Then all would start to jump ahead once again every minute after that.

If the master clocks on Titanic had been put back at midnight, or a little before, as planned on the night of the accident, then the slave clocks, located in various public spaces throughout the ship, would show a time that was close to 12 o'clock, and continue to do so for 23 or 24 minutes before moving ahead again. There is no way that these slave clocks would show a time close to 11:40pm when the ship struck the iceberg if the master clocks had been put back 23 or 24 minutes near midnight. As Third Officer Pitman said, the ship's crew had something else to think about.

### The Search for Reality

As we have seen before, the 3 hour 27 minute time difference between GMT and Titanic time first showed up in that wireless message from Carpathia's Captain Rostron to Olympic's Captain Haddock on Monday, April 15. In that message Rostron wrote: " Titanic foundered about 2.20am, 5.47 G.M.T., in 41.46 north. 50.14 west." The time information in that message, as previously noted, is exactly what Charles Lightoller repeated before the US Senate investigation. However, also notice that Rostron accepted as correct the erroneous distress position that was sent out by wireless from Titanic. It is almost certain that the information in that message had to have come from one of Titanic's surviving officers. Could it have come from Joseph Boxhall who was the officer who worked up the famous 41° 46'N, 50° 14'W SOS distress coordinates? Are those coordinates, which we now know to have been in error, some way tied to the 3 hour 27 minute time difference between ship's time and GMT that first appeared in Rostron's message to Haddock? I believe the answer is yes.

Consider the following. According to Boxhall, he worked up his distress position by starting out from a position derived from a set of celestial star sights taken around 7:30pm ship's time by Second Officer Charles Lightoller and Third Officer Hubert Pitman. Boxhall also said that "I worked it [the distress position] out for 11.46 as a matter of fact," and that he used a speed of 22 knots along a course of 266° true starting from that 7:30pm celestial fix. By taking Titanic's course and speed and running it up to the time he used for the collision, Boxhall came up with a set of coordinates at 41° 46'N, 50° 14'W. But today, since the discovery of the wreck in 1985, we know that his distress position was about 13 nautical miles too far west of where Titanic actually foundered. Undeniably, a mistake was made that night in calculating the ship's position. So let us consider the following steps using GMT as the time standard, the same time standard that is used by navigators worldwide even today.

1. We have previously pointed out that the difference between ship's time and GMT based on Titanic's estimated April 14th noontime position would have been 2 hours and 58 minutes. We also pointed out that a planned clock change did not take place on Titanic that night because of the accident. So using that navigationally derived time difference of 2 hours and 58 minutes between GMT and ship's time, we find that the star sights taken by Lightoller and Pitman at 7:30pm ship's time April 14, would have corresponded to 10:28pm GMT April 14.
2. We also know that many people, passengers and crew, placed the time of the accident at 11:40pm ship's time. Without any clock alterations, 11:40pm ship's time April 14th equates to 2:38am GMT April 15th using that navigationally derived 2 hour and 58 minute time difference.
3. Starting from 7:30pm (10:28pm GMT April 14) to 11:40pm (2:38am GMT April 15) is a run time of 4 hours and 10 minutes, or 4.17 hours.
4. Steaming at 22 knots over those 4.17 hours gives a travel distance of 91.74 nautical miles; the distance traveled from the celestial fix to the accepted time of the accident.

Now let us see what we get if we use the information given to us from Boxhall. Once again we will use GMT as the time standard.

1. According to Boxhall he used (without explanation) an impact time of 11:46pm ship's time, and that time was equated to 10:13pm NY time April 14, which is the same time as 3:13am GMT April 15.
2. Starting from 10:28pm GMT April 14, the time we derived for the celestial fix based on Titanic's noontime position, to Boxhall's accident time of 3:13am GMT April 15, is a run time of 4 hours 45 minutes, or 4.75 hours.
3. Steaming at 22 knots over 4.45 hours gives us a travel distance of 104.50 nautical miles; the distance traveled from the celestial fix to Boxhall's SOS position.

Now, if we take the difference between the two travel distances just derived, we find:

104.50 - 91.t4 = 12.76 nautical miles

What is interesting about this difference in distance is that it is almost the same as the distance between the Titanic wreck site and Boxhall's erroneous SOS position as shown in the figure below. This proves that if Joseph Boxhall had not made a mistake somehow in his calculations, he probably would have obtained a distress position that would have been very close to the location of the wreck instead of being about 13 miles too far to the west.

The reader should note that the precise time of when the celestial fix was actually taken does not really matter in this simple exercise. We were told by Third Officer Pitman that sights were taken, "between half past 7 and 20 minutes to 8." You can take the time of these sights at 7:30, as we did, or you can take 7:40, or any time in between, when doing this simple exercise. A different time for the fix will only increase or decrease the two run times that we obtained by a small amount exactly the same way. That amount will cancel out when taking the difference between the two travel distances that you get. You will still get a difference between distances of 12.8 nautical miles. The numbers cannot lie.

The results that we show here clearly suggests that the collision time of 3:13am GMT April 15th (10:13pm NY time April 14th) used by Fourth Officer Joseph Boxhall, is obviously coupled to the erroneous distress position that Boxhall obtained. Unfortunately, the erroneous location of the distress position had apparently led all of Titanic's surviving officers to later believe that clocks on Titanic at the time of collision and time of foundering were 1 hour 33 minutes ahead of clocks in New York, or 3 hours 27 minutes behind GMT.

The reality is that those clocks were 2 hours and 2 minutes ahead of clocks in New York as displayed on the two clocks that were kept in Titanic's Marconi cabin, and confirmed by junior wireless operator Harold Bride, and only 2 hours and 58 minutes behind GMT. The reality is that Titanic struck an iceberg at about 11:40pm ship's time (2:38am GMT; 9:38pm NY time), then slowly came to a stop and slowly drifted southward with the local current before foundering at 2:20am ship's time (5:18am GMT; 12:18am NY time) at 41° 43.5'N, 49° 57.8'W.

Titanic is a 1997 American epic historical romance film written and directed by James Cameron. Incorporating both historical and fictional aspects, it is based on accounts of the sinking of RMS Titanic in 1912. Leonardo DiCaprio and Kate Winslet star as members of different social classes who fall in love during the ship's ill-fated maiden voyage. The ensemble cast includes Billy Zane, Kathy Bates, Frances Fisher, Bernard Hill, Jonathan Hyde, Danny Nucci, David Warner and Bill Paxton.

Cameron's inspiration came from his fascination with shipwrecks. He felt a love story interspersed with human loss would be essential to convey the emotional impact of the disaster. Production began on September 1, 1995, [8] when Cameron shot footage of the Titanic wreck. The modern scenes were shot on board the Shirshov Institute of Oceanology research vessel Akademik Mstislav Keldysh, which Cameron had used as a base when filming the wreck. Scale models, computer-generated imagery (CGI), and a reconstruction of the Titanic built at Baja Studios were used to recreate the sinking. Titanic was initially in development at 20th Century Fox, but delays and a mounting budget resulted in Fox partnering with Paramount Pictures for financial help. It was the most expensive film ever made at the time, with a production budget of $200 million. Filming took place from July 1996 to March 1997.

Titanic premiered at the Tokyo International Film Festival on November 1, 1997, and was released in the United States on December 19. It was distributed by Paramount Pictures in the United States and Canada and by 20th Century Fox in other territories. It was praised for its visual effects, performances (particularly those of DiCaprio, Winslet, and Gloria Stuart), production values, direction, score, cinematography, story, and emotional depth. Among other awards, the film received fourteen nominations at the 70th Academy Awards and won eleven, including Best Picture and Best Director. In doing so, it tied both All About Eve (1950) for the record for the most Academy Award nominations, and Ben-Hur (1959) for the most Academy Awards won by a film, making Titanic the most successful individual film in Academy Award history. [a] 

With an initial worldwide gross of over $1.84 billion, becoming the highest-grossing film of 1997, Titanic was the first film to reach the billion-dollar mark, [b] and was the highest-grossing film of all time until Cameron's next film, Avatar (2009), surpassed it in 2010. Income from the initial theatrical release, retail video, and soundtrack sales and US broadcast rights exceeded $3.2 billion. [10] Re-releases pushed the worldwide theatrical total to $2.264 billion, making Titanic the second film to gross more than $2 billion worldwide after Avatar; as of 2026, it is the fifth-highest-grossing film. In 2017, the Library of Congress selected it for preservation in the United States National Film Registry as "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant".

## Plot

In 1996, aboard the research vessel Akademik Mstislav Keldysh, treasure hunter Brock Lovett and his team explore the wreck of RMS Titanic, hoping to find a necklace known as the Heart of the Ocean. Instead, they recover a safe containing a drawing of a young woman wearing the necklace. The sketch is dated April 14, 1912, the day the Titanic struck an iceberg and sank, resulting in about 1,500 deaths. [c] After seeing a television report about the discovery, centenarian Rose Dawson Calvert contacts Lovett, revealing she is the woman in the drawing. Hoping she can help locate the necklace, Lovett brings Rose and her granddaughter aboard the Keldysh, where Rose recounts her experience on Titanic.

In 1912, 17-year-old Rose DeWitt Bukater boards the Titanic in Southampton with her wealthy fiancé, Cal Hockley, and her mother, Ruth. Rose is unhappy in the loveless engagement, but Ruth stresses that the marriage will resolve their financial problems. Rose contemplates suicide by jumping from the ship's stern, but is stopped by Jack Dawson, a poor nomadic artist. Jack and Rose form a friendship, and Jack confesses his feelings for her. Though initially resistant, Rose realizes she has fallen in love with Jack, despite Cal's and Ruth's disapproval.

Rose brings Jack to her stateroom and asks him to draw her nude, wearing only the necklace. Afterward, they evade Cal's valet, Spicer Lovejoy, and have sex in a car in the cargo hold. On the forward deck, they witness the ship's collision with an iceberg and overhear officers discussing the severity of the situation. When Cal discovers Jack's sketch of Rose, he has Lovejoy plant the necklace on Jack, framing him for theft. Jack is arrested and locked in the master-at-arms' office, and Cal pockets the necklace.

As Titanic sinks, women and children are prioritized for the lifeboats. Rose rescues Jack, and they return to the deck, where Cal urges Rose to board a lifeboat, claiming he and Jack will board another. Cal unwittingly wraps his coat, containing the necklace, around her. As her lifeboat is lowered, Rose jumps back onto the ship, unwilling to leave Jack behind. Enraged, Cal grabs a pistol and chases them through the flooding ship, but gives up when they escape. Cal joins a lifeboat by pretending to be a child's father.

As the flooded bow sinks, the stern rises into the air, and Jack and Rose cling to the railing. The ship splits in two, and the stern sinks into the freezing water with the remaining passengers. Jack helps Rose onto floating debris and makes her promise to survive and live a full life. Jack dies from hypothermia, but Rose is saved by a returning lifeboat and rescued by the RMS Carpathia. Rose hides from Cal and her mother and gives her name as Rose Dawson on her arrival in New York City.

In the present, Rose reveals that Cal committed suicide after losing his fortune in the 1929 stock market crash. She tells the Keldysh crew that Jack saved her in every possible way, and laments that her memories are all that she has left of him. Touched by her account, Lovett abandons his search for the necklace. Alone at night on the stern of the Keldysh, Rose, who has kept the necklace in her possession, drops it into the sea above the wreck. Later, as she lies in her bed, photographs on her dresser depict a life of freedom and adventure inspired by Jack. [11] Aboard the pristine Titanic, a young Rose reunites with Jack at the Grand Staircase, applauded by the passengers and crew who died in the sinking.

### Historical characters

Although not intended to be an entirely accurate depiction of events, [18] the film includes portrayals of various historical figures:

The real Margaret Brown (right) providing Captain Arthur Henry Rostron with an award for his service in the rescue of Titanic' s surviving passengers

- Kathy Bates as Margaret "Molly" Brown. Brown is looked down upon by other first-class women, including Ruth, as "vulgar" and " new money". She is friendly to Jack and lends him a suit of evening clothes (bought for her son) when he is invited to dinner in the first-class dining saloon. She was dubbed the Unsinkable Molly Brown by historians because, with the support of other women, she commandeered Lifeboat 6 from Quartermaster Robert Hichens. [19] Some aspects of this altercation are portrayed in Cameron's film.
- Victor Garber as Thomas Andrews, the ship's builder. Andrews is portrayed as a kind, decent man who is modest about his grand achievement. After the collision, he tries to convince the others, particularly Ismay, that it is a "mathematical certainty" that the ship will sink. He is depicted during the sinking of the ship as standing next to the clock in the first-class smoking room, lamenting his failure to build a strong and safe ship. Although this has become one of the most famous legends of the sinking of the Titanic, this story, which was published in a 1912 book (Thomas Andrews: Shipbuilder) and thereafter perpetuated, came from John Stewart, a steward on the ship who in fact left the ship in boat no.15 at approximately 1:40 a.m. [20] There were testimonies of sightings of Andrews after that moment. [20] It appears that Andrews stayed in the smoking room for some time to gather his thoughts; he then continued assisting with the evacuation. [20]

### Pre-production

Director, writer and producer James Cameron (pictured in 2000)

> The story could not have been written better had it been fiction ...The juxtaposition of rich and poor, the gender roles played out unto death (women first), the stoicism and nobility of a bygone age, the magnificence of the great ship matched in scale only by the folly of the men who drove her hell-bent through the darkness. And above all the lesson: that life is uncertain, the future unknowable ... the unthinkable possible.

— James Cameron [45] [46] 

Cameron had long been fascinated by shipwrecks and felt Titanic was "the Mount Everest of shipwrecks". [47] [48] [49] He was almost past the point in his life when he felt he could consider an undersea expedition, but was restless to explore the life he had turned away from when he switched from the sciences to the arts in college. After an IMAX film, Titanica (1992), was made from footage of the Titanic wreck, Cameron sought Hollywood funding for his own expedition. He said he was more motivated by a desire to see the shipwreck than to make a film. [47] 

Cameron wrote a scriptment for a Titanic film, [50] met 20th Century Fox executives including Peter Chernin, and pitched it as " Romeo and Juliet on the Titanic". [48] [49] Cameron said the executives were unconvinced of the commercial potential, and had instead hoped for action scenes similar to his previous films. [51] They approved the project as they hoped for a long-term relationship with Cameron. [51] [52] [53] 

Cameron convinced Fox to promote the film based on the publicity afforded by shooting the Titanic wreck, [50] and organized several dives over two years. [45] He also convinced Fox that shooting the real wreck, instead of simulating it with special effects, would provide value: "We can either do [the shots] with elaborate models and motion control shots and CG and all that, which will cost X amount of money – or we can spend X plus 30 per cent and actually go shoot it at the real wreck." [48] 

### Undersea footage

The crew shot at the wreck, which lies in the Atlantic Ocean, 12 times in 1995. The work was risky, as the water pressure could kill the crew if there were even the tiniest flaw in the submersible structure. [52] Additionally, adverse conditions prevented Cameron from getting footage. [52] During one dive, one of the submersibles collided with Titanic' s hull, damaging both and leaving fragments of the submersible's propeller shroud scattered around the superstructure. The external bulkhead of the captain's quarters collapsed, exposing the interior, and the area around the entrance to the Grand Staircase was damaged. [54] 

Descending to the site emphasized to the crew that the Titanic disaster was not simply a story of fiction, but a real event with real loss of life. Cameron said: "Working around the wreck for so much time, you get such a strong sense of the profound sadness and injustice of it, and the message of it." He felt a "great mantle of responsibility" to convey the emotional message of the story, as he was aware there might never be another filmmaker to visit the wreck. [53] 

### Writing

After filming the underwater shots, Cameron began writing the screenplay. [50] He wanted to honor the people who died, and spent six months researching the Titanic' s crew and passengers. [45] He created a detailed timeline of the events of the voyage and sinking and had it verified by historical experts. [48] From the beginning of the shoot, the team had "a very clear picture" of what happened on the ship. Cameron said, "That set the bar higher in a way – it elevated the movie in a sense. We wanted this to be a definitive visualization of this moment in history as if you'd gone back in a time machine and shot it." [48] Cameron was influenced by A Night to Remember, the 1958 British film about the Titanic which he had seen as a youth. He liberally copied some dialogue and scenes, including the lively party of the passengers in steerage, [55] and the musicians playing on the deck during the sinking. [18] 

Cameron felt the Titanic sinking was "like a great novel that really happened", but that the event had become a mere morality tale; the film would give audiences the experience of living the history. [45] The treasure hunter Brock Lovett represented those who never connected with the human element of the tragedy. [41] He believed that the romance of Jack and Rose would be the most engaging element: when their love is finally destroyed, the audience would mourn the loss. [45] He said: "All my films are love stories, but in Titanic I finally got the balance right. It's not a disaster film. It's a love story with a fastidious overlay of real history." [53] Cameron created the character of the modern-day Rose, a survivor of the Titanic, to "see the present and the past" and "connects us in a way through history". [56] He framed the romance with the elderly Rose to make the intervening years palpable and poignant. [45] While Winslet and Stuart believed Rose dies at the end, [57] [58] Cameron said, "The answer has to be something you supply personally, individually." [11] 

### Scale modeling

The reconstruction of Titanic. The blueprints were supplied by the original ship's builder and Cameron tried to make the ship as detailed and accurate as possible. [59] [60] 

Harland & Wolff, Titanic' s builders, opened their private archives to the crew, sharing blueprints that were previously thought lost. [59] Fox acquired 40 acres (16 ha) of waterfront south of Playas de Rosarito in Mexico and began building a new studio on May 31, 1996. A horizon tank of 17 million US gallons (64 million litres) was built for the exterior of the reconstructed ship, providing 270 degrees of ocean view. The ship was built to full scale, but Lamont removed redundant sections on the superstructure and forward well deck for the ship to fit in the tank, with the remaining sections filled with digital models. The lifeboats and funnels were shrunk by ten percent. The boat deck and A-deck were working sets, but the rest of the ship was steel plating. Within was a 50-foot (15 m) lifting platform for the ship to tilt during the sinking sequences. The 60-foot (18 m) 1/8th scale model of the stern section was designed by the naval architect Jay Kantola using plans of the Titanic' s sister ship RMS Olympic. [60] Above the model was a 162-foot-tall (49 m) tower crane on 600 feet (180 m) of rail track, acting as a combined construction, lighting, and camera platform. [41] 

Production designers faithfully reconstructed the interior rooms of the Titanic based on authentic blueprints and period photographs. The central Grand Staircase, a prominent focal point, was built to a high standard of craftsmanship; however, it was structurally reinforced with steel framework and scaled 30% wider than the original vessel to enhance the visual grandeur and facilitate filming. Craftsmen from Mexico and Britain sculpted the ornate paneling and plasterwork based on Titanic' s original designs. [61]: 21 The carpeting, upholstery, pieces of furniture, light fixtures, chairs, cutlery and crockery with the White Star Line crest on each piece were among the objects recreated according to original designs. [61]: 35 For the ship's interiors, production designer Peter Lamont's team looked for artifacts from the era. The newness of the ship meant every prop had to be made from scratch. [59] Cameron hired two Titanic historians, Don Lynch and Ken Marschall, to authenticate the historical detail. [52] 

### Casting

Cameron said he needed the cast to feel they were really on the Titanic, to relive its liveliness, and "to take that energy and give it to Jack ... an artist who is able to have his heart soar". [56] Established actors including Chris O'Donnell and Stephen Dorff were considered, but Cameron felt they were too old for the part of a 20-year-old. [51] [52] Tom Cruise was interested, but his asking price was too high. [52] Cameron considered Jared Leto, but he refused to audition. [62] Billy Crudup was on the shortlist and was asked to audition, but he turned it down as he was not interested and chose to star in Without Limits (1998) instead. In 2000, Crudup said that the film would not be as successful if he had starred in it. [63] [64] Jeremy Sisto filmed a series of screen tests with Winslet and three other actresses vying for the role of Rose. [65] Mark Wahlberg met Cameron to discuss the part but Cameron was not interested. [66] Matthew McConaughey, [67] Ethan Hawke, [68] Christian Bale, [69] and Paul Rudd also auditioned. [70] McConaughey was disregarded because he refused to change his Southern drawl. [67] 

Leonardo DiCaprio, then 21 years old, was brought to Cameron's attention by the casting director, Mali Finn. [51] Initially, DiCaprio did not want the role and refused to read his first romantic scene. Cameron said, "He read it once, then started goofing around, and I could never get him to focus on it again. But for one split second, a shaft of light came down from the heavens and lit up the forest." Cameron believed in DiCaprio's ability and told him, "Look, I'm not going to make this guy brooding and neurotic. I'm not going to give him a tic and a limp and all the things you want." Cameron envisioned the character as like those played by James Stewart or Gregory Peck. [51] [71] After she screen-tested with DiCaprio, Winslet was so impressed she whispered to Cameron, "He's great. Even if you don't pick me, pick him." [51] DiCaprio turned down the lead role in Boogie Nights (1997) to star in Titanic. In 2025, he said he regretted this decision, saying Boogie Nights was "a profound movie of my generation". [72] 

Cameron described Rose as "an Audrey Hepburn type". As with DiCaprio, Finn brought Winslet to Cameron's attention. Gwyneth Paltrow, Winona Ryder, Claire Danes (who had worked with DiCaprio in Romeo + Juliet the previous year), Gabrielle Anwar, and Reese Witherspoon were considered for the role. [d] When they turned it down, with Paltrow choosing to star in Great Expectations (1998) instead and Danes feeling it was not right for her, Winslet campaigned for the role. She sent Cameron daily notes from England, which led Cameron to invite her to Hollywood for auditions. He was initially uncertain even after her screen test impressed him. [51] [76] [77] Winslet sent Cameron a single rose with a card signed, "From Your Rose", and lobbied him by phone. "You don't understand!" she pleaded one day when she reached him by mobile phone in his Humvee. "I am Rose! I don't know why you're even seeing anyone else!" Her persistence and talent eventually convinced him to cast her. [51] Cameron said Winslet "had the thing that you look for" and that there was "a quality in her face, in her eyes" that he "just knew people would be ready to go the distance with her". [56] Winslet said of Rose: "She has got a lot to give, and she's got a very open heart. And she wants to explore and adventure the world, but she [feels] that's not going to happen." [56] 

At 87, Gloria Stuart had to be made up to look older for the role of the elderly Rose. [52] Cameron instructed Finn to "find retired actresses from the Golden Age of the thirties and forties". [53] Cameron did not know who Stuart was. Fay Wray was also considered, but Cameron said, "[Stuart] was just so into it, and so lucid, and had such a great spirit. And I saw the connection between her spirit and [Winslet's] spirit. I saw this joie de vivre in both of them, that I thought the audience would be able to make that cognitive leap that it's the same person." [53] 

Cameron considered Michael Biehn for the role of Cal Hockley, whom he had previously collaborated with on The Terminator, Aliens, and The Abyss, [78] before offering it to Matthew McConaughey. [52] Rob Lowe said he also pursued it. [79] Reba McEntire turned down the role of Margaret Brown because it conflicted with her touring schedule. [80] 

### Filming

Principal photography began on July 31, 1996, [8] at Dartmouth, Nova Scotia. The modern-day expedition scenes were shot aboard the Akademik Mstislav Keldysh. [41] In September, the production moved to the newly built Fox Baja Studios in Rosarito, Mexico, where a full-scale Titanic replica had been constructed. [41] The poop deck was built on a hinge that could rise from zero to 90 degrees in a few seconds, just as the ship's stern rose during the sinking. [81] For the safety of the stuntmen, many props were made of foam rubber. [82] By November 15, the boarding scenes were being shot. [81] Cameron built his Titanic on the starboard side as a study of weather data revealed it was a prevailing north-to-south wind, which blew the funnel smoke aft. This posed a problem for shooting the ship's departure from Southampton, as it was docked on its port side. Implementation of written directions, as well as props and costumes, had to be reversed; for example, if someone walked to their right in the script, they had to walk left during shooting. In post-production, the film was flipped to the correct direction. [83] A full-time etiquette coach was hired to instruct the cast in the manners of the upper class gentility in 1912. [52] Despite this, several critics noted anachronisms. [84] [85] 

Cameron's sketch of Rose wearing the Heart of the Ocean. The scene was one of the first shot, as the main set was not ready. [53] 

Cameron sketched Jack's portrait of Rose; Winslet posed in a bathing suit. [86] [87] Cameron felt the scene had a backdrop of repression and freedom: "You know what it means for her, the freedom she must be feeling. It's kind of exhilarating for that reason," he said. [86] [53] The sketching scene was DiCaprio and Winslet's first scene together. Cameron said: "It wasn't by any kind of design, although I couldn't have designed it better. There's a nervousness and an energy and a hesitance in them. They had rehearsed together, but they hadn't shot anything together. If I'd had a choice, I probably would have preferred to put it deeper into the body of the shoot." Cameron said he and his crew "were just trying to find things to shoot" because the big set "wasn't ready for months, so we were scrambling around trying to fill in anything we could get to shoot." Cameron felt the final scene worked well. [53] 

The shoot was an arduous experience that "cemented Cameron's formidable reputation as 'the scariest man in Hollywood". He became known as an "uncompromising, hard-charging perfectionist" and a "300-decibel screamer, a modern-day Captain Bligh with a megaphone and walkie-talkie, swooping down into people's faces on a 162 ft crane." [88] Winslet chipped a bone in her elbow during filming and worried that she would drown in the 17-million-gallon (64-million-litre) water tank in which the ship would sink. She said she was sometimes afraid of Cameron's temper and that he would shout angrily at crew members. [88] Bill Paxton was familiar with Cameron's work ethic from his earlier experience, and said: "There were a lot of people on the set. Jim is not one of those guys who has the time to win hearts and minds." [88] The crew felt Cameron had an evil alter ego and nicknamed him "Mij" (Jim spelled backwards). [88] In response to the criticism, Cameron said, "Film-making is war. A great battle between business and aesthetics." [88] More than 800 crew members worked on the film. [89] 

On August 9, 1996, during the Akademik Mstislav Keldysh shoot in Canada, an unknown person, suspected to be a crew member, put the dissociative drug PCP into the soup that Cameron and various others ate one night in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia. [51] [90] [91] It sent more than 50 people to the hospital. [90] [91] Paxton and Cameron ate the soup and went to the hospital, however, Paxton decided to leave, telling Cameron, "Jim, I'm not gonna hang out here, this is bedlam. I'm gonna ... wander back down to the set and just drink a case of beer." [92] The actor Lewis Abernathy said "there were people just rolling around, completely out of it. Some of them said they were seeing streaks and psychedelics." [51] Cameron vomited before the drug took a full hold. Abernathy was shocked at the way he looked. "One eye was completely red, like the Terminator eye. A pupil, no iris, beet red. The other eye looked like he'd been sniffing glue since he was four." [51] [88] The Nova Scotia Department of Health confirmed that the soup had contained PCP on August 27, and the Halifax Regional Police Service announced a criminal investigation the next day. The investigation was closed in February 1999. [93] Though Cameron suggest it might have been a fired crew member that was behind the poisoning, the person was never caught. [91] [57] [94] 

 The filming schedule was intended to last 138 days but grew to 160 (filming officially wrapped on March 23, 1997). [8] Many cast members came down with colds, flu, or kidney infections after spending hours in cold water, including Winslet. She decided she would not work with Cameron again unless she earned "a lot of money". [94] Several others left the production, and three stuntmen broke their bones, but the Screen Actors Guild decided, following an investigation, that nothing was inherently unsafe about the set. [94] DiCaprio said there was no point when he felt he was in danger during filming. [95] Cameron believed in a passionate work ethic and never apologized for the way he ran his sets. He said:
